          "content:encoded": "<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Let's Start With What Most Articles Get Wrong</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Search \"direct listing GIFT IFSC\" today and you will find articles confidently explaining how companies can list their shares and raise foreign currency capital from global investors. Some even walk you through the fundraising process, pricing mechanics, and book building.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Almost all of them are describing something else — an IPO or a public offer on GIFT IFSC exchanges.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>A&nbsp;<strong>direct listing</strong>&nbsp;— specifically, a&nbsp;<em>listing without a public offer</em>&nbsp;under the IFSCA (Listing) Regulations, 2024 — is fundamentally different. No capital is raised. No new shares are issued. No money flows into the company. No book building. No underwriter. No subscription.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>What it does instead is simpler, and depending on your structure, far more strategic:&nbsp;<strong>existing shares are admitted for trading on an international exchange within India's regulatory perimeter.</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>That is the starting point. Everything else follows from here.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What Is GIFT IFSC — and Why Does It Matter for Listing?</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>GIFT City (Gujarat International Finance Tec-City) is India's first and only International Financial Services Centre, located in Gandhinagar, Gujarat. It is a jurisdiction within India that operates under a distinct regulatory regime — designed to replicate the environment of global financial hubs like Singapore, Dubai DIFC, and London.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>IFSCA is the unified authority for the development and regulation of financial products, financial services, and financial institutions in the IFSC. Prior to its establishment, domestic financial regulators — RBI, SEBI, PFRDA, and IRDAI — each separately regulated IFSC activities, creating overlap and inefficiency.&nbsp;<a href=\"https://www.ifsca.gov.in/\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noreferrer noopener\">International Financial Services Centres Authority</a></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Today, IFSCA is the single window. One regulator. One framework. This is not just administrative convenience — for cross-border capital market transactions, it materially reduces regulatory coordination risk.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The two recognised stock exchanges at GIFT IFSC are&nbsp;<strong>India INX</strong>&nbsp;(a wholly-owned subsidiary of BSE Ltd.) and&nbsp;<strong>NSE IFSC</strong>&nbsp;(promoted by NSE). Both operate under IFSCA's supervisory jurisdiction, trade in foreign currencies including USD, GBP, and EUR, and provide extended trading hours of 22 hours a day, making them among the longest-operating trading platforms globally.&nbsp;</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What Is a Direct Listing in GIFT IFSC?</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The concept finds its regulatory home in&nbsp;<strong>Chapter IV, Regulation 40</strong>&nbsp;of the IFSCA (Listing) Regulations, 2024 — titled&nbsp;<em>\"Listing of Specified Securities Without Public Offer.\"</em></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Under Regulation 40, companies can list their specified securities directly on IFSC exchanges without making a public offer. Eligible companies — Indian or foreign — can have their shares admitted for trading on India INX or NSE IFSC without undertaking the traditional IPO process.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The operative word is&nbsp;<em>without</em>. Without a public offer. Without new share issuance. Without capital raising.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The purpose is purely to achieve a&nbsp;<strong>listing</strong>&nbsp;— to make existing shares tradeable on an internationally recognised exchange, accessible to global investors, with price discovery happening in foreign currency, inside India's legal perimeter.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Think of it as what NYSE or Nasdaq call a direct floor listing — companies like Spotify and Coinbase used this route in the US. The GIFT IFSC architecture has created its equivalent, suited to Indian and cross-border company structures.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:gallery {\"linkTo\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-gallery has-nested-images columns-default is-cropped\"><!-- wp:image {\"id\":32016,\"sizeSlug\":\"large\",\"linkDestination\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image size-large\"><img src=\"https://csatwork.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/direct-listing-gift-ifsc-liquidity-price-discovery-quote-1024x576.png\" alt=\"Expert insight on direct listing in GIFT IFSC focusing on liquidity and price discovery rather than fundraising\" class=\"wp-image-32016\"/><figcaption class=\"wp-element-caption\">Direct listing at GIFT IFSC is about liquidity and price discovery—not raising capital</figcaption></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image --></figure>\n<!-- /wp:gallery -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The Important Caveat Every Promoter Must Know in 2026</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Here is where most advisors — and most articles — stop being accurate.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Regulation 40 exists in the statute. The operational framework under it has not yet been notified by IFSCA.</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The regulation creates the legal permission. But IFSCA is yet to issue the circular or framework specifying the detailed conditions, eligibility norms, procedural requirements, documentation standards, and exchange-level mechanics specifically for a listing without public offer under Regulation 40.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>That framework is expected in&nbsp;<strong>June 2026</strong>.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Until then, companies cannot simply walk into India INX or NSE IFSC and pursue a Regulation 40 listing. The plumbing — the operational infrastructure behind the regulation — is still being put in place.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is not a minor footnote. In our experience advising on cross-border structuring at GIFT IFSC, this is the single most common misconception we encounter — promoters who believe the route is already fully open because the regulation exists. The permission exists. The process does not yet.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:gallery {\"linkTo\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-gallery has-nested-images columns-default is-cropped\"><!-- wp:image {\"id\":32015,\"sizeSlug\":\"large\",\"linkDestination\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image size-large\"><img src=\"https://csatwork.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/regulation-40-gift-ifsc-framework-not-live-quote-1024x576.png\" alt=\"Regulation 40 GIFT IFSC insight explaining the gap between legal permission and operational framework\" class=\"wp-image-32015\"/><figcaption class=\"wp-element-caption\">Regulation 40 exists—but the operational framework is still awaited</figcaption></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image --></figure>\n<!-- /wp:gallery -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Why Is IFSCA Doing This? The Policy Rationale</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Understanding the intent behind Regulation 40 helps you understand whether this route makes sense for your company.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>IFSCA constituted a Standing Committee on Primary Markets (SCOP), chaired by Shri T.V. Mohandas Pai, in February 2024 to advise on policy and regulatory matters for the development of a vibrant and robust primary market in GIFT IFSC. The Committee recommended that IFSCA's regulatory framework should be aligned with international financial centres such as Singapore, Hong Kong, USA, and the UK.&nbsp;</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The direct listing route — listing without a public offer — sits squarely within that alignment agenda. In mature international markets, companies achieve exchange listing without necessarily raising capital from the public at the time of listing. This gives flexibility to promoters, PE-backed companies, and family businesses who want the benefits of a listed entity — transparency, global investor access, price benchmarking — without the obligations and dilution of a public offering.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Listing without public offer is permitted for startups and SMEs under the IFSCA framework — signalling that the route is intended to be accessible, not just for large conglomerates, but for growth-stage companies with existing institutional shareholders seeking global visibility.&nbsp;<a href=\"https://ifsca.gov.in/Document/Legal/IFSCA_Listing_Brochure.pdf\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noreferrer noopener\">International Financial Services Centres Authority</a></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What the Framework Will Cover — Based on Regulation 40's Architecture</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>While the detailed operational circular is pending, we can map what the framework is expected to address, based on what Regulation 40 itself provides and what comparable mechanisms in other IFSC-type jurisdictions require.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Eligibility.</strong>&nbsp;The framework will specify which entities can pursue a listing without public offer. For IPOs under the same regulations, an issuer must have operating revenue of at least USD 20 million in the last financial year, a pre-tax profit of at least USD 1 million, or a post-issue market capitalisation of at least USD 25 million. The Regulation 40 framework may carry similar or lighter thresholds, given that no public capital raising is involved.&nbsp;</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Minimum Public Shareholding.</strong>&nbsp;A key amendment to the IFSCA Listing Regulations reduced the minimum public shareholding requirement for companies listing in IFSCs from 25% to 10%. This is significantly more lenient than domestic listing requirements and is important for promoter-heavy cap tables typical of Indian family businesses and PE-backed companies.&nbsp;</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Accounting Standards.</strong>&nbsp;Companies reporting under IFRS, Ind AS, or US GAAP will all be accommodated. This matters particularly for foreign-incorporated issuers or Indian companies that have already adopted IFRS for international reporting.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Disclosure Obligations.</strong>&nbsp;Post-listing, listed entities will be subject to continuous disclosure requirements under Chapter XII of the Listing Regulations. Notably, the disclosure framework requires half-yearly financial statements rather than quarterly — a meaningful compliance reduction compared to domestic listed entities.&nbsp;</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>FDI Treatment.</strong>&nbsp;This is a layer that catches companies off-guard. All investments in shares listed at GIFT IFSC exchanges are treated as foreign direct investment under FEMA. Companies must stay within FDI sectoral caps and avoid sectors where FDI is prohibited. If your company operates in a sector with a 49% or 74% FDI cap, your post-listing shareholding structure needs to be carefully modelled before you proceed.&nbsp;&nbsp;</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What a Direct Listing at GIFT IFSC Is — and Is Not</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>A common mistake we see promoters make is conflating the different listing routes available at GIFT IFSC. Let us be precise.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>It is not a fundraise.</strong>&nbsp;Zero capital enters the company through the listing itself. If you want to raise capital, that would require a separate IPO or preferential issue process — a distinct track entirely.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>It is not an IPO.</strong>&nbsp;There is no offer document, no subscription process, no allotment, no book building, no anchor investors, no minimum subscription requirements.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>It is not a secondary listing.</strong>&nbsp;A secondary listing at GIFT IFSC is for companies already listed on a recognised foreign exchange who want an additional listing at GIFT. Regulation 40 is for primary listing of shares that are not yet publicly traded.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>It is not an overseas listing.</strong>&nbsp;GIFT IFSC sits within India's territorial and regulatory perimeter. FEMA, Companies Act, and IFSCA rules all apply. This is not the same as listing on NYSE or LSE.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>It is not yet operationally live.</strong>&nbsp;Regulation 40 exists. The framework circular is expected in June 2026. The window opens when that circular lands.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Who Should Be Watching This Space?</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>If you fall into any of the following categories, the Regulation 40 framework deserves serious attention as it approaches operationalisation:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>PE and VC-backed companies</strong>&nbsp;with multiple institutional shareholders who want a path to liquidity without a domestic IPO. A listing without public offer creates a tradeable market for existing shares — existing investors can transact, price discovery happens, and the company gets global visibility without dilution.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Promoter-led Indian companies</strong>&nbsp;with international business ambitions. A GIFT IFSC listing creates a foreign currency-denominated market cap, which is useful in cross-border M&amp;A, partnership discussions, and employee incentive structures.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Foreign companies</strong>&nbsp;seeking a regulated India-linked listing to access domestic and NRI investor pools without the full burden of a SEBI-regulated domestic listing.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Family businesses</strong>&nbsp;transitioning toward institutional governance. The lighter compliance burden at GIFT IFSC — half-yearly reporting, 10% minimum public shareholding — makes it a manageable first step toward a listed structure.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The Tax Architecture: Why GIFT IFSC Is Structurally Advantaged</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The listing benefit at GIFT IFSC is amplified by its tax architecture. Entities operating in GIFT IFSC enjoy 100% income tax exemption for 20 consecutive years out of 25 years, exemption from GST and Customs on services rendered to service providers in GIFT IFSC/SEZ units, and no Securities Transaction Tax (STT), Commodity Transaction Tax (CTT), or stamp duty on trades.&nbsp;</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For global investors, the absence of STT, CTT, and stamp duty meaningfully reduces the cost of acquiring and trading shares — a structural advantage that domestic exchange-listed shares cannot offer. This is a real pull factor for foreign institutional investors, sovereign wealth funds, and global family offices that are routinely sensitive to transaction cost structures.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What Happens After Listing? The Ongoing Obligations</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Once a company is listed under Regulation 40, it steps into the continuous listing obligations framework under Chapter XII of the IFSCA (Listing) Regulations, 2024. These include:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Financial Reporting.</strong>&nbsp;Half-yearly financial statements under IFRS, Ind AS, or US GAAP, disclosed within 45 days of the end of the half-year, following board approval. This timeline was specified under the amended regulation 96(2) introduced in October 2025.&nbsp;</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Material Event Disclosures.</strong>&nbsp;Any price-sensitive information — changes in control, significant transactions, litigation, regulatory actions — must be disclosed promptly to the exchange.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Governance Standards.</strong>&nbsp;The IFSCA framework replaces the Indian concept of \"promoter\" with \"controlling shareholder\" for foreign companies — aligning with how governance accountability is understood in global markets.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Corporate Actions.</strong>&nbsp;Any subsequent capital actions — rights issues, preferential allotments, QIPs — will require separate compliance under the respective chapters of the Listing Regulations. IFSCA issued a circular on April 22, 2026 prescribing the detailed framework for preferential issues and qualified institutions placements under the Listing Regulations — a sign that the post-listing capital market infrastructure is actively being built out.&nbsp;&nbsp;</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The June 2026 Framework: What to Do Right Now</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>If you are a promoter, CFO, or legal counsel evaluating this route, the period between now and June 2026 is not idle time. It is preparation time.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The questions to resolve before the framework lands are:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Structuring questions.</strong>&nbsp;Is your company a public company or does it need to be converted? If it is a private company, conversion is a prerequisite under Indian law before any listing — domestic or international.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Cap table analysis.</strong>&nbsp;What is your current FDI exposure? Who are your existing shareholders, and what is their residency status? How does the 10% minimum public shareholding requirement interact with your current shareholding?</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Financial reporting readiness.</strong>&nbsp;Are your financials currently prepared under Ind AS or IFRS? If you are on Indian GAAP, a transition may be required. The quality and audit standard of your financials will matter.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Sector compliance.</strong>&nbsp;Does your company operate in an FDI-restricted sector? If so, what is the sectoral cap, and does your anticipated post-listing shareholding structure comply?</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Depository arrangements.</strong>&nbsp;Shares listed at GIFT IFSC trade in dematerialised form through India International Depository IFSC Limited (IIDI). Your company will need to engage with depository infrastructure ahead of time.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>None of these are complex in isolation. But together they take time, and starting six months before the framework notification lands puts you in a position to move quickly when it does.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:image {\"id\":32014,\"sizeSlug\":\"large\",\"linkDestination\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image size-large\"><img src=\"https://csatwork.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/gift-ifsc-direct-listing-preparation-2026-framework-quote-1024x576.png\" alt=\"Preparation strategy for GIFT IFSC direct listing including structure cap table FDI and financial readiness\" class=\"wp-image-32014\"/><figcaption class=\"wp-element-caption\">Early preparation defines success in GIFT IFSC direct listing</figcaption></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>A Note on the Broader GIFT IFSC Listing Landscape</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The Regulation 40 direct listing sits alongside several other capital market routes at GIFT IFSC that are already operational and worth understanding in context.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>IPO on GIFT IFSC exchanges</strong>&nbsp;— open to unlisted Indian public companies and foreign companies, this involves a public offer, capital raising, and the full IPO process. Operationally live.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Secondary listing</strong>&nbsp;— for companies listed on recognised foreign exchanges who want an additional GIFT IFSC listing. Operationally live.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>SPAC listings</strong>&nbsp;— Special Purpose Acquisition Company frameworks are available for SPAC structures raising at least USD 50 million. Operationally live.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Debt listing</strong>&nbsp;— Indian and foreign companies can list debt securities, commercial paper, and certificates of deposit. From April 2025, issuers are required to obtain a credit rating from at least one CRA registered with IFSCA. Operationally live.&nbsp;<a href=\"https://www.ifsca.gov.in/Document/Legal/press-release_listing-regulations30082024050144.pdf\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noreferrer noopener\">International Financial Services Centres Authority</a></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The Regulation 40 listing without public offer is the missing piece — the route that gives companies equity market presence at GIFT IFSC without a capital raise. Once the June 2026 framework lands, it completes the suite.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Conclusion: The Permission Exists. The Process Is Coming.</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Direct listing at GIFT IFSC — listing without a public offer under Regulation 40 — is a genuinely useful structural tool. It creates international exchange presence, foreign currency price discovery, and a tradeable market for existing shares, all without the company raising a single dollar of new capital.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The regulatory intent is clear. The legal foundation is in place. IFSCA's track record of moving quickly on implementation — the Listing Regulations were notified in August 2024, amended in October 2025, and the preferential issue framework landed in April 2026 — gives reasonable confidence in the June 2026 timeline.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>But the framework is not yet here. Any advisor telling you the route is fully operational today is either confused or conflating it with the IPO route. The distinction matters — and in this space, acting on incorrect information can create real structural and compliance problems downstream.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The right move right now is to understand the architecture, stress-test your eligibility, and have the structural readiness work done — so that when IFSCA releases the framework, you are not starting from zero.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>If you are evaluating a direct listing in GIFT IFSC, working through Regulation 40 readiness, or structuring your company ahead of the June 2026 framework notification, feel free to reach out. We advise promoters, PE funds, and CFOs at every stage of the GIFT IFSC listing journey — from initial eligibility assessment through to exchange admission.</em></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>FAQs: Direct Listing in GIFT IFSC (Regulation 40)</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>1. What is a direct listing in GIFT IFSC?</strong><br>A direct listing under Regulation 40 allows companies to list existing shares on IFSC exchanges without issuing new shares or raising capital. It is purely a listing mechanism for liquidity and price discovery in foreign currency, not a fundraising exercise.&nbsp;</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>2. Is the direct listing route currently operational in India?</strong><br>No. While Regulation 40 legally permits listing without a public offer, the detailed operational framework is expected around June 2026. Until then, companies cannot execute a direct listing on IFSC exchanges.&nbsp;</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>3. How is a direct listing different from an IPO in GIFT IFSC?</strong><br>An IPO involves issuing new shares, raising capital, book building, and investor subscription. A direct listing has none of these—no capital raise, no dilution, and no underwriting. It simply enables trading of existing shares.&nbsp;</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>4. Who should consider a direct listing at GIFT IFSC?</strong><br>PE/VC-backed companies seeking liquidity, promoter-led businesses aiming for global visibility, and foreign companies wanting India-linked listing exposure—all without immediate capital raising—should evaluate this route.&nbsp;</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>5. What are the key compliance considerations before listing?</strong><br>Companies must evaluate FDI limits, ensure appropriate corporate structure (public company), align financial reporting (Ind AS/IFRS/US GAAP), and prepare for minimum public shareholding and disclosure requirements post-listing.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>6. What are the key advantages of listing at GIFT IFSC?</strong><br>Benefits include foreign currency trading, lower transaction costs (no STT/stamp duty), lighter compliance (half-yearly reporting), and access to global investors within India’s regulatory framework.&nbsp;</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">About the Author</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Prashant Kumar</strong>&nbsp;is a Company Secretary, Published Author, and a seasoned professional in corporate and financial services regulation.           "title": "Direct Listing vs IPO in GIFT IFSC: What Indian Companies Actually Need to Know in 2026",
          "link": "https://csatwork.in/direct-listing-vs-ipo-gift-ifsc/",
          "pubDate": "Thu, 30 Apr 2026 17:38:43 +0000",
          "dc:creator": "prashantmishra1986",

          "description": null,
          "content:encoded": "<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\"><strong>By CS Prashant Kumar | Company Secretary &amp; Compliance Officer, Global Horizons Capital Advisors (IFSC) Private Ltd </strong></h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The question used to be simple: do you want to go public or not?</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Not anymore. In 2026, Indian companies evaluating capital markets access must answer a more nuanced question —&nbsp;<em>which market, which mechanism, and for what objective?</em></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>India's Direct Listing Scheme — backed by amended FEMA (NDI) Rules, the Companies Act, and IFSCA's Listing Regulations, 2024 — has established the enabling architecture for a structurally different path to public markets. But architecture is not the same as an open door. The IFSCA's specific framework for direct listings under Regulation 40 is yet to be formally notified, and is expected sometime between June and July 2026. Getting the current state of play wrong — in either direction — is an expensive advisory error.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This article draws a clear line between the two routes, grounded in what the law actually says today and what is still pending — not what industry commentators are presenting as already operational.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What Exactly Is the Difference Between a Direct Listing and an IPO?</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The one-line answer:</strong>&nbsp;An IPO issues new shares and raises fresh capital. A direct listing gives existing shares a public market — without issuing anything new.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>But the implications of that single structural difference cascade across dilution, pricing, cost, FEMA treatment, investor access, and strategic positioning. Understanding those downstream effects is where the real advisory value lies.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:gallery {\"linkTo\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-gallery has-nested-images columns-default is-cropped\"><!-- wp:image {\"id\":32029,\"sizeSlug\":\"large\",\"linkDestination\":\"none\",\"className\":\"is-style-default\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image size-large is-style-default\"><img src=\"https://csatwork.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/direct-listing-vs-ipo-quote-1-1024x576.png\" alt=\"Expert insight on difference between IPO and direct listing India\" class=\"wp-image-32029\"/><figcaption class=\"wp-element-caption\"><strong>Understanding the fundamental difference between capital raising and liquidity creation.</strong></figcaption></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image --></figure>\n<!-- /wp:gallery -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The Regulatory Architecture You Need to Know</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Before comparing routes, the regulatory stack matters.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The enabling layer — what exists today:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The Ministry of Finance amended the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 in January 2024, notifying the Direct Listing Scheme and permitting eligible Indian public companies to list on international exchanges in GIFT IFSC. Simultaneously, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs issued the Companies (Listing of Equity Shares in Permissible Jurisdictions) Rules, 2024. These two instruments create the FEMA and Companies Act gateway.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>IFSCA's Listing Regulations, 2024 — further amended as of October 14, 2025 — include Regulation 40, which provides the statutory hook for direct listing on IFSC exchanges without a public offer.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What is still missing — the critical gap as of April 2026:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Regulation 40 exists on paper. But IFSCA's detailed operational framework for direct listings — the circular/notification that will specify eligibility criteria, documentation requirements, process timelines, pricing mechanics, and disclosure standards specific to this route — has not yet been notified. It is expected in June–July 2026.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This distinction matters enormously. The enabling statutes and the exchange-level regulations are in place. The operational rulebook that actually allows a company to execute a direct listing is pending. Any advisor or article telling you the direct listing route is currently \"live and available\" is conflating the legislative framework with an executable process.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Currently approved exchanges:</strong>&nbsp;India International Exchange (India INX, a BSE subsidiary) and NSE International Exchange (NSE IFSC). Both operate under IFSCA's unified regulatory authority. Once the IFSCA framework is notified, these exchanges will be the operational venues.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Separate gap for listed companies:</strong>&nbsp;For companies already listed on BSE or NSE who want to cross-list on IFSC exchanges, SEBI's operational guidelines also remain pending. NSE IX's MD &amp; CEO flagged this publicly at the Global Securities Markets Conclave in February 2026. This is a second, parallel regulatory gap — distinct from the IFSCA framework pending for unlisted companies.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>IPO in India: What You're Actually Signing Up For</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>A domestic IPO under SEBI's ICDR framework is a capital-raising exercise with market entry as its byproduct. The company issues fresh equity, which flows into the business as primary capital. Dilution is structural and non-negotiable.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>An IPO in GIFT IFSC follows the IFSCA (Listing) Regulations, 2024, and allows issue of equity shares in foreign currency (USD, GBP, EUR) to non-resident investors. Both fixed price and book-building mechanisms are available. The issuer must comply with the Direct Listing Scheme's pricing rules — for unlisted companies, the issue price cannot be less than fair market value as determined under NDI Rules.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What makes an IFSC IPO different from a domestic one?</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Shares are denominated and traded in foreign currency</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Investors are primarily non-residents, as IFSC-listed securities are currently accessible only to overseas investors. Resident Indians are not permitted to invest at this stage—even under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) in the case of Indian companies—although a pilot framework for limited resident participation is expected by mid-2026.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>No Securities Transaction Tax (STT), Commodities Transaction Tax (CTT), or stamp duty for investors</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Financial reporting under Ind AS (or IFRS, depending on the issuer's accounting framework)</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Oversight by IFSCA — not SEBI — for IFSC-specific compliance</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Direct Listing in GIFT IFSC: The Structure and Where It Stands</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Regulation 40 of the IFSCA Listing Regulations, 2024 provides the statutory basis for an eligible company to list shares directly on an IFSC exchange without making a public offer. The concept: no fresh issuance, no book-building for new capital, existing shares admitted to trading.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The enabling statutes — NDI Rules, Companies Act rules — are in place. What is awaited is IFSCA's operational notification (expected June–July 2026) that will specify how a company actually executes this route: documentation, disclosure standards, process timelines, pricing mechanics, and eligibility criteria specific to direct listings.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What the framework is designed to enable (once notified):</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Offer for Sale (OFS) by existing shareholders is anticipated to be permitted. This would allow promoters, PE funds, or early investors to achieve liquidity without the company itself raising capital — separating \"going public\" from \"raising capital\" in a way domestic markets do not permit.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>FEMA treatment:</strong>&nbsp;Investments under the Direct Listing Scheme are treated as Foreign Direct Investment — not FPI. FDI sectoral caps, prohibited activity restrictions, and land-border country approvals (prior government approval required for entities from countries sharing a land border with India) all apply.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Price discipline for listed companies (when SEBI guidelines arrive):</strong>&nbsp;For a listed Indian company, the price offered on IFSC exchanges cannot be less than the price offered to domestic investors — a safeguard against valuation arbitrage at the expense of retail shareholders.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The framework is coherent and well-designed. The wait is for the final IFSCA notification to convert the architecture into an executable process.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Five Dimensions Where the Routes Diverge Materially</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>1. Capital vs. Liquidity</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is the foundational distinction and should drive the decision before anything else.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>An IPO is chosen when the company needs capital — to fund capex, retire debt, finance acquisitions, or support a growth plan that requires external funding. The entire process — merchant banker engagement, DRHP, book-building, roadshows — is structured around demonstrating value to justify the capital raise.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>A direct listing is chosen when the company is already capitalised, and the objective is to create a public market for existing shares. The company gets a valuation benchmark, existing shareholders get liquidity, and the company gains global visibility — without bringing any fresh money in or accepting the dilution that comes with it.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Test question for business leaders:</strong>&nbsp;<em>Does the company need this capital to execute its next phase, or does it need a market to reflect the value already created?</em>&nbsp;The answer to that question should determine the route.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>2. Dilution and Ownership Dynamics</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>An IPO dilutes. Fresh shares are issued to public investors, reducing the proportionate ownership of promoters and existing shareholders. For growth-stage companies that need capital, this is acceptable — it is the price of funding. For founder-led businesses, family-controlled enterprises, or companies with complex cap tables from multiple private funding rounds, even modest dilution can shift board dynamics and future M&amp;A optionality.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>A direct listing avoids dilution entirely at the company level. If existing shareholders choose to sell via OFS, the dilution is at the shareholder level — the company's issued and paid-up share capital does not change. Promoters who do not sell retain their exact pre-listing ownership percentage.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The underappreciated implication:</strong>&nbsp;In a direct listing, there is no anchor investor mechanism, no stabilisation agent, and no underwriter absorbing unsold inventory. The market determines price from day one. This is efficiency in theory; volatility risk in practice.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>3. Pricing: Structured Discovery vs. Open Market</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>In a traditional Indian IPO — or an IFSC IPO — price is established through a structured book-building exercise where institutional investors bid within a price band, anchoring the issue. This provides predictability, reduces opening-day volatility, and often gives companies a floor they can point to in communications with stakeholders.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>In a direct listing, no price band exists. The opening price emerges from real-time supply and demand. India INX's 22-hour trading window (4 AM to 2 AM IST) and sub-4 microsecond latency infrastructure mean pricing can move fast in either direction before a company has had time to respond.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Who benefits from open market pricing:</strong>&nbsp;Companies with strong international brand recognition, existing institutional relationships with global investors, or those where the private market had already established robust valuation benchmarks (e.g., unicorns with well-documented funding rounds). For everyone else, the absence of a structured pricing mechanism is a risk, not a feature.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>4. Cost Structure</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The Ministry of Finance has estimated that listing costs in GIFT City via direct listing run 40–50% lower than equivalent ADR/GDR structures. The removal of underwriting fees, reduced intermediary costs, and the leaner disclosure timeline relative to domestic SEBI ICDR compliance drive this differential.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>However, \"cheaper\" does not mean \"simple.\" Direct listings still require:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>IFSCA-compliant disclosure documentation</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Ind AS financial statements (three years audited)</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Continuous listing compliance under Chapter XII of the IFSCA Listing Regulations, 2024</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>FEMA compliance, FDI reporting, and NDI Rules adherence</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Legal opinions on sectoral cap compliance and prohibited activities</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The cost advantage is real. But companies that enter a direct listing without proper advisory support underestimate what \"simpler process\" actually demands in execution.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>5. Investor Base and Global Positioning</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is where GIFT IFSC's structural advantage over domestic IPOs is clearest. An Indian IPO — even with QIB participation — is overwhelmingly a domestic capital event. FPI participation exists, but foreign investors are engaging with a domestic instrument, not an internationally-denominated one.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>GIFT IFSC listings are designed for non-resident investors — sovereign wealth funds, global institutional investors, family offices across the Middle East, Southeast Asia, and Europe. India INX and NSE IFSC exchanges already attract participation from investors across 75+ countries. Securities are denominated in USD, GBP, or EUR. Settlement interfaces with global custodian networks. The investor profile is categorically different.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For Indian companies with global revenue exposure, international operations, or cross-border M&amp;A ambitions, this alignment between capital market presence and business footprint is strategically significant — and not achievable through a domestic NSE/BSE listing alone.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The Tax Architecture for IFSC Listings: What Non-Resident Investors Actually Care About</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The GIFT IFSC tax regime is one of its most powerful selling points for global investor attraction. Non-resident investors transacting on IFSC exchanges benefit from:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>No capital gains tax</strong> on transfer of securities (bonds, derivatives, specified securities) on recognised IFSC stock exchanges, where consideration is in foreign currency</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>No STT, CTT, or stamp duty</strong> on IFSC exchange transactions</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>No withholding tax</strong> requirements on specified payments to IFSC units during the tax holiday period (under Section 147 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, formerly Section 80LA)</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>MAT at 9%</strong> of book profits (versus standard rates) for IFSC units — or lower corporate tax of 17.16%/25.17% with no MAT applicability</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For institutional investors comparing GIFT IFSC against Singapore's SGX or London's LSE, this zero-tax environment on capital gains and transaction taxes is a direct competitive differentiator.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The Two Regulatory Gaps: What the Market Is Not Saying Clearly</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>There are two distinct pending pieces, and conflating them creates confusion in advisory conversations.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Gap 1 — IFSCA's Direct Listing Framework (Expected June–July 2026)</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Regulation 40 of IFSCA's Listing Regulations, 2024 creates the statutory hook. But IFSCA's detailed operational circular — which will specify eligibility, documentation, pricing mechanics, disclosure standards, and process timelines for a direct listing — has not yet been notified as of April 2026. It is expected in June–July 2026.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Until that notification, no Indian company — listed or unlisted — can actually execute a direct listing on GIFT IFSC exchanges. The enabling law exists. The operational rulebook does not yet.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Gap 2 — SEBI's Guidelines for Listed Indian Companies</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Even after IFSCA notifies its framework (covering unlisted public companies primarily), a separate SEBI circular is required before companies already listed on domestic exchanges (BSE/NSE) can cross-list on IFSC exchanges.&nbsp;</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>NSE IX's MD &amp; CEO publicly called this out at the Global Securities Markets Conclave in February 2026. The IFSCA working group has already outlined the structure for this — Class A shares on domestic exchanges, Class B shares on IFSC, fungibility mechanisms — but SEBI has not converted it into formal operating guidelines.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What this means in practice:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:table -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-table\"><table class=\"has-fixed-layout\"><tbody><tr><td><strong>Company type</strong></td><td><strong>Current status</strong></td></tr><tr><td>Unlisted public Indian company</td><td>Awaiting IFSCA operational notification (June–July 2026)</td></tr><tr><td>Listed Indian company (BSE/NSE)</td><td>Awaiting both IFSCA framework + SEBI guidelines</td></tr><tr><td>Foreign company</td><td>Separate framework; cross-border dual listing provisions exist</td></tr></tbody></table></figure>\n<!-- /wp:table -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Advisors who present direct listing in GIFT IFSC as currently executable are ahead of the regulatory reality. The correct framing is: the architecture is ready, the opportunity is real, and the operational window is opening — likely in the second half of 2026.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:gallery {\"linkTo\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-gallery has-nested-images columns-default is-cropped\"><!-- wp:image {\"id\":32030,\"sizeSlug\":\"large\",\"linkDestination\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image size-large\"><img src=\"https://csatwork.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/gift-ifsc-direct-listing-framework-quote-1-1024x576.png\" alt=\"\" class=\"wp-image-32030\"/><figcaption class=\"wp-element-caption\"><strong>Why understanding the regulatory gap is critical before planning a listing.</strong></figcaption></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image --></figure>\n<!-- /wp:gallery -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>IPO vs. Direct Listing in GIFT IFSC: The Decision Matrix</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:table -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-table\"><table class=\"has-fixed-layout\"><tbody><tr><td><strong>Parameter</strong></td><td><strong>Domestic IPO</strong></td><td><strong>IFSC IPO</strong></td><td><strong>GIFT IFSC Direct Listing</strong></td></tr><tr><td><strong>Capital raised</strong></td><td>Yes (primary)</td><td>Yes (primary, in FX)</td><td>Only via OFS (secondary)</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Dilution</strong></td><td>Yes</td><td>Yes</td><td>No (unless OFS by shareholders)</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Eligible companies</strong></td><td>Listed/unlisted</td><td>Unlisted public cos</td><td>Unlisted public cos (framework pending)</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Operational status</strong></td><td>Live</td><td>Live</td><td>IFSCA notification expected Jun–Jul 2026</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Investors</strong></td><td>Domestic + FPIs</td><td>Non-residents (FDI)</td><td>Non-residents (FDI)</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Pricing mechanism</strong></td><td>Book-building</td><td>Book-building / Fixed</td><td>Open market</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Currency</strong></td><td>INR</td><td>USD/GBP/EUR</td><td>USD/GBP/EUR</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Regulator</strong></td><td>SEBI (ICDR)</td><td>IFSCA + NDI Rules</td><td>IFSCA + NDI Rules</td></tr><tr><td><strong>STT/CTT</strong></td><td>Applicable</td><td>Not applicable</td><td>Not applicable</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Cost vs ADR/GDR</strong></td><td>N/A</td><td>40–50% lower</td><td>40–50% lower (projected)</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Resident investor access</strong></td><td>Yes</td><td>Not yet</td><td>Not yet</td></tr></tbody></table></figure>\n<!-- /wp:table -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Who Should Consider Which Route</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Choose a domestic IPO if:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The company needs INR capital for domestic operations</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The core investor base and brand recognition is Indian</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Regulatory familiarity and process certainty are priorities</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The company is in a sector with FDI restrictions that would constrain IFSC eligibility</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Choose an IFSC IPO if:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The company wants to raise foreign currency capital</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The business has international operations or revenue</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The company wants to bypass the ADR/GDR route without offshore incorporation</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Valuation benchmarking against global peers is a strategic objective</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Choose a GIFT IFSC Direct Listing if (from H2 2026 onwards, once IFSCA notifies the framework):</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The company does not need primary capital</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Existing shareholders — PE investors, promoters — need a liquidity event</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The company wants a global public market presence without dilution</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The company has strong institutional investor relationships internationally and can support open-market price discovery</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The company is an unlisted public entity not restricted by FDI sectoral caps</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The Bigger Picture: Why GIFT IFSC Is a Structural Shift, Not a Trend</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>India's approach to GIFT IFSC is deliberate: the stated objective is to \"onshore the offshore\" — to bring back India-related financial transactions that have historically routed through Singapore, Mauritius, London, or Cayman. The direct listing framework is one part of that larger architecture.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>IFSCA's vision documents project over USD 1 trillion in listed securities turnover by FY2030. Indian companies have already done secondary bond listings worth over USD 52 billion on IFSC exchanges. The equity listing ecosystem — for both unlisted and, eventually, listed companies — is the next frontier, and the regulatory scaffolding is largely in place.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>What is imminent is the operational notification. When IFSCA notifies the direct listing framework in the coming months, and when SEBI follows with listed-company guidelines, GIFT IFSC's relevance to the broader CFO and promoter community will shift from theoretical to immediately actionable. Companies that understand the architecture now will not be learning the framework under time pressure when the window opens.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:gallery {\"linkTo\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-gallery has-nested-images columns-default is-cropped\"><!-- wp:image {\"id\":32031,\"sizeSlug\":\"large\",\"linkDestination\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image size-large\"><img src=\"https://csatwork.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/capital-markets-strategy-quote-1024x576.png\" alt=\"\" class=\"wp-image-32031\"/><figcaption class=\"wp-element-caption\"><strong>Why GIFT IFSC represents a long-term structural shift in global capital access for Indian companies — not just a new listing option.</strong></figcaption></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image --></figure>\n<!-- /wp:gallery -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Conclusion</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Direct listing and IPO are not interchangeable. They are not even competing options in most situations — they serve different objectives, different company profiles, and different stages of capital market evolution.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For Indian companies in 2026, the decision framework starts with:&nbsp;<em>What do you need from markets — capital, liquidity, or global positioning?</em>&nbsp;Answer that first. Then map the regulatory route.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The GIFT IFSC direct listing framework is real, well-designed, and imminent — but not yet operationally open. The IFSCA notification expected in June–July 2026 will be the moment the conversation shifts from planning to execution. The right time to understand the structure is before that window opens, not after.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The structure follows strategy. The question is whether your advisory team is close enough to the regulatory calendar to position you correctly — not just conceptually, but at the right moment.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Frequently Asked Questions</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Can an unlisted Indian company list directly on GIFT IFSC right now?</strong>&nbsp;Not yet — and this is the most important clarification to get right. While the enabling framework exists (amended NDI Rules, Companies Act rules, and Regulation 40 of IFSCA Listing Regulations, 2024), IFSCA's specific operational notification for direct listings has not been issued as of April 2026. It is expected in June–July 2026. Until that notification, there is no executable process in place.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Can a company already listed on BSE or NSE use the direct listing route in GIFT IFSC?</strong>&nbsp;No — on two counts. First, the IFSCA direct listing operational framework is pending notification. Second, even after that notification (which will primarily address unlisted companies), listed Indian companies require a separate SEBI circular before they can cross-list on IFSC exchanges. That SEBI circular is also pending, with no confirmed timeline as of April 2026.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Is investment in GIFT IFSC direct listings treated as FDI or FPI?</strong>&nbsp;It is treated as Foreign Direct Investment under NDI Rules. FDI sectoral caps, prohibited activity restrictions, and land-border country approvals all apply.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Are there tax benefits for investors in GIFT IFSC listed securities?</strong>&nbsp;Yes. Non-resident investors transacting on IFSC exchanges benefit from zero capital gains tax, no STT, no CTT, and no stamp duty on qualifying transactions — subject to consideration being received in foreign currency.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Can Indian residents invest in shares listed on GIFT IFSC exchanges?</strong>&nbsp;Currently, resident Indians cannot directly invest in IFSC-listed equity securities. A pilot for resident participation is underway, with full rollout anticipated by mid-2026 subject to FEMA and regulatory framework finalisation.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Does a direct listing eliminate disclosure and governance obligations?</strong>&nbsp;No. Continuous disclosure, governance standards, and reporting obligations under Chapter XII of the IFSCA Listing Regulations, 2024 apply in full. Regulatory simplicity refers to process, not to accountability standards.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>About the Author</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Prashant Kumar is a Company Secretary, Published Author, and a seasoned professional in corporate and financial services regulation. He currently serves as Company Secretary &amp; Compliance Officer at Global Horizons Capital Advisors (IFSC) Private Limited, an IFSCA-licensed Investment Banker based in GIFT City, with direct, on-ground exposure to capital market transactions within the IFSC ecosystem.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>He brings hands-on experience in IPOs, direct listings, and exchange listings, along with deep expertise in GIFT IFSC structuring, fund setup (FME &amp; AIF), corporate governance, and regulatory compliance. He regularly advises fund managers, startups, and institutions on building globally aligned, execution-ready structures.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For professional discussions on GIFT IFSC, IPOs, listings, fund structuring, and regulatory strategy, he can be reached at +91 9821008011 or&nbsp;prashant.kumar@global-horizons.in.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->",
