          "title": "India's Direct Listing Framework Is Architecturally Sound and Operationally Incomplete — And That Gap Is Where Every Advisory Error Is Being Made",
          "link": "https://csatwork.in/gift-ifsc-direct-listing-framework-analysis/",
          "pubDate": "Thu, 30 Apr 2026 17:59:12 +0000",
          "dc:creator": "prashantmishra1986",
          "guid": {
            "#text": "https://csatwork.in/?p=32034",
            "@attributes": {
              "isPermaLink": "false"
            }
          },
          "description": null,
          "content:encoded": "<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\"><strong>By CS Prashant Kumar | Company Secretary &amp; Compliance Officer, Global Horizons Capital Advisors (IFSC) Private Limited</strong></h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>There is a particular kind of regulatory optimism that grips the Indian capital markets ecosystem whenever a new framework is announced. The press release goes out. The industry conferences put it on the agenda. Advisors begin positioning it to clients. Articles appear explaining \"how to use\" the new route. And somewhere in that enthusiasm, a critical question gets quietly set aside:&nbsp;<em>is the framework actually executable yet?</em></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>India's direct listing framework at GIFT IFSC is currently living inside that gap.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The enabling architecture — the January 2024 amendment to FEMA's Non-Debt Instruments Rules, the MCA's Companies (Listing of Equity Shares in Permissible Jurisdictions) Rules, 2024, and Regulation 40 of IFSCA's Listing Regulations, 2024 — is real, well-designed, and genuinely significant. But IFSCA's operational notification that will convert this architecture into an executable process has not been issued as of April 2026. It is expected in June–July 2026.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>That two-year gap between statutory enablement and operational readiness is not an administrative delay. It reflects the genuine complexity of what this framework is attempting — and understanding that complexity is the difference between advising clients correctly and advising them confidently but wrong.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This piece makes five arguments about the GIFT IFSC direct listing framework that are not being made in the mainstream commentary. Taken together, they suggest the framework is more strategically significant than most analysts have appreciated — and more operationally complicated than most articles have acknowledged.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Argument One: This Is Not a Capital Markets Reform. It Is a PE Exit Architecture.</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The official framing of India's direct listing framework positions it as a capital markets development — a mechanism for Indian companies to access global investors and achieve international valuations. That framing is accurate but incomplete. It describes the instrument without identifying the problem it is actually solving.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The real problem is this: India has produced a generation of PE-backed, VC-funded unlisted companies that have raised multiple private rounds, reached significant scale, and now face a structural impasse. Their investors — domestic PE funds, global VCs, family offices — need liquidity. But the available exit routes are unsatisfying. A domestic IPO on BSE or NSE requires navigating SEBI's ICDR framework, accepting INR-denominated pricing from a largely domestic investor base, and often listing at a valuation that global investors consider a discount to what comparable companies command internationally. A strategic sale is an option, but not always available or desired. An offshore listing via ADR or GDR requires routing through foreign intermediaries, foreign jurisdiction regulation, and structural complexity that most mid-sized Indian companies cannot absorb.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The direct listing framework solves precisely this problem. It allows existing shareholders — promoters, PE funds, early investors — to offer their shares on an international exchange at GIFT IFSC, denominated in foreign currency, accessible to global institutional investors, without the company itself issuing a single new share. No fresh capital. No dilution. No SEBI ICDR compliance. Just a public market for shares that already exist, priced by investors who understand global benchmarks.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is not primarily a mechanism for companies to raise capital. It is a mechanism for India's PE ecosystem to achieve internationally-priced exits without exporting the transaction to Singapore or Cayman. The fact that it also gives companies global visibility and a valuation benchmark is a secondary benefit — valuable, but not the load-bearing structural purpose.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This reframing matters for advisors. Companies that are evaluating the direct listing framework asking \"how do we use this to raise capital?\" are asking the wrong question. The right question is: \"which of our existing shareholders needs liquidity, at what valuation, from which investor base, and on what timeline?\" The answer to that question determines whether direct listing is relevant — and, if so, who the real client in the transaction is.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Argument Two: The FDI Treatment of Direct Listing Is Not a Technical Detail. It Is a Structural Surprise.</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Every investment made through the GIFT IFSC direct listing route is treated as Foreign Direct Investment under India's NDI Rules — not as Foreign Portfolio Investment. This classification is stated clearly in the regulatory framework and is routinely noted in articles about the scheme. What is not being said clearly is what it actually means in practice — and for many unlisted companies, it will be the most consequential regulatory fact in their entire transaction.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>FPI is light-touch from an Indian regulatory perspective. A foreign investor buys shares on an exchange, holds them, sells them. The compliance burden sits largely on the custodian and the exchange. The investor does not have a direct relationship with India's foreign exchange regulatory framework in any meaningful operational sense.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>FDI is different in kind, not just in degree. When a non-resident investor acquires shares through the direct listing route, that investment is FDI. This means:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Sectoral cap compliance is not a checkbox — it is a ceiling.</strong>&nbsp;A company in a sector with a 49% or 74% FDI cap must actively manage its total non-resident holdings across all foreign investors combined. In a domestic IPO with FPI participation, the exchange monitoring systems handle this largely automatically. In an international direct listing where new non-resident investors are acquiring shares that were previously held domestically, the compliance mechanics of tracking aggregate FDI against sectoral ceilings in real time is a non-trivial operational problem that nobody has fully solved yet.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Land-border restrictions create investor list complications.</strong>&nbsp;Prior Government approval is required for investments from entities that are citizens of, or beneficial-owned by residents of, countries sharing a land border with India — China, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar. On an international exchange accessible to global investors, managing which orders can be accepted and which require prior approval before settlement is an exchange-level operational challenge that the detailed IFSCA notification will need to address with precision. How this works in practice — whether through investor-level eligibility screening before admission, or through exchange-level controls at the order stage — is one of the key unresolved questions in the pending notification.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Reporting obligations are immediate and specific.</strong>&nbsp;FDI investments require reporting to the Reserve Bank of India through the FIRMS portal within specified timelines. For a company executing a direct listing where potentially thousands of non-resident investors are acquiring shares simultaneously on the exchange, the mechanics of aggregating and reporting these as FDI transactions — rather than the standardised FPI reporting that exchanges handle for domestic listings — is genuinely complex.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The companies that will be most surprised by the FDI treatment are those that have significant existing non-resident shareholding close to their sectoral FDI ceiling. For them, a successful direct listing could inadvertently trigger a regulatory breach if the incoming investor demand is not actively capped and managed. This is not a hypothetical concern — it is a real execution risk that the detailed IFSCA framework will need to address, and that advisors need to be actively modelling before recommending the route.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Argument Three: GIFT IFSC Is Not Competing With NYSE or NASDAQ. It Is Disrupting Mauritius and Singapore.</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The narrative around GIFT IFSC positioning in the capital markets commentary almost universally frames it as India's answer to NASDAQ, the NYSE, or the LSE — a world-class international exchange that can compete with the best. That is aspirational positioning, and there is nothing wrong with ambition. But it misidentifies who is actually threatened by GIFT IFSC's success.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The entities facing genuine disruption from the GIFT IFSC direct listing framework are not NYSE or NASDAQ. They are Mauritius, Singapore, and Cayman Islands — the three jurisdictions through which India-origin capital has historically been structured, managed, and exited.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Consider the actual transaction flow that GIFT IFSC is designed to replace. A PE fund investing in an Indian company typically structures through a Mauritius or Singapore holding entity — historically for tax treaty benefits, increasingly for regulatory familiarity and investor comfort. When the fund seeks an exit, it either routes through a domestic IPO (accepting INR pricing and domestic investor base), a secondary sale to another PE fund (often through the same offshore structure), or — for larger companies — an ADR or GDR listing through a foreign depositary. Each of these routes involves capital leaving India, being processed through an offshore jurisdiction, and returning in a different form. The transaction costs, the treaty risks, and the regulatory complexity are all managed offshore.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The GIFT IFSC direct listing framework, when fully operational, allows the entire transaction to stay onshore — in a jurisdiction that is treated as offshore for FEMA purposes, priced in foreign currency, accessible to non-resident investors, with a competitive tax regime that eliminates STT, CTT, stamp duty, and capital gains tax for qualifying non-resident transactions. For a PE fund exiting a mid-market Indian company with global investors as natural buyers, this is a materially better architecture than routing through Singapore or Mauritius — if the operational framework is robust.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is what the Government means when it describes GIFT IFSC's objective as \"onshoring the offshore.\" It is not a metaphor. It is a precise description of the transaction flows being targeted: the India-related financial activity that currently happens in Singapore's SGX, in Mauritius's stock exchange, in Cayman-structured fund vehicles, being brought within India's regulatory and fiscal jurisdiction without losing its international character.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The implications for Indian companies are significant. If your growth capital came through a Mauritius or Singapore holding structure, your exit route planning needs to account for whether GIFT IFSC offers a better terminal option than continuing to route through those jurisdictions. The answer will depend on treaty positions, fund vintage, investor base, and timing — but the question is now legitimately on the table in a way it was not before January 2024.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Argument Four: The Pricing Problem for Unlisted Companies Is the Single Largest Unresolved Technical Challenge in the Framework.</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>A direct listing, by structural definition, has no issue price. There is no book-building exercise, no price band, no anchor investor determining where the market opens. Price emerges from the interaction of supply and demand on the exchange from the first moment of trading.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>On the NYSE or NASDAQ, where the US direct listing model originated (Spotify's 2018 listing being the landmark example), this works because the company has a deep, liquid private market history. Institutional investors who participated in private rounds have publicly disclosed valuations. Investment banks publish reference price estimates based on comparable public companies, secondary market transactions, and 409A valuations. By the time Spotify opened for trading, the market had a reasonable basis for price discovery even without a formal book-building exercise.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>India's unlisted company ecosystem is structurally different. Most companies eligible for the GIFT IFSC direct listing route — PE-backed, multi-round funded, significant scale — have private valuations determined through negotiated investment rounds, not through competitive market clearing. The most recent round valuation may be twelve or eighteen months old. There is no secondary market of the depth and transparency that existed for Spotify or Slack before their direct listings. The \"comparable public companies\" are often listed on domestic Indian exchanges at valuations that may not reflect what global investors would pay.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The NDI Rules require that the issue price for initial listing of an unlisted company's shares shall not be less than fair market value as determined under those rules. This creates a floor. It does not create a mechanism for orderly price discovery.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The unresolved question — which the detailed IFSCA notification will need to answer — is how the exchange handles the opening of trading for a company with a regulatory floor price, no prior trading history, and potentially thin liquidity in early sessions. On a domestic exchange, the SEBI-mandated book-building process and the mandatory 10% retail allocation create initial liquidity and price stabilisation mechanisms. None of those mechanisms exist in the direct listing structure as currently contemplated.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The practical consequences are three. First, companies with weak institutional investor outreach before listing will face genuine price discovery risk on opening day — the absence of a book-building process that normally functions as an investor education exercise creates the possibility of an opening price that either dramatically overshoots or undershoots fair value. Second, the 22-hour trading window at India INX, while commercially attractive, means pricing events can happen when the issuer's management team is asleep and unable to respond to market communications. Third, for sectors where comparable international valuations are significantly higher than domestic benchmarks — deep technology, biotech, specialised manufacturing — the fair market value floor under NDI Rules may actually constrain the upside price discovery that was the primary motivation for choosing GIFT IFSC in the first place.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>None of this is an argument against the framework. It is an argument for building pre-listing investor relationships, international-standard financial disclosure, and robust IR infrastructure before the listing event — not as a nice-to-have, but as a structural prerequisite for the direct listing to function as intended.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Argument Five: The Two Regulatory Gaps Are Being Treated as One. They Are Not.</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The commentary around GIFT IFSC direct listing regularly acknowledges that \"guidelines are pending.\" What is almost never clearly articulated is that there are two separate pending regulatory actions, from two different regulators, covering two different company populations — and that the timeline and complexity of each is different.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Gap One: IFSCA's Operational Framework (Expected June–July 2026)</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is the notification that will operationalise Regulation 40 of IFSCA's Listing Regulations, 2024 — specifying the actual process by which an unlisted Indian public company executes a direct listing on India INX or NSE IFSC. Until this notification, no company — listed or unlisted — can execute a direct listing at GIFT IFSC. The statutory enablement exists. The exchange infrastructure exists. The rulebook that connects them does not yet.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The questions this notification must resolve include: eligibility criteria beyond those in the NDI Rules, documentation and disclosure standards comparable to a prospectus but structurally different from one, pricing mechanics that accommodate the fair value floor while enabling market discovery, investor eligibility screening for land-border restrictions at the exchange level, and the FDI reporting mechanics described in Argument Two above. These are not straightforward drafting exercises — they require IFSCA to make policy choices on questions that have not been fully resolved in comparable jurisdictions.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Gap Two: SEBI's Operational Guidelines for Listed Indian Companies</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is entirely separate. Once an Indian company is already listed on BSE or NSE, any cross-listing on GIFT IFSC exchanges requires SEBI's specific operational guidelines — not IFSCA's framework. The IFSCA working group has already proposed the architecture: Class A shares on domestic exchanges, Class B shares on IFSC, fungibility between the two through a defined conversion mechanism. But SEBI has not converted this into operative circular. NSE IX's MD and CEO flagged this explicitly at the Global Securities Markets Conclave in February 2026.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The complexity here is greater than for unlisted companies — because cross-listing a domestically-listed company on IFSC exchanges raises questions about minimum public shareholding compliance across both exchanges, SAST Regulations applicability when the same acquirer holds both Class A and Class B shares, voting rights parity, information flow obligations between exchanges, and the treatment of corporate actions (dividends, rights, buybacks) across two exchange ecosystems with different currency denominations and investor populations. SEBI has not yet published its answers to these questions. The IFSCA framework notification alone will not unlock this route.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:gallery {\"linkTo\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-gallery has-nested-images columns-default is-cropped\"><!-- wp:image {\"id\":32035,\"sizeSlug\":\"large\",\"linkDestination\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image size-large\"><img src=\"https://csatwork.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/gift-ifsc-global-capital-structural-shift-1024x576.png\" alt=\"\" class=\"wp-image-32035\"/></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image --></figure>\n<!-- /wp:gallery -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The Advisory Consequence</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The practical reality as of April 2026:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For an&nbsp;<em>unlisted</em>&nbsp;Indian public company: the route is legislatively enabled, structurally sound, and operationally pending. The right posture is to begin internal preparation now — governance structuring, Ind AS financial statements, international IR groundwork, FEMA compliance audit — so that when the IFSCA notification comes, the company is not starting from zero.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For a&nbsp;<em>listed</em>&nbsp;Indian company: the route requires two sequential regulatory actions, from two different regulators, with the second (SEBI's guidelines) having no confirmed timeline. Any listed company being advised that GIFT IFSC direct cross-listing is a near-term option should seek a second opinion.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What Regulation 40 Actually Says — And What It Doesn't</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For those who want the regulatory text grounded in the argument above: Regulation 40 of IFSCA's Listing Regulations, 2024 provides that an eligible issuer may list specified securities on a recognised stock exchange in IFSC without making a public offer. It requires compliance with the Direct Listing Scheme under the NDI Rules. It specifies that Indian companies must meet the pricing requirements of that Scheme.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>What Regulation 40 does not do is specify the operational process — how the listing application is made, what documents are required, how investor eligibility is verified, how the opening of trading is managed, what ongoing disclosure obligations apply specifically to direct-listed companies as distinct from IPO-listed companies. Those details will come from the IFSCA notification. The regulation creates the right. The notification will create the mechanism.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This distinction — between a statutory right and an operational mechanism — is the most important regulatory precision in this entire discussion.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The Comparison That Actually Matters: Direct Listing vs. IPO as Strategy, Not Structure</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Having established what the framework is, what it isn't, and where the real complexity lies, the comparison between direct listing and IPO can be made at the level that is actually useful — strategy, not structure.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>An IPO, whether domestic or at IFSC, is a financing event that happens to produce a public market. The company enters the transaction needing something — capital, debt repayment capacity, acquisition currency — and exits with a public listing as a byproduct of having obtained it. The process is oriented around the company's needs.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>A direct listing is a market event that serves existing shareholders more than the company itself. The company gains visibility, a valuation benchmark, and enhanced credibility with future counterparties. But the primary beneficiaries of a direct listing are those who already hold shares — and who now have a public, internationally-priced market in which to sell them if they choose to. This is why the framework's most natural users are not growth-stage companies that need capital. They are mature, well-capitalised companies with sophisticated investor bases who are optimising for exit quality, not entry capital.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The decision between the two routes, therefore, is not primarily a capital markets question. It is a shareholder strategy question. Who owns the company today? What do they need? On what timeline? At what price? From which investor base? The answers to those questions determine the route — and the regulatory framework is the vehicle, not the driver.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What Companies Should Be Doing Right Now</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The IFSCA notification in June–July 2026 will not give unlisted companies that begin preparation then any meaningful head start. The companies that will execute cleanly in the first wave are those that are using the current window to:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Get Ind AS right.</strong>&nbsp;Three years of audited Ind AS financials is a baseline requirement. Companies still on Indian GAAP need to begin the transition now — not because the notification will demand it immediately, but because restating three years of financials retrospectively under time pressure produces poor disclosures and poor valuations.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Build international IR infrastructure.</strong>&nbsp;A direct listing with no pre-existing relationships with non-resident institutional investors is a price discovery event without an audience. The international roadshow that would normally accompany an IPO book-building needs to be replicated informally before listing, through investor education, analyst coverage, and structured engagement with global institutions.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Audit FEMA compliance comprehensively.</strong>&nbsp;Every historical foreign investment — from incorporation through all funding rounds — needs to be mapped against FDI sectoral compliance. Pricing compliance for past issuances. Reporting compliance with RBI. Downstream investment regulations if the company has subsidiaries. A FEMA gap that surfaces during a direct listing process is not a paperwork problem — it can be a transaction-stopping event.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Resolve cap table complexity.</strong>&nbsp;Companies with multiple ESOP schemes, convertible instruments, or fractional ownership arrangements need clean, IFSCA-compliant cap tables before a listing event. The exchange will require it. Global investors will expect it.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Engage legal advisors who have actually read the working group reports.</strong>&nbsp;The IFSCA working group reports, the SEBI expert committee reports, and the detailed regulatory correspondence on this subject are publicly available. The number of advisors who have read them carefully is smaller than the number who are advising on the subject. Ask your advisor what they think about the Class A / Class B share fungibility proposal and the FDI reporting mechanics — the answer will tell you what you need to know about their depth.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:gallery {\"linkTo\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-gallery has-nested-images columns-default is-cropped\"><!-- wp:image {\"id\":32036,\"sizeSlug\":\"large\",\"linkDestination\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image size-large\"><img src=\"https://csatwork.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/gift-ifsc-global-capital-markets-shift-1024x576.png\" alt=\"\" class=\"wp-image-32036\"/></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image --></figure>\n<!-- /wp:gallery -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Conclusion: The Framework Is Ready. The Market Is Not.</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>India's GIFT IFSC direct listing framework represents a genuinely sophisticated policy intervention — one that, when fully operational, will reshape how PE-backed Indian companies think about exits, how global investors access Indian growth stories, and how India competes with Singapore and Mauritius for the management of India-origin capital.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The regulatory architecture is coherent. The intent is unambiguous. The international positioning is credible. The exchange infrastructure — 22-hour trading, sub-4 microsecond latency, USD/GBP/EUR denomination, zero STT/CTT/capital gains for non-residents — is world-class by any measure.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>What is not yet ready is the market — by which I mean not the exchange, but the ecosystem of companies, advisors, investors, and intermediaries who need to understand this framework deeply enough to use it well. The IFSCA notification expected in June–July 2026 will open the window. Whether Indian companies walk through it intelligently or stumble through it unprepared will depend almost entirely on the quality of advisory work done between now and then.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The gap between regulatory enablement and advisory readiness is not unusual in Indian capital markets. It is, however, the gap where the most consequential mistakes are made. This piece is an attempt to close it — at least partially.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>A Note on Regulatory Status (April 2026)</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For readers using this article for advisory or planning purposes, the following is the precise current regulatory position:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>— The Direct Listing Scheme under NDI Rules:&nbsp;<strong>Notified (January 2024)</strong>&nbsp;— Companies (Listing of Equity Shares in Permissible Jurisdictions) Rules, 2024:&nbsp;<strong>Notified</strong>&nbsp;— Regulation 40, IFSCA Listing Regulations, 2024:&nbsp;<strong>In force</strong>&nbsp;— IFSCA Operational Framework for Direct Listings:&nbsp;<strong>Pending — expected June–July 2026</strong>&nbsp;— SEBI Guidelines for Listed Companies' Cross-Listing on IFSC:&nbsp;<strong>Pending — no confirmed timeline</strong>&nbsp;— Resident Indian Investor Participation in IFSC-listed Equity:&nbsp;<strong>Pending — pilot underway</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Any representation that the direct listing route is currently executable is factually incorrect. Any representation that the framework is not advancing is equally incorrect. The accurate position is: the architecture is complete, the operational notification is imminent, and the preparation window is now.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>About the Author&nbsp;</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Prashant Kumar is a Company Secretary, Published Author, and a seasoned professional in corporate and financial services regulation. He currently serves as Company Secretary &amp; Compliance Officer at Global Horizons Capital Advisors (IFSC) Private Limited, an IFSCA-licensed Investment Banker based in GIFT City, with direct, on-ground exposure to capital market transactions within the IFSC ecosystem.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>He brings hands-on experience in IPOs, direct listings, and exchange listings, along with deep expertise in GIFT IFSC structuring, fund setup (FME &amp; AIF), corporate governance, and regulatory compliance. He regularly advises fund managers, startups, and institutions on building globally aligned, execution-ready structures.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For professional discussions on GIFT IFSC, IPOs, listings, fund structuring, and regulatory strategy, he can be reached at +91 9821008011 or&nbsp;prashant.kumar@global-horizons.in.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>© 2026 CS Prashant Kumar.           "content:encoded": "<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\"><strong>By CS Prashant Kumar | Company Secretary &amp; Compliance Officer | Global Horizons Capital Advisors (IFSC) Private Limited </strong></h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>A practitioner's deep-dive into enforcement realities, deal structuring, tax economics, and why GIFT City is no longer just a policy experiment — it is becoming a genuine leasing jurisdiction.</em></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Why Are Leasing Companies Moving to GIFT City?</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>If someone asks you — \"Why are aircraft and ship leasing companies setting up in GIFT City?\" — the honest, direct answer is this:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Because, for the first time, India offers the combination that global lessors actually need: enforceable asset recovery, tax-neutral structuring, full USD operability, and a single regulatory authority — all within the same jurisdiction.</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>That may sound like a policy brochure. But the shift is real, and it is being driven by commercial logic, not patriotism.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Let me walk you through exactly why — drawing on both the legal framework and the deal economics.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What Is GIFT City, and Why Does It Matter for Leasing?</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>GIFT City — Gujarat International Finance Tec-City — is India's first operational International Financial Services Centre (IFSC), located near Gandhinagar in Gujarat. It operates under the&nbsp;<strong>International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA)</strong>, a unified regulator that governs banking, insurance, capital markets, and leasing activity within the zone.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>What makes GIFT structurally different from the rest of India is this:&nbsp;<strong>it operates closer to an offshore jurisdiction in regulatory character, while being physically onshore.</strong>&nbsp;Transactions are conducted in foreign currency, tax treatment is distinct from the domestic regime, and regulatory approvals flow through a single authority rather than multiple overlapping bodies.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For aircraft and ship leasing — businesses that are inherently cross-border, USD-denominated, and dependent on swift asset recovery — this architecture matters enormously.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The Historical Problem: Why India Was Left Out of Its Own Leasing Market</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Here is a fact that should be uncomfortable for any Indian policy-maker: for decades, Indian airlines leased hundreds of aircraft, but almost none of those leases were structured in India.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The ownership sat in&nbsp;<strong>Dublin, Singapore, or Dubai.</strong>&nbsp;The financing flowed from&nbsp;<strong>European and American lenders.</strong>&nbsp;India was the end-consumer — a large and growing one — but it had no role in the value chain above the airline level.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Why?</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Three compounding problems:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>First, enforcement uncertainty.</strong>&nbsp;Under the Cape Town Convention, a lessor owns the aircraft and can reclaim it upon default. But when an Indian airline entered insolvency proceedings under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), an automatic moratorium applied. That moratorium froze all recovery actions — including the lessor's right to repossess an asset it legally owned. Aircraft sat grounded for months. Values eroded. Lessors absorbed losses that were entirely avoidable from a legal standpoint.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Second, tax friction.</strong>&nbsp;Withholding tax on lease rentals, GST complexity, and the absence of a tax-neutral holding structure made it expensive to route leasing transactions through India. Every percentage point of avoidable tax leakage directly hits IRR in a business that operates on thin margins.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Third, currency mismatch.</strong>&nbsp;Aircraft and ship values are set in USD globally. Lease rentals are paid in USD. Maintenance reserves are benchmarked in USD. Putting that into a rupee-centric regulatory framework created hedging costs, FEMA compliance complexity, and structural inefficiency.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>GIFT City addresses all three — not perfectly, but materially enough that the economics of choosing India over Ireland or Singapore have fundamentally changed.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:gallery {\"linkTo\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-gallery has-nested-images columns-default is-cropped\"><!-- wp:image {\"id\":32042,\"sizeSlug\":\"large\",\"linkDestination\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image size-large\"><img src=\"https://csatwork.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/india-leasing-value-chain-gift-city-ifsc-1024x576.png\" alt=\"India shifting from leasing consumer to global leasing hub through GIFT City IFSC\" class=\"wp-image-32042\"/></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image --></figure>\n<!-- /wp:gallery -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Enforcement: The Single Biggest Unlock for Lessors</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Let us be precise about what changed — because vague references to \"improved enforcement\" obscure the actual mechanism.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The Cape Town Convention and Its Indian Implementation</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>India ratified the Cape Town Convention and its Aircraft Protocol, which created an international legal framework for secured interests in aircraft assets. In theory, this gave lessors the right to repossess aircraft quickly upon default.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The practical problem was the interaction with Indian insolvency law. The IBC's moratorium provision under Section 14 did not clearly carve out lessors' rights, leading to litigation-heavy recoveries every time an airline went under.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>What has shifted:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Courts and tribunals have become more sophisticated in applying Cape Town principles</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Regulatory coordination between DGCA (aircraft deregistration), NCLT (insolvency proceedings), and lessors has improved</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>IFSCA's framework for GIFT-based leasing entities incorporates clearer recovery rights</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The shift is from&nbsp;<strong>\"legal right, uncertain execution\"</strong>&nbsp;to&nbsp;<strong>\"legal right, increasingly predictable execution.\"</strong>&nbsp;That distinction — seemingly semantic — is worth hundreds of millions of dollars across a leasing portfolio.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What a Lessor Actually Cares About</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>When I talk to lessors about India risk, the conversation is not theoretical. They want to know:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><em>If an airline defaults tomorrow, how many days does it take to get my aircraft back?</em></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><em>Will I be able to deregister the aircraft from the Indian registry without litigation?</em></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><em>What is my exposure during a moratorium period — in days, not principles?</em></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The honest answer is still:&nbsp;<em>India is not yet Ireland or Singapore in speed.</em>&nbsp;But the gap has narrowed significantly. And for a lessor that wants Indian market exposure — which almost every global platform does, given the growth trajectory of Indian aviation — the question is whether the risk is now manageable, not whether it is zero.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Increasingly, the answer is yes.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Tax Efficiency: How GIFT City Changes the Economics of Every Deal</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is where practitioners sometimes lose non-specialists, so let me make it concrete.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>How Lease Economics Work</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>A lessor buys an aircraft for, say, $50 million. It finances $40 million through lenders at a cost of 5%. It leases the aircraft to an airline for a monthly rental that gives it a net spread — the difference between what it earns and what it costs to own and finance the asset.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>That spread, over a 10–12 year lease, is the lessor's return. It is not large in absolute percentage terms. Which means&nbsp;<strong>every tax leakage point matters.</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What GIFT Offers</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Entities registered in GIFT's IFSC can access:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Tax holidays</strong> under the Income Tax Act for IFSC units (currently a 20-year holiday on profits, subject to conditions)</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Reduced or exempted withholding tax</strong> on certain lease payments, reducing the gross-up cost for airlines</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>GST clarity</strong> — leasing transactions structured within the IFSC do not attract GST in the same way domestic transactions do</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>No Minimum Alternate Tax</strong> (MAT) exposure for IFSC units under certain conditions</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The aggregate effect is a structurally lower tax cost compared to routing the same transaction through the domestic regime.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>To illustrate: if a GIFT-based structure saves 150–200 basis points in effective tax cost versus an offshore structure, the lessor can either pocket that improvement or pass part of it to the airline as lower lease rates — making Indian lessors genuinely competitive on pricing.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is not a niche advantage. Over a portfolio of 20–30 aircraft, it is a material commercial difference.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Foreign Currency Flexibility: Aligning India With the Global Standard</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Ask any aviation finance professional what the standard currency for aircraft leasing is, and the answer is immediate:&nbsp;<strong>US Dollars.</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is not a preference — it is structural. Aircraft are purchased from Boeing and Airbus in USD. Maintenance events are priced in USD. Residual values are benchmarked in USD. Lenders price financing in USD. Lease rentals follow the same currency.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Historically, India's regulatory architecture was rupee-centric. This created genuine friction: FEMA-related compliance for cross-border payments, hedging requirements, and currency mismatch between asset economics and local regulatory structure.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>GIFT IFSC eliminates this friction for entities set up within it. Transactions can be&nbsp;<strong>fully structured, executed, and serviced in USD</strong>&nbsp;— no currency translation, no hedging mandated by regulatory compliance, no INR leg introduced artificially.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For a leasing company evaluating where to domicile its India-facing structures, this is not a minor operational detail. It is fundamental to whether the structure is clean or complicated.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The Market Access Argument: India's Growth, Without India's Legacy Risk</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>India's aviation sector is among the fastest-growing in the world. IndiGo alone operates one of the largest single-airline order books globally. New carriers are entering. Passenger numbers are growing structurally, driven by demographics, rising incomes, and expanding route networks.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Global lessors cannot afford to be absent from this market. They need Indian airline exposure.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The traditional choice was: access India through your Dublin or Singapore entity, accepting the jurisdictional complexity that comes with cross-border enforcement. This worked — imperfectly, expensively, but it worked.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>GIFT offers a different architecture:&nbsp;<strong>structure your India-facing leasing through a GIFT entity, and get the market access with significantly reduced structural friction.</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The GIFT entity is not subject to the full weight of the domestic Indian regulatory regime. It operates under IFSCA. It can hold aircraft in foreign currency. And it benefits from the enforcement improvements discussed above.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Think of it as:&nbsp;<strong>Irish benefits, Indian proximity, improving Indian enforcement.</strong>&nbsp;That combination — even if imperfect in execution today — is directionally transforming India's role in global leasing value chains.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Regulatory Architecture: The Advantage of One Authority</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is underappreciated by commentators who focus primarily on tax.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>In the domestic Indian regime, a company involved in aviation finance might interact with: DGCA (for aircraft registration and deregistration), RBI (for FEMA and external commercial borrowings), SEBI (for capital market instruments), the Ministry of Civil Aviation, and various tax authorities. Each has its own process, timeline, and institutional culture.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>GIFT entities deal primarily with&nbsp;<strong>IFSCA</strong>&nbsp;— a single, purpose-built authority designed for international financial services. IFSCA has taken a proactive approach to issuing guidance on aircraft leasing, ship leasing, and related financing structures, often in direct consultation with industry.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The practical result: faster approvals, clearer regulations, and a regulator that understands the commercial context of what you are trying to do.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For a leasing company that needs to structure a new transaction, respond to a default, or seek approval for a novel structure, dealing with one informed authority rather than five bureaucratic ones is not a minor convenience. It is a genuine competitive advantage.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Capital Markets and Lender Confidence: How GIFT Changes the Financing Equation</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Leasing is a capital-intensive business. No lessor funds its portfolio from equity alone. Banks, insurance companies, pension funds, and capital market investors provide the debt that makes leasing economics work.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>These lenders underwrite jurisdictional risk. Before extending a $30 million facility to a GIFT-based leasing entity, a lender's credit team will ask:&nbsp;<em>if this deal goes wrong, can the borrower recover the aircraft and repay us?</em></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Three years ago, the honest answer to that question — for an India-based structure — was uncertain enough to command a significant risk premium, if lenders were willing to lend at all.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Today, with improved enforcement frameworks, IFSCA regulatory clarity, and growing precedent of successful GIFT-based transactions, lenders are becoming more comfortable. Comfort translates to lower risk premiums. Lower risk premiums translate to lower cost of capital. Lower cost of capital means better deal economics.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is a reinforcing cycle: as more transactions are executed successfully through GIFT, lender confidence grows, capital becomes cheaper, more deals get done.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Ireland went through precisely this cycle between 1975 and 1995. GIFT is at an earlier stage of the same trajectory.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Ship Leasing: The Next Frontier</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Aircraft leasing has seen faster traction at GIFT — partly because the Cape Town Convention provides a more mature international legal framework for aircraft than for ships, and partly because Indian aviation growth is more visible than maritime finance.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>But the fundamentals for ship leasing are equally compelling:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>India is one of the world's largest importers and exporters by volume</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Indian shipping companies operate significant fleets, most of which are financed offshore</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The maritime sector is capital-intensive, making tax-efficient financing highly valuable</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The current gap is enforcement maturity. The legal framework for ship mortgages and recovery in the event of default is less internationally standardised than the aircraft regime. This is not an insurmountable problem — it is a legislative and regulatory gap that can be addressed.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>IFSCA has already issued frameworks for ship leasing within the IFSC, and early transactions are being structured. The market is smaller than aircraft leasing today, but the long-term potential — tied to India's trade growth — is substantial.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>A Real-World Structuring Example: Sale and Leaseback at GIFT City</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Let me make this concrete with a transaction type that is common in aviation finance: the&nbsp;<strong>sale and leaseback.</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The Scenario</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>An Indian airline takes delivery of 10 new aircraft from Airbus. It needs to pay for them, but also wants to preserve liquidity for operations. The solution: sell the aircraft to a lessor immediately upon delivery, then lease them back under a long-term operating lease.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>How This Works Through GIFT</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list {\"ordered\":true} -->\n<ol class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>A leasing company incorporated in GIFT's IFSC purchases the 10 aircraft from Airbus, paying in USD under a direct import transaction.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The GIFT entity simultaneously enters into a lease agreement with the Indian airline, denominated in USD, for a 12-year term.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The GIFT entity finances the purchase through a combination of equity and a USD-denominated loan facility from a foreign bank (lending into GIFT under the permissible framework).</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Lease rentals flow from the airline to the GIFT entity in USD. The GIFT entity services its debt and retains its spread.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What GIFT Adds to This Structure</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The lease rental withholding tax position is more favourable than a pure offshore-to-Indian-airline structure</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The GIFT entity benefits from the IFSCA regulatory framework, reducing approval complexity</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>If the airline defaults, the GIFT entity can invoke Cape Town enforcement mechanisms with improving predictability</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The entire structure — ownership, financing, leasing — sits within a single, coherent regulatory perimeter</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Both sides benefit: the airline gets liquidity and removes the aircraft from its balance sheet; the lessor gets a well-structured, tax-efficient Indian asset exposure.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Frequently Asked Questions About GIFT City Leasing</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What types of leasing companies can set up in GIFT City?</strong>&nbsp;Aircraft leasing companies, ship leasing companies, and helicopter leasing entities can all register under IFSCA's leasing framework. The regulator has issued specific guidelines for each category.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Is GIFT City leasing only for large global lessors?</strong>&nbsp;No. While global platforms like SMBC Aviation Capital and AerCap have strategic reasons to explore GIFT, the framework is also accessible to mid-sized platforms, family office-backed leasing vehicles, and Indian-promoted entities looking to structure international leasing activity.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What is the minimum capital requirement for a GIFT City leasing entity?</strong>&nbsp;IFSCA has prescribed minimum capital requirements for IFSC leasing entities. These vary based on the nature of the entity and the type of assets being leased. Specific requirements should be verified against current IFSCA circulars, as they are updated periodically.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>How does GIFT City compare to Ireland for aircraft leasing?</strong>&nbsp;Ireland has a 50-year head start, an established ecosystem of lessors, lawyers, lenders, and technical managers, and a fully tested enforcement track record. GIFT is earlier in its development but offers advantages Ireland cannot: direct access to the Indian market, improving enforcement in the world's fastest-growing aviation market, and a regulatory authority that is actively facilitating growth. The comparison is not Ireland versus GIFT — most sophisticated lessors will run structures in both jurisdictions depending on the asset and counterparty.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Are ship leasing transactions currently being executed through GIFT City?</strong>&nbsp;Yes, though in smaller numbers than aircraft leasing. The IFSCA has issued ship leasing frameworks and early transactions are being structured. The market is expected to grow as enforcement frameworks mature.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What This Means for India's Economic Positioning</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Stepping back from the transactional detail, what GIFT City's leasing ecosystem represents is a&nbsp;<strong>fundamental change in India's role in global asset finance.</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For decades, India was a consuming nation — a market for aircraft, ships, and capital, but not a participant in structuring, financing, or managing those assets. The value added by Irish lessors, Singaporean SPVs, and Dubai-based holding companies flowed to those jurisdictions, not to India.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>GIFT City, if it continues on its current trajectory, changes that equation. Indian-domiciled structures will originate, finance, and manage leasing transactions. The fees, the tax base, the employment in legal and financial services — these will accrue within India.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is the deeper ambition behind the policy architecture. And unlike many policy ambitions, this one has genuine commercial momentum behind it — because the underlying business case is real.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:gallery {\"linkTo\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-gallery has-nested-images columns-default is-cropped\"><!-- wp:image {\"id\":32043,\"sizeSlug\":\"large\",\"linkDestination\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image size-large\"><img src=\"https://csatwork.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/gift-city-global-finance-india-ifsc-positioning-1024x576.png\" alt=\"GIFT City redefining India role in global finance and leasing ecosystem\" class=\"wp-image-32043\"/></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image --></figure>\n<!-- /wp:gallery -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Conclusion: A Structural Shift That Practitioners Should Take Seriously</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The movement of aircraft and ship leasing to GIFT City is not a government press release. It is a commercial reality in formation — driven by the convergence of enforcement improvement, tax efficiency, currency flexibility, and market access that global lessors actually need.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>It is not complete. Enforcement predictability still lags Ireland. The ecosystem of advisors and technical specialists is still developing. And ship leasing is at a much earlier stage than aircraft leasing.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>But the direction is clear. And the practitioners who understand both the legal framework and the deal economics — who can structure transactions that leverage GIFT's advantages while managing its current limitations — are the ones who will build meaningful practices in this space.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For Indian aviation and maritime businesses, the opportunity is equally significant. Access to capital through GIFT-based lessors, structured in a tax-efficient and legally clear manner, could materially change the cost and availability of fleet financing.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>India is no longer just a consumer of leased assets. It is building the infrastructure to be a financier of them.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong><em>About the Author</em></strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>CS Prashant Kumar is a Company Secretary, Published Author, and a seasoned professional in corporate and financial services regulation. He currently serves as Company Secretary &amp; Compliance Officer at Global Horizons Capital Advisors (IFSC) Private Limited, an IFSCA-licensed Investment Banker based in GIFT City, with direct, on-ground exposure to capital market transactions within the IFSC ecosystem.</em></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>He brings hands-on experience in IPOs, direct listings, and exchange listings, along with deep expertise in GIFT IFSC structuring, fund setup (FME &amp; AIF), corporate governance, and regulatory compliance. He regularly advises fund managers, startups, and institutions on building globally aligned, execution-ready structures.</em></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>For professional discussions on GIFT IFSC, IPOs, listings, fund structuring, and regulatory strategy, he can be reached at +91 9821008011 or&nbsp;prashant.kumar@global-horizons.in.</em></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->",

          "link": "https://csatwork.in/ifsca-fund-management-regulations-gift-ifsc-funds/",
