          "title": "IFSCA Introduces Trust and Company Service Providers (TCSPs) at GIFT City: What It Means for Leasing, SPVs, and Cross-Border Structuring",
          "link": "https://csatwork.in/ifsca-tcsp-gift-city-leasing-spv-cross-border-structuring/",
          "pubDate": "Fri, 15 May 2026 14:50:18 +0000",
          "dc:creator": "prashantmishra1986",
          "guid": {
            "#text": "https://csatwork.in/?p=32060",
            "@attributes": {
              "isPermaLink": "false"
            }
          },
          "description": null,
          "content:encoded": "<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">CS Prashant Kumar | Company Secretary &amp; Compliance Officer | Global Horizons Capital Advisors (IFSC) Private Limited</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">What Just Changed at GIFT City?</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>On May 5, 2026, the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) quietly issued a notification that could meaningfully reshape how special purpose vehicles (SPVs), leasing structures, and cross-border entity management work out of GIFT IFSC.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The&nbsp;<strong>IFSCA (TechFin and Ancillary Services) (Amendment) Regulations, 2026</strong>&nbsp;inserts a brand new Chapter VA into the principal TechFin and Ancillary Services Regulations, 2025 — formally introducing the concept of a&nbsp;<strong>Trust and Company Services Provider (TCSP)</strong>&nbsp;within India's only IFSC at GIFT City, Gandhinagar.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This isn't just a regulatory tweak. It is a foundational building block for a full-service international financial centre — the kind of infrastructure that Singapore, the Cayman Islands, the DIFC, and the BVI have long had. India is now building it, deliberately, within a regulated framework.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">What Exactly Is a TCSP Under IFSCA Regulations?</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>In plain language, a&nbsp;<strong>TCSP (Trust and Company Services Provider)</strong>&nbsp;is a regulated intermediary that provides corporate and trust administration services — things like acting as a nominee director, forming companies or trusts on behalf of clients, providing registered office addresses, and arranging trustee services.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>These are services that any sophisticated international financial centre needs. In the offshore world, corporate service providers (CSPs) do this every day in the Cayman Islands, BVI, and Singapore. At GIFT IFSC, this function now has a proper regulatory home.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Under the new regulations, a TCSP is defined as:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:quote -->\n<blockquote class=\"wp-block-quote\"><!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>\"An entity which has been granted registration as a TechFin and Ancillary Services Provider under these regulations to undertake Trust and Company Services Provider services for leasing activities permitted by the Authority.\"</em></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph --></blockquote>\n<!-- /wp:quote -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The immediate and explicit context is&nbsp;<strong>leasing activities</strong>&nbsp;— aircraft leasing, ship leasing, and equipment leasing structures that IFSCA has been aggressively developing. But the architecture is clearly designed with broader application in mind.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Why Does This Matter? The Big Picture First</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Before getting into the regulatory details, it's worth pausing to appreciate what this regulation is trying to solve.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>International leasing structures — say, an aircraft leasing SPV — need to be legally incorporated, administered, and governed. They need a registered office. They need directors (often nominee directors from the service provider). They need a compliance function. They may need a trustee if the structure involves a trust layer.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Until now, promoters had to either bring in offshore service providers (adding cost, complexity, and jurisdictional friction) or self-manage, which creates its own governance risks.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The TCSP framework means that&nbsp;<strong>a regulated, IFSCA-registered entity can now provide all of these services</strong>&nbsp;from within GIFT IFSC itself. This keeps the entire structuring ecosystem onshore — or rather, in the IFSC, which operates on a quasi-offshore basis for regulatory and tax purposes — without needing to rely on Cayman or Singapore intermediaries.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For India's ambition to make GIFT IFSC a genuine global financial hub, this is a significant missing piece being put in place.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Breaking Down the TCSP Framework: What the Regulations Actually Say</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">1. Registration Is Mandatory Before Commencement</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Any entity wanting to provide TCSP services at GIFT IFSC must obtain a&nbsp;<strong>certificate of registration from IFSCA</strong>&nbsp;before commencing operations. There is no grandfather exception for existing TechFin service providers — existing registered entities must separately apply for TCSP approval.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The registration remains valid until suspended, cancelled, or voluntarily surrendered — and voluntary surrender requires IFSCA's acceptance, meaning you can't simply walk away from obligations by filing a letter.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Practitioner note:</strong>&nbsp;The application process follows the existing TechFin registration route under Regulation 6(1) of the principal regulations, with an additional declaration of arm's length separation between TCSP activities and other services the entity may provide.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">2. Legal Form and Eligibility: Who Can Apply?</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The applicant must be incorporated as either a&nbsp;<strong>company or an LLP in the IFSC</strong>, or such other form as IFSCA may permit.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The FATF filter is specifically built into eligibility: all promoters or partners must be from jurisdictions&nbsp;<strong>not listed as High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to Call for Action</strong>&nbsp;in FATF's public statement.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is a clean, globally-aligned anti-money laundering threshold. It effectively pre-screens out high-risk jurisdictions at the promoter level, rather than only at the client level.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">3. Permissible Services: The Fifth Schedule</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The services that a TCSP can offer are set out in the&nbsp;<strong>Fifth Schedule</strong>&nbsp;to the regulations. These are:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>(i) Acting as an agent for setting up</strong>&nbsp;trusts, companies, LLPs, or any other body corporate.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>(ii) Acting as (or arranging for another person to act as):</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Trustee for an express trust or equivalent function for any other type of trust</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Director, company secretary, or nominee shareholder in the case of a company</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Partner or designated partner in the case of an LLP</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Any equivalent person in the case of a body corporate</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>(iii) Providing a registered office, business address, correspondence or administrative address</strong>&nbsp;for a trust, company, LLP, or body corporate</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>(iv) Any other services as IFSCA may permit</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The catch-all in (iv) is deliberate — IFSCA is building in flexibility to expand the scope as the market evolves without needing fresh legislative intervention.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">4. Governance and Controls: This Is Not a Light-Touch Regime</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The governance requirements under Regulation 10F are substantive and clearly modelled on FATF recommendations for trust and company service providers.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Key requirements include:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Governing Body:</strong>&nbsp;Every TCSP must have a governing body that formulates a governance framework commensurate with the scale, nature, complexity, and risk profile of its activities. This is not a box-ticking exercise — the framework must be proportionate.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Internal Audit / Independent Review:</strong>&nbsp;TCSPs must establish an internal audit or independent review mechanism to assess:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Adequacy of governance and control frameworks</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Effectiveness of AML/CFT/KYC systems and procedures</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Accuracy and completeness of client and entity records</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Adherence to regulatory approvals and service scope</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>IFSCA has also reserved the power to appoint&nbsp;<strong>external auditors</strong>&nbsp;for special audits where a TCSP's risk profile warrants it.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Record-Keeping:</strong>&nbsp;TCSPs must maintain accurate and up-to-date records (in physical or electronic form) of:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Each legal person or arrangement administered</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Details of directors, trustees, protectors, partners, and nominee shareholders</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Trust deeds, constitutional documents, shareholders' agreements</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Services provided, service agreements, and engagement duration</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>These records must be accessible to IFSCA or any government authority at any time, retained for&nbsp;<strong>a minimum of five years</strong>&nbsp;after cessation of the client relationship, and protected with appropriate data security safeguards.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Segregation of Duties:</strong>&nbsp;No single function or individual can have end-to-end control over client acceptance, service delivery, transaction execution, and compliance oversight. This is standard four-eyes principle applied at the process level.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Ring-Fencing:</strong>&nbsp;The TCSP business must be run as a&nbsp;<strong>distinct and adequately resourced line of business</strong>&nbsp;with its own governance arrangements, policies, systems, controls, and key personnel. Cross-contamination with other services the entity provides is explicitly prohibited.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">5. Principal Officer and Compliance Officer: Residency and Qualification Requirements</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Every TCSP must appoint a&nbsp;<strong>Principal Officer and a Compliance Officer</strong>, both of whom must:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Be <strong>based in the IFSC</strong> (not remote or offshore)</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Be <strong>full-time employees</strong> of the TCSP (no shared resources or consultants)</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Qualifications:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Both must hold a professional or post-graduate qualification in finance, law, commerce, or a related field</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The <strong>Principal Officer</strong> must have at least <strong>five years of post-qualification experience</strong> in financial services</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>One practical concession: a Compliance Officer already appointed under another applicable law or regulation (say, under SEBI or RBI framework for a regulated entity operating in IFSC) can be redesignated as the TCSP Compliance Officer, provided they meet the minimum requirements.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">6. Who Can Be a Service Recipient? The Non-Resident Requirement and the SPV Exception</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is one of the most commercially significant provisions in the entire framework.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The general rule: TCSPs may only provide services to&nbsp;<strong>non-resident</strong>&nbsp;service recipients from non-FATF-blacklisted jurisdictions.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The&nbsp;<strong>SPV exception</strong>&nbsp;is the crucial carve-out: A TCSP may provide services to an&nbsp;<strong>IFSC-based SPV even where the SPV has been sponsored, originated, or financed by a person resident in India</strong>&nbsp;— provided the SPV itself is the primary service recipient.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The explanation is equally important: An Indian resident who sponsors or finances an SPV is&nbsp;<strong>not treated as a service recipient</strong>&nbsp;merely by reason of that association. The TCSP's contractual and fiduciary obligations run to the SPV in IFSC, not to the Indian sponsor.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Why this matters:</strong>&nbsp;Many legitimate IFSC leasing structures — aircraft leasing, infrastructure asset leasing — involve Indian promoters setting up SPVs at GIFT IFSC. Without this carve-out, the non-resident requirement would have effectively prevented TCSPs from servicing the most common use case. IFSCA has intelligently threaded this needle.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">7. Professional Indemnity Insurance</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Every TCSP must maintain&nbsp;<strong>professional indemnity (PI) insurance</strong>&nbsp;commensurate with the scale and risk profile of its business, covering claims from negligence, errors, omissions, or breach of duty.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The regulation doesn't specify minimum cover amounts — this will likely be addressed through circulars. But the obligation itself is unconditional.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">8. Conflict of Interest Framework</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>TCSPs must identify and (where appropriate) disclose conflicts of interest, and maintain a&nbsp;<strong>documented conflict management policy</strong>.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Given that a TCSP acting as both trustee and nominee director for the same structure can have inherent conflicts, this isn't merely a compliance formality — it's operationally significant.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">9. Reporting and Enforcement</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Financial reporting to IFSCA must be in&nbsp;<strong>US Dollars</strong>&nbsp;(unless IFSCA specifies otherwise). Operational reporting must follow IFSCA's prescribed format, interval, and manner.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>On enforcement: violations of the regulations, guidelines, circulars, or directions can attract enforcement action&nbsp;<strong>including suspension or cancellation of registration</strong>. The due process standard is expressly preserved — no enforcement action without a reasonable opportunity of written submissions.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Practical Implications: Who Should Be Paying Attention?</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Aircraft and Ship Lessors at GIFT IFSC</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is the most immediate audience. IFSCA has been building out the aircraft leasing ecosystem aggressively. The TCSP framework provides the last-mile administrative infrastructure — the ability to have properly governed, locally-registered service providers who can manage SPV incorporation, nominee services, and registered office functions right within GIFT IFSC.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Fund Managers and Alternative Asset Managers</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Fund structures often use trust layers and nominee arrangements. Having a regulated TCSP within IFSC who can serve as trustee or nominee removes the need to route these arrangements through offshore intermediaries.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Law Firms, CA Firms, and Corporate Secretarial Firms</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The TCSP framework creates a new regulated category of financial service that professional services firms can potentially step into — subject to registration requirements and eligibility. For CA firms and law firms with an IFSC practice, this is worth a strategic evaluation.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Indian Promoters Structuring Outbound Investments via IFSC</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The SPV carve-out in Regulation 10H is specifically designed to enable Indian promoters to use IFSC-based TCSPs for their SPV management needs. This eliminates the offshore corporate service provider from the chain for many structures.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Global Family Offices and Private Wealth Structures</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>As IFSCA expands TCSP scope beyond just leasing (via the catch-all in Fifth Schedule Clause iv), trust and family holding structures could increasingly be serviced from GIFT IFSC.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">How Does This Compare Globally?</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:table -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-table\"><table class=\"has-fixed-layout\"><thead><tr><th>Jurisdiction</th><th>Regulatory Framework</th><th>TCSP Oversight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><strong>Singapore</strong></td><td>Trust Companies Act; MAS licensing</td><td>Comprehensive; MAS licensed trust companies</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Cayman Islands</strong></td><td>Companies Management Law</td><td>CIMA registered CSPs</td></tr><tr><td><strong>DIFC (Dubai)</strong></td><td>DIFC Companies Law; DFSA oversight</td><td>DNFBP regime for CSPs</td></tr><tr><td><strong>BVI</strong></td><td>Financial Services Commission oversight</td><td>Registered agents mandatory</td></tr><tr><td><strong>GIFT IFSC (India)</strong></td><td>IFSCA TechFin &amp; Ancillary Regs (2025/2026)</td><td>New TCSP registration regime; FATF-aligned</td></tr></tbody></table></figure>\n<!-- /wp:table -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>India's framework is closer to the Singapore model — a formal licensing/registration regime with substantive governance and AML/CFT requirements — rather than the lighter-touch models seen in some Caribbean jurisdictions. That's the right call for a jurisdiction positioning itself as a credible, G20-aligned financial centre.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Key Compliance Obligations at a Glance</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For any entity considering a TCSP registration at GIFT IFSC:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Pre-commencement:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Incorporate as a company or LLP in IFSC</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Verify promoter/partner FATF eligibility</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Apply to IFSCA under Regulation 6(1)</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Submit arm's length declaration</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Structural:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Appoint Principal Officer (5+ years experience) and Compliance Officer — both full-time, IFSC-based</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Establish governance framework, internal audit mechanism</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Implement segregation of duties controls</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Ring-fence TCSP business line from other services</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Ongoing:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Maintain client and entity records (5-year minimum post-engagement)</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Report to IFSCA in USD in prescribed format</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Maintain professional indemnity insurance</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Maintain documented conflict management policy</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>AML/CFT/KYC compliance</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">What to Watch For Next</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>1. IFSCA Circulars:</strong>&nbsp;The Fifth Schedule's catch-all provision (Clause iv — \"any other services as may be permitted\") signals that IFSCA will expand the service menu through circulars. Watch for guidance on trust administration, family office services, and potentially fund administration.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>2. Minimum PI Insurance Thresholds:</strong>&nbsp;These will almost certainly come via circular. Promoters planning TCSP registration should build this into financial projections.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>3. Reporting Format Specifications:</strong>&nbsp;IFSCA is yet to prescribe the specific reporting format and intervals. This will shape the operational compliance burden significantly.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>4. Expansion Beyond Leasing:</strong>&nbsp;The current framework explicitly anchors TCSP services to \"leasing activities permitted by the Authority.\" Any expansion of the TCSP concept to other IFSC activities (fund management, insurance, banking SPVs) will require either a regulatory amendment or a broad reading of the catch-all. Likely the former.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>5. PMLA Applicability:</strong>&nbsp;TCSPs providing trust and nominee services are classic Designated Non-Financial Businesses and Professions (DNFBPs) under FATF's framework. The interface between IFSCA's TCSP regulations and India's Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) obligations for IFSC entities will need clarity.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">The Bottom Line</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The IFSCA TCSP framework is a mature, well-constructed regulatory intervention. It brings GIFT IFSC closer to the administrative infrastructure of mature offshore jurisdictions — but does so within a robust, FATF-compliant governance architecture rather than the lighter-touch regimes that created reputational problems elsewhere.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For leasing structures, this is immediately actionable. For the broader IFSC ecosystem — fund managers, family offices, investment holding structures — this is a foundation that IFSCA is clearly intending to build upon.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The message from IFSCA is clear: GIFT IFSC is being built not just as a place to book transactions, but as a full-service financial centre with the institutional infrastructure to match. The TCSP framework is another piece of that architecture clicking into place.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>This article is based on the IFSCA (TechFin and Ancillary Services) (Amendment) Regulations, 2026 published in the Gazette of India on May 7, 2026 (F. No. IFSCA/GN/2026/008). It is intended for informational purposes and does not constitute legal or regulatory advice. For specific structuring or compliance queries, please consult a qualified advisor with IFSC expertise.</em></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>About the Author</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Prashant Kumar is a Company Secretary, Published Author, and seasoned professional in corporate and financial services regulation. He currently serves as Company Secretary and Compliance Officer at Global Horizons Capital Advisors (IFSC) Private Limited, an IFSCA-licensed Investment Banker based in GIFT City, with direct, on-ground exposure to capital market transactions and regulatory structuring within the IFSC ecosystem.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>He brings hands-on experience in IPOs, direct listings, and exchange listings, along with deep expertise in GIFT IFSC structuring, fund setup across FME and AIF frameworks, corporate governance, and regulatory compliance. He regularly advises fund managers, startups, and institutions on building globally aligned, execution-ready structures within the GIFT IFSC framework.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>His current role at an IFSCA-licensed entity in GIFT City gives him direct working familiarity with the regulatory environment, the IFSCA registration process, and the practical compliance requirements that govern financial services activity within the IFSC — including the setup and ongoing governance of leasing structures for aircraft and ships.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>If you are evaluating a GIFT IFSC aircraft or ship leasing structure — whether at the pre-incorporation stage, mid-setup, or for compliance review of an existing entity — Prashant Kumar and the team at Global Horizons Capital Advisors are positioned to provide structured, regulation-grounded advisory on the complete setup process, from entity incorporation and DC Letter of Approval through IFSCA registration, sector-specific clearances, and tax election under Section 147 of the Income Tax Act, 2025.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For professional discussions on GIFT IFSC leasing structures, fund setup, IPOs, listings, and regulatory strategy, he can be reached at +91 9821008011 or&nbsp;<a href=\"mailto:prashant.kumar@global-horizons.in\">prashant.kumar@global-horizons.in</a>.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->",

          "title": "The Social Security (Central) Rules, 2026: A Complete Guide for Employers, HR Heads &amp; Founders",
          "link": "https://csatwork.in/social-security-central-rules-2026-guide-employers-india/",
          "pubDate": "Sun, 24 May 2026 17:11:19 +0000",
          "dc:creator": "prashantmishra1986",
          "guid": {
            "#text": "https://csatwork.in/?p=32075",

          "description": null,
          "content:encoded": "<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>By CS Prashant Kumar | </strong>Company Secretary &amp; Compliance Officer | Global Horizons Capital Advisors (IFSC) Private Ltd</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>On 8 May 2026, the Ministry of Labour &amp; Employment notified the Social Security (Central) Rules, 2026 — finally bringing the Code on Social Security, 2020 to life. Twelve old laws have been replaced. Gig workers are now formally inside the social security net. Crèche obligations have expanded. Gratuity rules have quietly changed for fixed-term staff. Here is everything in the new Rules, explained in plain English — with my notes on what each part actually means for your business.</em></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">First, the big picture: what just changed and why it matters</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Think of it this way. For nearly a century, India's labour welfare laws lived in twelve separate rulebooks — one for ESI, one for gratuity, one for the old Employee's Compensation Act of 1923, one for the BOCW cess, and so on. Each had its own forms, its own registers, its own deadlines, and its own inspector. Anyone running a business knew the frustration: comply with one, you still had nine more to worry about.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The Code on Social Security, 2020 was Parliament's attempt to fold all of that into one law. But a law needs operational rules to come alive, and those rules took six years to arrive. They have now arrived. The&nbsp;<strong>Social Security (Central) Rules, 2026</strong>, notified through Gazette S.O. 344(E), span&nbsp;<strong>14 chapters, 67 rules and 30 prescribed forms</strong>.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>My quick take:</strong>&nbsp;these Rules are better drafted than most of us in the profession expected. They are clearer than the Code itself in many places. And they are significantly more consequential than the press coverage has suggested. If you run a company in India — any size, any sector — at least three or four chapters here will require operational changes in the next ninety days.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Let me walk you through what each chapter says and what you should actually do about it.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter I — How registration now works</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Every establishment covered by the Code must register electronically on the&nbsp;<strong>Shram Suvidha Portal</strong>&nbsp;in&nbsp;<strong>Form-I</strong>. Your PAN and UAN are verified online at the point of submission. If the authority does not reject your application within seven days, registration is&nbsp;<strong>deemed granted</strong>&nbsp;— the certificate is issued automatically.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>You must also keep your registration current. Any change in particulars — a new address, a change in directors, a switch in nature of business — must be updated within&nbsp;<strong>30 days</strong>. Cancellation of registration is permitted only after all dues are paid and self-certified.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What this means in practice:</strong>&nbsp;the era of running between four different labour offices to get four different certificates is over. One portal, one form, one window. The seven-day deemed-approval clock is genuinely useful — keep evidence of submission carefully, because if the authority misses the deadline, you have a valid registration whether or not you receive a physical certificate. I would also recommend a monthly internal review of establishment data so the 30-day update obligation is never missed.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter II — Who runs these social security organisations</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This chapter governs the four main statutory bodies under the Code: the Central Board (which runs the EPF), the ESIC, the National Social Security Board, and the Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Boards.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Trustees of the Central Board hold office for&nbsp;<strong>four years</strong>; Executive Committee members for&nbsp;<strong>two years</strong>. Members are capped at a maximum of two terms. Vacancies are filled through elections among employer and employee representatives.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Plain take:</strong>&nbsp;this is governance plumbing. For most employers, it does not directly affect day-to-day compliance. But it is useful to know that the people taking decisions on EPF investments, ESIC fund allocation and welfare board priorities have defined terms and are partly elected by industry — which means industry associations have a genuine seat at the table if they choose to use it.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>📲&nbsp;<strong>Stay updated in real-time</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The labour codes are still rolling out. New clarifications, FAQs from the Ministry, state-level adaptations and procedural circulars will follow over the coming months. For real-time updates and practitioner notes on the Social Security (Central) Rules, 2026 — and on GIFT IFSC, SEBI, MCA and other regulatory developments — join my WhatsApp channel:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><a href=\"https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VbCuVOFJf05ex3adUF1I\" data-type=\"link\" data-id=\"https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VbCuVOFJf05ex3adUF1I\">Join my WhatsAPP Channel Here</a></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter III — Appeals before the EPF Tribunal</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>If you are an employer and the EPFO determines you owe a sum under Section 125 of the Code, you can appeal — but the Rules now require:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>A filing fee of ₹2,000</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>A 25% pre-deposit</strong> of the disputed amount before the appeal is admitted</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>My honest opinion:</strong>&nbsp;the 25% pre-deposit is the more important number. The government has, in effect, said: if you want to dispute an EPFO order, you must put some skin in the game. This is the same playbook used in GST and customs appeals, and the goal is to compress the volume of frivolous litigation that has historically clogged the tribunal. For a genuine dispute it is still worth appealing. For a borderline case it changes the calculus — the working-capital cost of the pre-deposit may push more matters into negotiated settlement, which is probably what the government wants.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter IV — ESIC, simplified</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The ESIC framework continues largely as before, with three meaningful modernisations:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list {\"ordered\":true} -->\n<ol class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The <strong>Director General</strong> of ESIC has clearly defined powers over fund administration and benefit disbursement.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>ESIC investments are now aligned with <strong>Central Government investment guidelines</strong> — meaning the fund must follow the same prudential rules as other public welfare corpora.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Most importantly for insured workers: a <strong>mandatory annual medical examination for insured persons aged 40 and above</strong>. This is preventive screening, free of cost, and is intended to catch lifestyle diseases — diabetes, hypertension, cardiac risk — early.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>My take:</strong>&nbsp;the 40+ annual medical examination is a quiet but genuinely good policy. For a workforce that has historically only engaged with the ESIC system when something has already gone wrong, building in routine preventive care is overdue. HR teams should publicise this benefit internally; my experience is that most ESI-covered employees do not realise this entitlement exists.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter V — Gratuity (read this one twice)</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The gratuity chapter contains the single most under-discussed change in the entire Rules.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For&nbsp;<strong>regular employees</strong>, the rules are familiar:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Form-III nomination, now requiring the <strong>Aadhaar of the nominee</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The employer must respond to a gratuity claim in <strong>15 days</strong> and pay within <strong>30 days</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Payment is permitted only by <strong>demand draft or direct bank credit</strong> (no cash, no cheques anymore)</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>For minor nominees, the amount must be deposited in an SBI or nationalised bank term deposit until majority</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For&nbsp;<strong>fixed-term employees (FTEs)</strong>, the change is significant: gratuity now accrues from the&nbsp;<strong>completion of one year of service</strong>, not five years. And in the year of separation,&nbsp;<strong>six or more months of service rounds up to a full year</strong>.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Why this matters — and what to do about it:</strong>&nbsp;for decades, the five-year continuous service threshold has been the unspoken reason why a great deal of Indian employment is structured on 11-month or 12-month renewable contracts. Companies that have built their workforces on FTE structures — IT services, ITeS, retail and quick-commerce, BFSI back-offices, electronics assembly, auto components — are now carrying a gratuity liability they have historically not provisioned for.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>I would suggest three immediate steps for any company with a meaningful FTE base:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Instruct your actuary</strong> to recompute the gratuity liability on the new year-one basis. This is not a wait-and-watch matter; your auditors will ask in the next quarter.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Audit your contracts</strong> to identify which FTEs now trigger accrual. Some renewal patterns that were previously safe — repeated 11-month contracts — now compound against you because of the six-month rounding rule.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Refresh your nomination database.</strong> Pull the Aadhaar of every nominee. The day you actually need a nomination — typically when an employee passes away in service — is the worst time to discover it is unenforceable.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:gallery {\"linkTo\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-gallery has-nested-images columns-default is-cropped\"><!-- wp:image {\"id\":32078,\"sizeSlug\":\"large\",\"linkDestination\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image size-large\"><img src=\"https://csatwork.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/fte-gratuity-social-security-rules-2026-1024x576.png\" alt=\"\" class=\"wp-image-32078\"/></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image --></figure>\n<!-- /wp:gallery -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter VI — Maternity benefits, with the crèche rule that has expanded</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This chapter standardises maternity certification, nursing breaks and crèche obligations across all sectors — not just factories.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Key thresholds:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Crèche is now mandatory for <strong>any establishment with 50 or more employees</strong> (not 50 women employees — any 50 employees)</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Located <strong>within 1 km</strong> of the workplace (relaxable in industrial parks and clusters)</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Minimum <strong>10 sq ft of floor area per child</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>A trained woman-in-charge plus <strong>one ayah for every ten children</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Operating hours must match the workplace's working hours, including shifts</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Nursing mothers are entitled to <strong>two breaks of 15 minutes each</strong>, plus up to 15 minutes of travel time per break</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>My take:</strong>&nbsp;the Maternity Benefit Act, 2017 already required this for \"every establishment having fifty or more employees\", but the design specifications were vague and enforcement was patchy. The Rules now make every parameter explicit. Many service-sector employers — IT campuses, BPOs, financial services back-offices — have historically interpreted the obligation loosely. I expect inspections to begin testing these specifications during FY 2027.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>If you are above the 50-employee threshold and do not currently provide a crèche, this is a Q3 priority, not a \"we will get to it\" item. The cleanest solutions I have seen are tie-ups with professional crèche operators (Klay, Founding Years, Little Elly are the main organised players); building in-house is rarely cost-effective unless you have multiple thousand employees on one campus.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter VII — BOCW cess: how construction projects are now assessed</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess regime has been restructured for clarity:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Cess is <strong>self-assessed by a chartered engineer</strong> at the commencement of the project</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>For government and public-sector projects, cess is <strong>deducted at source</strong> by the contracting authority</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Collected cess must be transferred to the relevant <strong>State Welfare Board within 30 days</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Plain take:</strong>&nbsp;the self-assessment-by-chartered-engineer model is a workable improvement. It moves the cess determination away from a slow case-by-case authority review to a professional certification model, similar to how project costs are audited for income tax. Real-estate developers and infrastructure contractors should ensure their chartered engineer's assessment certificates are properly maintained — that is the document the welfare board will ask for in any future scrutiny.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter VIII — Gig workers and aggregators (the chapter that will reshape the platform economy)</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is the headline chapter, and it deserves to be understood properly.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For the first time, India has operational rules governing the relationship between platform aggregators — Ola, Uber, Zomato, Swiggy, Urban Company, Zepto, Blinkit, Rapido, Porter, and every comparable platform — and the gig and platform workers they engage.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What every aggregator must do:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Within 45 days</strong> of these Rules coming into force, share gig and platform worker details with the designated portal via API for UAN generation</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>New worker onboarding and exit reporting must be transmitted in <strong>real time</strong> (or at minimum, daily) via API</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Contribute <strong>between 1% and 2% of turnover</strong> to the Social Security Fund, capped at <strong>5% of total payouts to gig and platform workers</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>File the <strong>provisional contribution in Form-XX by 30 June</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>File the <strong>final return in Form-XXI by 31 October</strong>, after statutory audit under the Income-Tax Act 2025, Companies Act 2013, or LLP Act 2008 as applicable</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Default in contribution attracts <strong>1% interest per month</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The captive structure trap</strong>&nbsp;is critical. Many platforms have, over the years, parked workers in associate companies, holding companies, subsidiaries, vendor LLPs and third-party manpower agencies — partly for tax efficiency, partly for labour-law cushioning. The new Rules expressly extend the 5% computation to workers engaged through any of these arrangements. The denominator is unified. Restructuring will not save you.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:gallery {\"linkTo\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-gallery has-nested-images columns-default is-cropped\"><!-- wp:image {\"id\":32079,\"sizeSlug\":\"large\",\"linkDestination\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image size-large\"><img src=\"https://csatwork.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/fte-gratuity-social-security-rules-2026-2-1024x576.png\" alt=\"\" class=\"wp-image-32079\"/></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image --></figure>\n<!-- /wp:gallery -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>When does a gig worker become eligible for benefits?</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The worker must have been engaged for:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>At least 90 days with a single aggregator</strong>, OR</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>At least 120 days across multiple aggregators</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>…in the preceding financial year. A \"day\" is any calendar day on which the worker earned income from the aggregator, regardless of amount. Working with three aggregators on one calendar day counts as three engagement days. Benefits cease at age sixty.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>My honest view:</strong>&nbsp;this chapter is a watershed. The 1-2% turnover contribution sounds small on paper but for unicorn-scale food delivery and ride-hailing platforms operating on thin or negative contribution margins, it is a real number that will need to be priced into unit economics. The captive-structure trap is well drafted and closes a loophole that several large platforms have quietly relied on. The 90/120 day eligibility threshold is, in my reading, deliberately calibrated to capture genuine platform-dependent workers — the full-time delivery executive, the full-time driver — while excluding genuinely casual side-income earners. It is a defensible policy line.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>If you run a platform business, this is the chapter that should be on your CEO's desk this week. The 45-day API integration window is tight. Most aggregators will need external technology support to build the data pipeline; that procurement decision needs to be made now.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter IX — Finance, accounts and write-offs</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This chapter governs how the various welfare funds are administered financially.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Two points worth knowing:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Dues that are <strong>irrecoverable</strong> can be written off where the establishment has been closed for more than <strong>five years</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>ESIC accounts are subject to <strong>CAG audit</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Plain take:</strong>&nbsp;this is mostly internal financial-administration plumbing. For employers, the only practical implication is that you should not assume historical EPF or ESI dues will quietly disappear — the five-year-closure threshold for write-off is genuinely tight, and active or recently-active establishments will continue to face recovery action on legacy dues.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter X — Records, registers and the unified annual return</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This chapter is small in length but large in operational impact.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>All registers must now be maintained <strong>electronically</strong>, in a format consistent with the Wages (Central) Rules, 2026</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Five-year retention</strong> of all records and registers</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The legacy multiplicity of annual returns under EPF, ESI, Maternity Benefit and BOCW is replaced by a <strong>single unified annual return in Form-XXIII</strong>, due by <strong>28 (or 29) February</strong> each year</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>My take:</strong>&nbsp;this is the chapter that genuinely simplifies life for compliance teams. One return, one deadline, one format. If your organisation is still running paper-based attendance, wage and contribution registers, this is the time to migrate. Several HR-tech platforms (Keka, Darwinbox, GreytHR) are already updating their compliance modules for Form-XXIII; the migration should not take more than a quarter for most mid-sized employers.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter XI — Offences and compounding</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Where a violation can be compounded, the compounding notice is now issued&nbsp;<strong>electronically in Form-XXIV</strong>, and the compounded amount must be&nbsp;<strong>deposited within 15 days</strong>.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Plain take:</strong>&nbsp;electronic compounding is faster and more transparent than the old paper-based regime. The 15-day deposit window is firm — missing it converts a compoundable matter back into a prosecutable one. Compliance officers should set up internal alerts for any compounding notice received, with escalation if the deposit is not actioned within seven days.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter XII — Career Centres and vacancy reporting</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The old Employment Exchanges framework has been replaced by&nbsp;<strong>Career Centres</strong>. The notable change: private establishments with&nbsp;<strong>20 or more employees</strong>&nbsp;must now report vacancies, with unique vacancy reporting numbers issued in&nbsp;<strong>three working days</strong>&nbsp;(seven in the North-Eastern States).</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>My take:</strong>&nbsp;the 20-employee threshold is genuinely low and catches a wide swathe of mid-sized Indian companies that have previously had no employment-reporting obligation at all. This is not a heavy procedural burden, but it does mean that for the first time, mid-sized private employment data will flow systematically to the central authority. Over time, this data will feed into sectoral wage and employment analytics. Compliance teams should not dismiss this as a formality — set up an internal workflow that routes every new vacancy through the Career Centre reporting portal before posting it on job boards.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter XIII — Employee's Compensation</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>If you delay paying compensation due to an injured employee or their dependants beyond&nbsp;<strong>30 days</strong>, you owe&nbsp;<strong>12% per annum simple interest</strong>&nbsp;on the unpaid amount.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The chapter also provides a mechanism for the cross-border transfer of compensation to dependants residing outside India — a useful provision for organisations with expatriate workforces or for dependants of Indian workers in international postings.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Plain take:</strong>&nbsp;the 12% interest number is meaningful. For a company that delays a substantial compensation payout by a year, the interest cost alone can exceed the legal fee for handling the matter properly in the first place. Process discipline here directly protects the bottom line.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter XIV — Miscellaneous: the Social Security Fund and exemptions</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This final chapter governs the Social Security Fund (which receives aggregator contributions and other earmarked moneys) and the exemption mechanism under Section 143 of the Code.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The exemption bar is high.</strong>&nbsp;An establishment seeking exemption from EPF and other welfare obligations on the ground that it operates substantially similar or superior schemes must now demonstrate:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>A <strong>three-year compliance history</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>At least <strong>500 contributing members</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>A <strong>corpus of ₹50 crore</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Positive net worth for the three preceding years</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Full Aadhaar seeding</strong> of all members</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>My take:</strong>&nbsp;these thresholds are deliberately stringent. They effectively close the exemption route for all but the largest legacy private-sector schemes — typically those of public-sector undertakings, large banks and a handful of conglomerates with their own provident fund trusts. The policy direction is unambiguous: the government wants money in the central Social Security Fund, not in fragmented private trusts. If you are presently operating under an exemption, expect renewed scrutiny on whether you continue to meet the new thresholds.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">The cross-cutting themes (the patterns to internalise)</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Stepping back from chapter-by-chapter detail, four patterns run through the Rules that define the texture of the new regime.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Digital-first is no longer optional.</strong>&nbsp;Almost every interaction with the regulator — registration, returns, nominations, compounding, appeals, vacancy reporting — is now mandatorily electronic, with the Shram Suvidha Portal as the central pipe. If your compliance workflow still depends on physical filings, plan the migration this quarter.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Aadhaar has become structural.</strong>&nbsp;Every welfare benefit nomination requires Aadhaar. Every exemption application requires Aadhaar seeding. Old debates about Aadhaar's role in welfare have effectively been settled in favour of universal seeding.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Deemed approvals are a real procedural tool.</strong>&nbsp;Seven days for registration, sixty days for certain exemption decisions. If the authority does not act, the applicant gets the benefit. Use it — keep clean evidence of submission timestamps, because if a clock runs out in your favour, that document is your shield.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Inter-statute integration is accelerating.</strong>&nbsp;The aggregator audit linkage to the Income-Tax Act, 2025 is a small but telling detail. The era of treating labour, tax and corporate compliance as separate silos is closing. Expect the next round of rules — under the other three labour codes, which are also in pipeline — to push this integration further.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">The compliance calendar in one place</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:table -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-table\"><table class=\"has-fixed-layout\"><thead><tr><th>Trigger</th><th>Deadline</th><th>Action</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Change in establishment particulars</td><td>30 days</td><td>Update on Shram Suvidha Portal</td></tr><tr><td>Aggregator API onboarding (one-time)</td><td>45 days from notification</td><td>Share worker data via API</td></tr><tr><td>Aggregator provisional contribution</td><td>30 June</td><td>File Form-XX</td></tr><tr><td>Aggregator final return</td><td>31 October</td><td>File Form-XXI</td></tr><tr><td>Unified annual return</td><td>28 / 29 February</td><td>File Form-XXIII</td></tr><tr><td>Gratuity claim response</td><td>15 days</td><td>Respond to claimant</td></tr><tr><td>Gratuity payment</td><td>30 days</td><td>Pay via DD or bank credit</td></tr><tr><td>Compounding deposit</td><td>15 days from notice</td><td>Pay compounded amount</td></tr><tr><td>Records retention</td><td>5 years</td><td>Maintain electronically</td></tr><tr><td>Delayed employee's compensation</td><td>Beyond 30 days</td><td>12% p.a. simple interest</td></tr><tr><td>Aggregator contribution default</td><td>Per month</td><td>1% interest per month</td></tr></tbody></table></figure>\n<!-- /wp:table -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Three questions every board should ask this quarter</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For senior management and audit committees now reviewing the impact of these Rules, three questions cut to the heart of likely exposure.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>On gratuity:</strong>&nbsp;have we recomputed our gratuity liability assuming year-one accrual for fixed-term employees? Is the increased actuarial provision reflected in the next financial statements? Have nomination records been refreshed with Aadhaar?</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>On platform exposure:</strong>&nbsp;if our business model depends on gig or platform workers — directly or through any group entity — are we ready in 45 days? Is the API integration scoped and resourced? Have we modelled the 1-2% turnover contribution against current EBITDA?</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>On operational readiness:</strong>&nbsp;are our registrations, returns and registers ready for migration to the unified electronic regime? Do our HR policies on crèche, maternity, nursing breaks and vacancy reporting reflect the new thresholds? Do we know which legacy filings disappear and which replace them?</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:gallery {\"linkTo\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-gallery has-nested-images columns-default is-cropped\"><!-- wp:image {\"id\":32080,\"sizeSlug\":\"large\",\"linkDestination\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image size-large\"><img src=\"https://csatwork.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/fte-gratuity-social-security-rules-2026-3-1024x576.png\" alt=\"\" class=\"wp-image-32080\"/></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image --></figure>\n<!-- /wp:gallery -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">The bottom line</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The Social Security (Central) Rules, 2026 are the largest single consolidation of Indian labour welfare law since Independence. For most employers, the procedural changes are manageable — provided they are actioned in time. For employers with large fixed-term workforces, the gratuity exposure is real and largely unprovisioned. For aggregators, the 45-day clock has already started.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>These Rules reward those who move first. The cost of inaction is now measurable — in interest, in actuarial provisions, in deferred audit qualifications, and in reputational risk.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The Code is no longer theoretical. The Rules are here. The compliance calendar has begun.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>About the Author</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Prashant Kumar is a Company Secretary, Published Author, and seasoned professional in corporate and financial services regulation.
