          "title": "The Code on Wages (Central) Rules, 2026: A Complete Guide for Employers, HR Heads &amp; Founders",
          "link": "https://csatwork.in/code-on-wages-central-rules-2026-india/",
          "pubDate": "Mon, 25 May 2026 05:45:41 +0000",
          "dc:creator": "prashantmishra1986",
          "guid": {
            "#text": "https://csatwork.in/?p=32082",
            "@attributes": {
              "isPermaLink": "false"
            }
          },
          "description": null,
          "content:encoded": "<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">CS PRASHANT KUMAR | Company Secretary &amp; Compliance Officer | Global Horizons Capital Advisors (IFSC) Private Ltd</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>On 8 May 2026, the Ministry of Labour &amp; Employment notified the Code on Wages (Central) Rules, 2026 — finally bringing the Code on Wages, 2019 to life. Seventeen old laws have been replaced. Minimum wage calculation has been standardised. The bonus framework now applies across every covered establishment. Disciplinary deductions follow a strict 7-day / 15-day procedural code. And appeals against wage claims now require a 100% pre-deposit. Here is everything in the new Rules, explained in plain English — with my notes on what each part actually means for your business.</em></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">First, the big picture: what just changed and why it matters</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For nearly ninety years, India's wage administration sat across at least four separate statutes — the Payment of Wages Act of 1936, the Minimum Wages Act of 1948, the Payment of Bonus Act of 1965, and the Equal Remuneration Act of 1976 — each with its own rules, its own forms, its own registers, and its own inspector. Compliance was scattered. Litigation was fragmented. And the same wage dispute could move through multiple authorities depending on which Act it came under.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The Code on Wages, 2019 was Parliament's first attempt at unifying all of this into a single statute. But a law needs operational rules to come alive, and those rules took seven years to arrive. They have now arrived. The&nbsp;<strong>Code on Wages (Central) Rules, 2026</strong>, notified through Gazette S.O. 343(E), span&nbsp;<strong>8 chapters, 54 rules, 9 forms and 4 appendices</strong>.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is the second labour code to come into force in 2026 (the Social Security Rules were notified the same day). The Industrial Relations Code and the Occupational Safety, Health &amp; Working Conditions Code are next.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>My quick take:</strong>&nbsp;these Rules do something the four parent Acts never managed in 90 years — they create a single, unified compliance framework for wage administration in India. The most consequential design choices are not in the headline-grabbing minimum wage chapter but in the procedural chapters: the 100% pre-deposit on employer wage-claim appeals, the 7-day / 15-day disciplinary framework, and the unified employee register that now sits across multiple labour codes. If you run a business in India, at least four chapters here will require operational changes in the next 90 days.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Let me walk you through what each chapter says and what you should actually do about it.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter I — How the Rules define the playing field</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The opening chapter establishes scope and definitions. Two things deserve attention.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>First, the definition of&nbsp;<strong>\"electronically\"</strong>&nbsp;has been deliberately expanded. It now covers email, designated portals, mobile applications, websites, and any digital payment mode. This is not casual drafting — it is the statutory basis for the entire Code being administered through electronic compliance.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Second, the Rules introduce a&nbsp;<strong>four-tier skill classification</strong>&nbsp;— highly skilled, skilled, semi-skilled, and unskilled — that anchors minimum wage fixation throughout the Code. Each tier has a specific definition tied to training, experience, judgment, and supervisory requirements.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What this means in practice:</strong>&nbsp;every employee in your organisation now needs to be tagged into one of these four skill tiers in your HR records. This is not a nominal exercise — minimum wage notifications, bonus computations, and overtime calculations will reference these tiers going forward. If your job descriptions are still vague or your skill classifications are inconsistent across departments, this is a Q3 priority. I would also recommend documenting the basis on which each tier is assigned, because skill-classification disputes are likely to become a fresh head of wage litigation over the next two years.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter II — How minimum wages are now calculated</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This chapter is the operational heart of the Code on Wages. It standardises minimum wage computation across the country in a way no previous statute managed.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The basics:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Minimum wages are fixed on a <strong>daily basis</strong>, with detailed criteria notified separately by the Central Government</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Daily rate ÷ 8</strong> = hourly rate</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Daily rate × 26</strong> = monthly rate</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Rounding works in the employee's favour: halves and above round up, below half drops</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Central Government employees are expressly excluded</strong> — they continue under their existing pay scales</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The variable dearness allowance (VDA):</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Revised <strong>twice every year</strong> — before 1 April and before 1 October</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Computed by reference to the Average Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers, published by the Labour Bureau, Ministry of Labour &amp; Employment</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Working hours and rest:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Normal working day = <strong>8 hours</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Weekly cap = <strong>48 hours</strong>, regardless of how many days are worked</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>One weekly rest day mandatory — Sunday in a six-day week; Saturday + Sunday in shorter weeks</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The employer can substitute the rest day, but <strong>no more than 10 consecutive working days are permitted without a rest day</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Work performed on a rest day must be paid at <strong>overtime rate (minimum twice the normal wage)</strong> plus a substituted rest day at normal rate</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Night shifts that extend past midnight are treated specially — the rest day clock starts when the shift ends</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>My take:</strong>&nbsp;the 48-hour weekly cap is the headline number for HR teams to internalise. It is more permissive than the 40-hour cap that some states had been moving toward, and it formally enables traditional six-day workweeks at eight hours each — which still characterises most of India's organised manufacturing, retail, BFSI back-office, and services sectors.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The 10-consecutive-days rule is the new compliance trap. Any shift roster that pushes an employee through more than ten working days without a rest day is now expressly non-compliant, even if the employee is paid overtime. For sectors that run continuous operations — IT/ITeS night shifts, manufacturing campaigns, retail festive seasons, hospitality, healthcare — this requires a roster audit. I have already seen draft rosters in client organisations that violate this rule without anyone realising it.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The twice-yearly VDA revision is also new. Most payroll systems are configured to update minimum wages annually on Central Government notification. From now, the April and October dates are hard. Build them into your payroll calendar as recurring events, not as discretionary updates.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter III — The national floor wage</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This chapter is short but politically significant. The&nbsp;<strong>Central Government will fix a national floor wage</strong>&nbsp;in consultation with the Central Advisory Board and State Governments, taking into account food, clothing, housing, and minimum living standard.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The floor wage is reviewed&nbsp;<strong>every five years</strong>, with periodic adjustments for cost-of-living variations.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Plain take:</strong>&nbsp;the floor wage sets a national baseline below which no State can fix its own minimum wage. For employers operating across multiple states, this introduces a measure of standardisation that has been politically debated since the Code was passed in 2019.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The actual floor wage number is not in these Rules — it will be notified separately. When it is announced, the impact will fall hardest on states that currently have minimum wages below the new floor. For multi-state employers — particularly retail chains, logistics, hospitality, and manufacturing with plants in lower-wage states — this could mean an immediate wage bill increase in select locations. Run a state-wise minimum wage gap analysis now, so that when the floor wage is notified you have your exposure quantified within 48 hours.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter IV — Payment of wages and the new disciplinary framework</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is the chapter most HR practitioners will spend the most time with, because it governs the day-to-day mechanics of wage administration and disciplinary deductions.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>For contractual employees:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Where workers are employed through a contractor, the&nbsp;<strong>principal employer (the company, firm, or association that owns the establishment) must pay the contractor</strong>&nbsp;the wage amount due, and the contractor pays the workers. If the contractor defaults, the principal employer steps in. The legal exposure does not vanish by routing employment through a vendor — a principle that has been reaffirmed across the new labour codes.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The 50% deduction cap:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Total authorised deductions cannot exceed&nbsp;<strong>50% of an employee's wages in any wage period</strong>. Where deductions exceed this cap, the excess is carried forward to the next wage period — but again subject to the same 50% cap on that month's wages. In effect, no single month can ever see more than half of the wage absorbed by deductions.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The 7-day / 15-day disciplinary framework:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Whether the employer is imposing a fine, making a deduction for absence from duty, or deducting for damage or loss, the procedure is now identical:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The employer must give <strong>electronic or written notice</strong> specifying the act or omission</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The employee has <strong>7 days</strong> to respond with cause</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>If charges are established, the fine or deduction is imposed</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The employee must be <strong>intimated within 15 days</strong> of imposition</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The notice listing acts and omissions for which fines can be levied must be&nbsp;<strong>displayed in Hindi, English and the local language</strong>&nbsp;at a conspicuous place in the workplace, AND a copy sent to the Inspector-cum-Facilitator having jurisdiction.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The \"approving authority\" for fines under Section 19 of the Code is the&nbsp;<strong>Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner (Central)</strong>of the jurisdiction.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Recovery of advances and loans:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Recovery of any advance or loan in instalments cannot push total deductions in any wage period beyond the 50% cap. Recoverable interest on loans follows Central Government guidelines issued from time to time.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>My take:</strong>&nbsp;the 7-day notice and 15-day intimation framework is non-negotiable due process. Every disciplinary deduction in your payroll system must now flow through this gate. Skipping the notice, missing the 7-day window, or failing to intimate within 15 days will make the deduction challengeable — and in my experience, employees who do challenge such deductions tend to recover not just the disputed amount but interest and procedural costs.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For HR teams, I would suggest three immediate steps:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Build the 7-day / 15-day timeline into your HR information system as automated workflow gates. No fine or deduction should be capable of being processed in payroll without these checkpoints clearing.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Audit your existing list of \"acts and omissions\" for which fines are imposed. It must be displayed in three languages and registered with the Inspector-cum-Facilitator. Most workplaces I have seen still display this only in English.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Update employee contracts and HR policy manuals to reflect the new disciplinary procedure. The Code does not grandfather old procedures — every disciplinary action from notification date onward must follow the new framework.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter V — Bonus, set-on, set-off, and the new universal application</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The bonus chapter retains the substance of the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965, but extends it operationally to every covered establishment under the Code.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>For contractual workers:</strong>&nbsp;if a contractor fails to pay bonus due under Section 26, the&nbsp;<strong>principal employer must pay the minimum bonus</strong>&nbsp;on written notice from the workers or their registered trade union.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The set-on / set-off mechanism:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>If allocable surplus in any year&nbsp;<strong>exceeds the maximum bonus</strong>&nbsp;(20% of wages):</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The excess is <strong>set on</strong> — carried forward to the next year</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Capped at 20% of the total wage bill in the carrying year</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Available for the next <strong>4 accounting years</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>If allocable surplus&nbsp;<strong>falls short of the minimum bonus</strong>&nbsp;(8.33%):</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The shortfall is <strong>set off</strong> — carried forward</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Same 4-year window</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Used to top up minimum bonus in deficit years</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Appendix A</strong>&nbsp;illustrates this with a worked 10-year example. Appendix B and C set out the gross profit computation methodology — separately for&nbsp;<strong>banking companies (Appendix B)</strong>&nbsp;and&nbsp;<strong>all other establishments (Appendix C)</strong>. Appendix D lists the&nbsp;<strong>prior charges</strong>&nbsp;to be deducted from gross profit before bonus computation, including preference dividends, 8.5% of paid-up capital, 6% of reserves, and so on, varying by employer category.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>My take:</strong>&nbsp;the substantive bonus mechanism is unchanged — anyone who has computed bonus under the 1965 Act will find familiar territory in Appendices A through D. What is genuinely new is the&nbsp;<strong>scope of application</strong>. Under the old Act, the bonus obligation was largely confined to establishments with twenty or more employees. The Code on Wages broadens this materially.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For mid-sized employers who have historically been outside the bonus net, this is now a fresh annual compliance and a fresh financial liability. The 8.33% minimum bonus on the wage base of an excluded mid-sized workforce can run into significant rupee numbers. I would suggest two immediate steps:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Run the Appendix C gross profit calculation on your last three years of financial statements to understand the baseline. If your allocable surplus has been negative or thin, set-off planning matters.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Build the bonus computation into your annual financial close process. Several mid-sized employers historically computed bonus only when challenged. The new framework leaves no room for that approach.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter VI — The Central Advisory Board, in brief</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This chapter governs the constitution and functioning of the Central Advisory Board that advises the government on minimum wage and equal remuneration matters.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Key features worth knowing:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>3-year terms</strong> for members, capped at two terms</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Quorum</strong> = one-third of members, with <strong>at least one representative each from employers and employees</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Meetings called with <strong>15 days' notice</strong> (7 days for emergencies)</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Decisions by majority; Chairperson holds the casting vote</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Decisions by circulation require <strong>two-thirds majority</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Disqualification grounds: unsound mind, undischarged insolvency, or conviction involving moral turpitude</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Plain take:</strong>&nbsp;governance plumbing. Directly relevant only to industry associations and trade unions that nominate Board members or engage with its consultations. For most employers, the practical relevance is that the Board is the channel through which industry can shape minimum wage and floor wage decisions. If your industry association has a Board seat, use it.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter VII — Nominations, undisbursed dues, and the death-in-service workflow</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This chapter deals with what happens when an employee passes away or cannot be traced and wages remain undisbursed. It is administratively important and procedurally strict.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The nomination framework (Rule 45):</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Every employee must file a&nbsp;<strong>Form-VII nomination</strong>&nbsp;designating who receives undisbursed dues on their death. The rules are clear:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>If the employee has a family, the nomination must be in favour of the <strong>spouse, or the spouse along with one or more family members</strong> — a nomination outside the family is invalid where a family exists</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>A fresh nomination is required after marriage</strong> — any nomination made before marriage is deemed invalid once marriage occurs</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>For minor nominees, the employee can appoint a guardian within the family</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Multiple nominees must have specified shares totalling 100% of the dues</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>If dues remain undisbursed:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Unpaid for <strong>3 months after death</strong> or because the employee's whereabouts are unknown → the employer must deposit the amount with the <strong>Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner (Central)</strong> of jurisdiction</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The DCLC has <strong>2 months</strong> to identify the nominee and disburse</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Unpaid for <strong>6 months</strong> for any other reason → also deposited with the DCLC, within 15 days of the end of that 6-month period</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Deposits must be made by <strong>bank transfer or crossed demand draft</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The DCLC publishes notice in <strong>two local newspapers in the vernacular</strong> of the work area AND <strong>two local newspapers in the vernacular of the employee's home area</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>If the deposit remains unclaimed for <strong>7 years</strong>, it is dealt with as the Central Government directs</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>My take:</strong>&nbsp;the nomination database is the under-recognised compliance risk in most Indian organisations. Two checkpoints HR teams must build in:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>A fresh-nomination workflow on marriage.</strong> Most HRMS platforms do not currently flag this. When an employee updates marital status, the system should automatically prompt for a refreshed Form-VII. This single workflow change closes the largest practical gap most employers have on this Rule.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Automated tracking of the 3-month and 6-month deposit clocks.</strong> Once dues become payable after death, the clock starts running. The employer's obligation to deposit with the DCLC is unconditional after 3 months for death cases and 6 months otherwise. Missing this is not a paperwork issue — it is a statutory default.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The vernacular-newspaper notification requirement is also worth flagging to clients with employees from multiple language regions. The DCLC handles the notification, but the employer's deposit obligation includes furnishing accurate home-address information to enable it.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Chapter VIII — Forms, registers, wage slips, claims and compounding</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is the longest operational chapter and the one that defines daily compliance.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Registers every employer must maintain</strong>&nbsp;— electronically or in physical form:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Form-I — Employee Register</strong>: 36 fields covering identity, family, UAN, PAN, Aadhaar, EPS/NPS membership, ESIC IP number, bank details, nominee, posting history, photo, specimen signature, mark of identification, date and reason for exit</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Form-IV — Register of Wages, Overtime, Advances, Fines &amp; Deductions for Damage and Loss</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Form-IX — Attendance Register-cum-Muster Roll</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Retention:</strong>&nbsp;all registers must be preserved for&nbsp;<strong>5 years</strong>&nbsp;after the date of the last entry.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Wage slips</strong>&nbsp;must be issued on or before the wage payment date in&nbsp;<strong>Form-V</strong>, electronically or physically. Required fields cover basic, DA, allowances, attendance, overtime, gross wages, all deductions (PF, ESI, others), and net wages paid.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Returns</strong>&nbsp;are now filed electronically in the formats prescribed under the&nbsp;<strong>Occupational Safety, Health &amp; Working Conditions Code, 2020</strong>&nbsp;— so the wage return is unified with the OSH return. One filing covers both Codes.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Claims procedure (Rule 49):</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>A <strong>single application</strong> can be filed on behalf of multiple employees with similar claims relating to the same wage period or the same incident of discrimination</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Filed in <strong>Form-II</strong> before the authority under Section 45</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Notice to employer in <strong>Form-VIII</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Authority can decide <strong>ex-parte</strong> if the employer fails to appear</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>The application is dismissed if the applicant fails to appear without reasonable cause</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Appeals procedure (Rule 50):</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Filed in <strong>Form-III</strong> before the appellate authority</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>An employer's appeal is not admitted unless the full claim amount is deposited at the time of filing</strong></li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Same ex-parte / dismissal logic applies</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Compounding of offences (Rule 54):</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Application in <strong>Form-VI</strong> to the notified Gazetted Officer</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Composition amount = <strong>50% of the maximum fine</strong> prescribed for that offence under the Code</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Payment within <strong>30 days</strong> of the composition order</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Composition certificate issued within <strong>10 days</strong> of receipt of payment</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>If the accused fails to deposit within the specified time, prosecution proceeds before the competent court</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>My take:</strong>&nbsp;the&nbsp;<strong>100% pre-deposit</strong>&nbsp;rule on employer wage-claim appeals is the single most consequential procedural design in these Rules, and it is not getting the attention it deserves.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>In every other comparable Indian statute — GST, customs, EPF — the pre-deposit for an appeal sits somewhere between 7.5% and 25% of the disputed amount. The Code on Wages now requires the&nbsp;<strong>entire claim amount</strong>&nbsp;to be deposited before an appeal is even admitted. This will fundamentally change the economics of wage-claim litigation in India.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For employers, this means three things:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Every wage claim should be <strong>defended seriously at the authority stage</strong>, because the cost of losing and then appealing is now the full disputed amount tied up upfront.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Borderline claims should be <strong>settled rather than appealed</strong>, even where the employer believes the merits are on its side. The opportunity cost of capital is meaningful.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Internal payroll and disciplinary processes need to be <strong>bulletproof</strong> — because procedural defects (missed 7-day notice, missed 15-day intimation, missing wage slip) are now the easiest routes to a successful employee claim.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>I would also suggest that any organisation with open wage-claim litigation should re-evaluate its dispute strategy in light of this change. Cases that were worth taking up on appeal under the old 25%-style pre-deposit assumptions may not be worth it now.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">The cross-cutting themes practitioners should internalise</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Stepping back from the chapter-by-chapter detail, five patterns run through these Rules that define the new regime.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Digital-first by default.</strong>&nbsp;Almost every interaction — registration, returns, wage slips, nominations, claims, appeals, compounding — is now electronic. Physical alternatives are permitted but treated as the exception. The Shram Suvidha Portal is the central pipe.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Unified registers across the labour codes.</strong>&nbsp;Form-I (Employee Register), Form-IV (Wages Register), and Form-IX (Attendance Register) are now common across the Code on Wages, the Code on Social Security, and (when their rules come) the OSH and IR Codes. Payroll-software vendors are already updating their compliance modules. If your organisation maintains separate registers across statutes, consolidate now.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Skill-tier classification is now structural.</strong>&nbsp;Highly skilled / skilled / semi-skilled / unskilled is the basis for minimum wage fixation. Every employee record must be properly tagged. Inconsistent classification will become a fresh head of wage litigation over the next two years.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Twice-yearly VDA revision.</strong>&nbsp;April and October. Auto-update your payroll systems for these dates as recurring events, not as discretionary updates.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The 100% pre-deposit on employer wage appeals is a hard de-litigation tool.</strong>&nbsp;It will reshape how wage disputes are managed. Front-load your compliance discipline so disputes do not arise — because once a claim is filed and the authority rules against you, your appeal route is economically expensive.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">The compliance calendar in one place</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:table -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-table\"><table class=\"has-fixed-layout\"><thead><tr><th>Trigger</th><th>Deadline</th><th>Action</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>VDA revision</td><td>Before 1 April and 1 October each year</td><td>Recompute and update payroll</td></tr><tr><td>Show-cause notice for fine / deduction</td><td>7 days</td><td>Employee response window</td></tr><tr><td>Intimation of fine / deduction imposed</td><td>15 days from imposition</td><td>Notify employee electronically or in writing</td></tr><tr><td>Wage slip</td><td>On or before wage payment date</td><td>Issue in Form-V</td></tr><tr><td>Undisbursed dues on death of employee</td><td>3 months from due date</td><td>Deposit with DCLC (Central)</td></tr><tr><td>Undisbursed dues for any other reason</td><td>6 months from due date</td><td>Deposit with DCLC (Central)</td></tr><tr><td>Records retention</td><td>5 years from last entry</td><td>Preserve all registers</td></tr><tr><td>Composition of offence</td><td>30 days from order</td><td>Pay 50% of maximum fine</td></tr><tr><td>Composition certificate issued</td><td>10 days from payment</td><td>Form-VI Part B</td></tr><tr><td>Employer wage-claim appeal</td><td>At time of working days</td><td>10</td><td>Without a rest day</td></tr></tbody></table></figure>\n<!-- /wp:table -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:quote -->\n<blockquote class=\"wp-block-quote\"><!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>📲&nbsp;<strong>Stay updated in real-time</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The labour codes are still rolling out. New clarifications, FAQs from the Ministry, state-level adaptations, and the upcoming Industrial Relations and OSH Code rules will follow over the coming months. Have we tagged every employee record in Form-I with the correct skill tier? Are wage slips being issued in Form-V on or before the payment date — electronically or physically?</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>On disciplinary procedure:</strong>&nbsp;are the 7-day notice and 15-day intimation timelines built into our HR information system as hard gates? Is our list of fineable acts and omissions displayed in Hindi, English, and the local language at the workplace, and registered with the Inspector-cum-Facilitator? Have we trained line managers on the new procedural requirements?</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>On dispute strategy:</strong>&nbsp;are we prepared for the 100% pre-deposit rule on wage-claim appeals? Does this change how we approach our existing open wage disputes? Have we evaluated whether borderline matters should be settled rather than litigated under the new economics?</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">The bottom line</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The Code on Wages (Central) Rules, 2026 do something the four parent Acts never accomplished in 90 years: they create a single, unified compliance framework for wage administration in India. The headline change is consolidation, but the practical changes that will affect employers daily are procedural — the 7-day / 15-day disciplinary framework, the 100% pre-deposit on appeals, the twice-yearly VDA, the unified registers across labour codes, and the four-tier skill classification.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For most employers, the operational changes are manageable provided they are actioned in time. For employers running multi-state operations with complex shift rosters and fixed-term workforces, the scope of work is more substantial — and the deadlines are tight.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The Code on Wages is no longer a 2019 statute waiting for its rules. The Rules are here. The compliance calendar has begun.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>These Rules, taken together with the Social Security (Central) Rules, 2026 notified the same day, represent the largest single consolidation of Indian labour and wage law in modern memory. The two codes that remain — Industrial Relations, and Occupational Safety, Health &amp; Working Conditions — are next in the pipeline. The texture of the new regime, however, is already visible. It rewards employers who move first.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>About the Author</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Prashant Kumar is a Company Secretary, Published Author, and seasoned professional in corporate and financial services regulation.           "description": null,
          "content:encoded": "<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">A plain-language guide to the June 2026 IFSCA cyber advisory — and exactly what your organisation needs to do (and document) before an inspection.</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>I've been tracking IFSCA's regulatory output closely, and one thing I've learned is that when IFSCA issues something titled \"advisory,\" the word doesn't mean optional. The June 4, 2026 circular on heightened cyber security risks from Frontier AI models is effective immediately, sits on top of the existing March 2025 Cyber Security Guidelines, and introduces obligations that need to be operationalised — not filed and forgotten.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Before we go further, here's the circular:&nbsp;<a href=\"https://ifsca.gov.in/CommonDirect/GetFileView?id=91427247c5628a865846d173bc9cc2f5&amp;fileName=Advisory_on_Heightened_Cyber_Security_Risks_arising_from_Frontier_Artificial_Intelligence_Models_20260604_0359.pdf\">IFSCA Advisory on Heightened Cyber Security Risks from Frontier AI Models</a></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Read it in full. Then use this note as your practical implementation guide — what needs to happen, who needs to own it, what policies need revision, what Board approvals are needed, and what documentation must exist when IFSCA comes calling.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:gallery {\"linkTo\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-gallery has-nested-images columns-default is-cropped\"><!-- wp:image {\"id\":32094,\"sizeSlug\":\"large\",\"linkDestination\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image size-large\"><img src=\"https://csatwork.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/ChatGPT-Image-Jun-5-2026-at-10_22_22-PM-1024x576.png\" alt=\"\" class=\"wp-image-32094\"/></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image --></figure>\n<!-- /wp:gallery -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Why This Circular Exists — And Why It Matters More Than Most</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>To understand what IFSCA is asking for, you need to understand what changed in the threat environment that prompted this circular.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For years, when a software vulnerability was publicly disclosed, financial institutions had a reasonable window — days, sometimes weeks — to assess exposure and deploy patches before attackers could build working exploits. That window shaped how patch management policies were written, how vendor SLAs were structured, and how incident response plans were calibrated.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Frontier AI models have eliminated that window.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>These models can now scan complex codebases, identify known and previously unknown vulnerabilities, reason about how to exploit them, and generate working attack code — in hours, not weeks. The expertise and resources previously required to mount a sophisticated cyberattack have been compressed and democratised by AI. What used to require a nation-state-level team can now be initiated by a moderately capable attacker with access to the right model.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>IFSCA's position is that even though the most capable models aren't freely available today, that restriction will not last. The circular is a forward-looking signal: restructure your security posture now, before AI-assisted attacks become routine, not after your entity is on the wrong end of one.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This context is important because it shapes how you should approach the compliance response. This isn't about ticking eleven boxes in Annexure A. It's about fundamentally recalibrating your organisation's operating tempo around cyber risk — and ensuring that recalibration is documented, approved, and evidenced at every level.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Who Needs to Drive This — And It's Not Just the CISO</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Let me address something upfront that often causes compliance gaps in cyber security circulars. The instinct in most entities is to route these to the IT or information security team and consider the compliance obligation discharged. That approach will not hold up with IFSCA.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This circular explicitly requires Board-level governance of AI cyber risk. It requires policies to be updated. It requires risk assessments to be placed before the Board. It requires vendor obligations to be contractually embedded. These are governance and compliance functions, not just technical ones.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The Compliance Officer and Principle Officer need to own the governance trail. The CISO owns technical implementation. The Compliance Officer owns the evidence that the entity has met its regulatory obligations. Both roles need to be actively engaged — and the documentation needs to reflect that.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:gallery {\"linkTo\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-gallery has-nested-images columns-default is-cropped\"><!-- wp:image {\"id\":32096,\"sizeSlug\":\"large\",\"linkDestination\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image size-large\"><img src=\"https://csatwork.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/ChatGPT-Image-Jun-5-2026-at-10_24_36-PM-1024x576.png\" alt=\"\" class=\"wp-image-32096\"/></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image --></figure>\n<!-- /wp:gallery -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>With that framing, let's walk through what needs to happen, in the sequence that makes organisational sense.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">First: Review and Revise Your Policies</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is where most compliance teams should begin, because the policies are the foundation on which everything else rests. An IFSCA inspector examining your compliance with this circular will start by looking at your governing documents — and if those documents predate the circular and make no reference to AI-driven threats, everything else you show them carries less weight.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The Cyber Security Policy</strong>&nbsp;is the primary document that needs revision. Your current policy was almost certainly written against a threat landscape that didn't account for AI-assisted attacks. It needs to be updated to explicitly recognise Frontier AI models as a defined threat category, to reflect the hours-level response expectation for critical vulnerabilities, and to set out the governance framework for AI tool usage within the entity. This isn't cosmetic editing — it's a substantive policy revision.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The Patch Management Policy</strong>&nbsp;needs to be reviewed separately. If it currently prescribes response timelines of 72 hours or longer for critical vulnerabilities, those timelines need to be compressed. The circular's expectation is that critical CVEs are treated as exploitable within hours of disclosure. Your policy needs to say that, and your procedures need to operationalise it.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The Third Party Risk Management Policy</strong>&nbsp;needs an AI-specific module. Currently, most TPRM frameworks assess vendors against standard security questionnaires. This circular introduces a specific additional obligation — critical vendors must demonstrate preparedness for AI-driven threats and accelerated exploit timelines. Your TPRM policy needs to reflect this as a formal requirement, not an ad hoc check.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The Incident Response Policy</strong>&nbsp;needs updating to include AI-attack scenarios specifically — automated credential attacks, rapid reconnaissance, AI-speed exploit attempts — and must set response SLAs calibrated to minutes for credential compromise scenarios, not hours.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The Software Development Lifecycle Policy</strong>&nbsp;needs a new mandatory control: AI-generated or AI-remediated code must undergo rigorous security testing and human review before production deployment. If your SDLC policy doesn't currently address AI-generated code at all, this is a gap that needs closing now.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>The AI Tools Usage Policy</strong>&nbsp;— if one doesn't exist, it needs to be created. This circular effectively mandates that entities have a governance framework for their internal use of AI tools. The policy should cover: what constitutes an AI tool for these purposes, the authorisation process for adopting new AI tools, data classification requirements governing what information can be processed by which tools, and the review requirements for AI vendor data handling terms.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Every one of these policy revisions needs to go through your normal policy approval process — which, for an IFSCA-regulated entity, means Board approval or approval by a Board-delegated committee, depending on your governance framework. The revised policies need to be dated after June 4, 2026, and the approval needs to be documented in Board or committee minutes.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:gallery {\"linkTo\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-gallery has-nested-images columns-default is-cropped\"><!-- wp:image {\"id\":32104,\"sizeSlug\":\"large\",\"linkDestination\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image size-large\"><img src=\"https://csatwork.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/ChatGPT-Image-Jun-5-2026-at-10_28_24-PM-5-1024x576.png\" alt=\"\" class=\"wp-image-32104\"/></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image --></figure>\n<!-- /wp:gallery -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What must be documented:</strong>&nbsp;Version-controlled copies of each revised policy showing tracked changes from the previous version. Board or committee meeting minutes approving each revised policy, with the date of approval. A policy register showing the current effective version and approval date of each policy. Distribution records confirming that updated policies were communicated to relevant staff.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Second: Update Your Risk Assessment and Take It to the Board</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Once your policies are being revised, the next step is the Cyber Security Risk Assessment — and this one has a specific Board approval requirement embedded in the circular.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The CSRA must be updated to include Frontier AI Model Risk as a formally assessed, named threat scenario. This means more than adding a paragraph. It means working through the standard risk assessment methodology — what is the threat, what is the likelihood for your specific entity, what is the potential impact given your technology environment and business model, what controls are currently in place, and what residual risk remains after those controls.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The depth of this assessment will depend on your entity's nature and scale, but it needs to be genuine. Generic boilerplate about \"AI presenting emerging risks to the financial sector\" will not satisfy an inspector who asks you to walk them through your assessment methodology.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What the Compliance Officer needs to do here:</strong>&nbsp;Don't leave the CSRA revision entirely with the IT team. Sit with the CISO and understand the AI threat in the context of your specific entity. If your entity runs a fund management operation with limited direct technology exposure, that shapes the risk assessment differently than if you're running a trading platform or a banking unit with complex API-driven infrastructure. The assessment needs to reflect your reality.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Once updated, the CSRA must be presented to and approved by the Board. For MIIs, it additionally goes before the Standing Committee on Technology. The Principle Officer needs to own the scheduling of this — it should be a substantive agenda item at the next Board meeting, with adequate pre-reading circulated in advance so the Board can engage meaningfully rather than rubber-stamp.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The Board presentation itself should cover: the nature of the AI threat and why it represents a step-change from previous cyber risk, your entity's specific exposure, the controls proposed or already implemented, identified gaps and remediation timelines, and the updated risk rating after controls.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>After the presentation, the minutes need to reflect a real discussion. Inspectors can tell the difference between minutes that record genuine Board engagement and minutes that record a formality. The Board should ask questions, the minutes should capture them, and any actions arising should be recorded with owners and timelines.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What must be documented:</strong>&nbsp;The updated CSRA, dated after June 4, 2026, with Frontier AI Model Risk as a named scenario including full risk assessment methodology, likelihood and impact ratings, control mapping, and residual risk. Board meeting agenda showing the CSRA as a substantive item. Board presentation deck or paper circulated as pre-reading. Board meeting minutes recording the discussion, questions raised, Board acknowledgment, and any actions arising with owners and timelines. For MIIs, equivalent Standing Committee on Technology minutes. Evidence of the periodic review cycle — the circular requires this to be done regularly, so you need a documented schedule for future reviews.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Third: Build and Maintain the Operational Documentation</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>With governance in place — policies revised, Board informed and on record — the next layer is the operational documentation that proves your controls are actually working, not just written into policies.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:gallery {\"linkTo\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-gallery has-nested-images columns-default is-cropped\"><!-- wp:image {\"id\":32099,\"sizeSlug\":\"large\",\"linkDestination\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image size-large\"><img src=\"https://csatwork.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/ChatGPT-Image-Jun-5-2026-at-10_32_57-PM-1024x576.png\" alt=\"\" class=\"wp-image-32099\"/></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image --></figure>\n<!-- /wp:gallery -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Software Bill of Materials:</strong>&nbsp;The SBOM is a complete inventory of every software component in your production environment — proprietary code, open-source libraries, third-party dependencies. It needs to exist, be version-controlled, be updated on every deployment, and be connected to your vulnerability management process so that when a CVE is published, you can immediately check your exposure. The compliance team doesn't build the SBOM — but the Compliance Officer needs to confirm it exists and understand how it feeds into the patch process.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>Documents needed:</em>&nbsp;The SBOM itself in version-controlled form, the SOP describing how it's maintained and updated, and evidence of the link to your CVE monitoring process.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Patch Management Log:</strong>&nbsp;Your revised Patch Management Policy says critical CVEs are treated as exploitable within hours. This log is the evidence that your operations match your policy. For every critical vulnerability, the log should record: date and time of public disclosure, date and time of internal impact assessment completion, date and time of patch deployment, and SLA compliance status. Gaps between policy and log are exactly what inspectors look for.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>Documents needed:</em>&nbsp;The Patch Management Log, maintained contemporaneously, with all fields completed for every critical CVE from the date the policy came into effect.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>MFA Coverage Register:</strong>&nbsp;A structured record of every internet-facing system and every privileged account, showing the MFA type currently deployed and any gaps with documented remediation timelines. Also needed alongside this: the MFA Enrolment and Device Change SOP, showing the identity verification steps required to register a new MFA device or modify an existing one.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>Documents needed:</em>&nbsp;The MFA Coverage Register with current status and gap remediation plan. The MFA Enrolment SOP. Evidence of periodic review.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>API Inventory:</strong>&nbsp;A comprehensive register of every API your entity exposes or consumes, the applications that use each, access control settings, rate-limiting configurations, and the whitelist of authorised entities. Evidence of quarterly review and decommissioning of unused APIs.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>Documents needed:</em>&nbsp;The API Inventory Register with all fields completed. Review records showing quarterly verification and any APIs decommissioned.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>SOC Detection Rules Documentation:</strong>&nbsp;Written confirmation that your SOC detection capabilities have been tuned to identify AI-speed attack patterns — automated reconnaissance, abnormally rapid scanning, access sequences exceeding human-plausible timelines. The CISO should be able to produce a document summarising these rules and their last review date.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>Documents needed:</em>&nbsp;SOC detection configuration summary or rules document, with last review date. Evidence of periodic review.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Tabletop Exercise and Drill Reports:</strong>&nbsp;IFSCA will want to see that you've tested your incident response capabilities, not just documented them. At minimum, conduct one tabletop exercise simulating an AI-driven attack scenario — including credential compromise with automated response — and document the outcome, gaps identified, and improvement actions taken.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>Documents needed:</em>&nbsp;Tabletop exercise or simulation reports, including scenario description, participants, findings, and action items with owners and timelines. Evidence of follow-up on action items.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Incident Response Records:</strong>&nbsp;For any actual security events, maintain records showing the timeline from detection to containment. For credential compromise specifically, the record must demonstrate minutes-level response. These records are both an operational tool and an inspection exhibit.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>Documents needed:</em>&nbsp;Incident response records for all events, with timestamps at each stage of the response.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Fourth: Extend Your Compliance Obligations to Your Vendors</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The vendor requirement in this circular is, in my view, the most practically challenging — and the one where documentation gaps are most common. The circular makes clear that your critical service providers' preparedness for AI-driven threats is your regulatory responsibility, not just their commercial obligation.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What the Compliance Officer needs to do:</strong>&nbsp;Begin by formally identifying your critical service providers under your TPRM framework, with documented criteria for that classification. Then issue a formal AI Cyber Risk Questionnaire to each — not a casual email, a structured questionnaire that asks specifically about their SBOM practices, patch timelines for critical vulnerabilities, AI threat assessment processes, and incident response capabilities. Get written responses. File them.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Then review your vendor contracts. If they don't currently include obligations around AI cyber risk assessment and vulnerability remediation timelines, they need to. For new contracts, incorporate this as standard language. For existing critical vendor contracts, negotiate an addendum. The obligation being in writing matters — a verbal assurance from a vendor's account manager has no inspection value.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Where vendor vulnerabilities are identified, your remediation tracker needs to show that you're actively managing closure — with owner, timeline, and evidence of completion.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What must be documented:</strong>&nbsp;Critical Service Provider Register with classification criteria. AI Cyber Risk Questionnaires issued — keep copies of what you sent, not just responses received. Written vendor responses, dated and filed. For inadequate responses, evidence of follow-up or escalation. Vendor contract addenda incorporating AI risk obligations. Vendor Remediation Tracker with open items, timelines, and closure evidence.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Fifth: Govern Your Own Use of AI Tools — And Get Board Sign-Off</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is the dimension of the circular that most entities haven't yet thought through systematically. The focus tends to be on defending against AI. But the circular equally addresses your own use of AI tools — and creates specific governance obligations around it.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Many teams across IFSC entities are already using AI tools without a formal governance framework: developer code assistants, AI-powered security scanners, cloud-based vulnerability analysis platforms, AI-assisted SIEM tools. The circular requires that every such tool be formally authorised, that you know what data it processes and where that data goes, and that you've reviewed the vendor's data handling terms and concluded they're adequate.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What the Compliance Officer needs to do:</strong>&nbsp;Commission an internal survey of every AI tool in use across the entity. The results will almost always be broader than leadership expects — tools adopted at team level without central IT approval are common. Once the inventory is complete, work with legal and the DPO to review vendor terms for every tool that processes sensitive or regulated data. Then take a consolidated AI Tool Governance framework — covering authorisation process, data classification requirements, vendor review criteria, and DLP controls — to the Board for approval as a policy matter.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This Board approval is important. The circular creates a specific obligation around AI tool governance that goes beyond routine IT procurement. Bringing it to the Board signals that the entity has understood the obligation and taken it seriously at the governance level.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What must be documented:</strong>&nbsp;An AI Tool Register listing every tool in use, the data types it processes, approval status, and authorisation date. Legal or DPO review records for each tool processing sensitive data, with a conclusion on adequacy of vendor terms. The Board-approved AI Tools Usage Policy, with minutes of approval. DLP configuration records. Where tools are found to be unapproved or inadequately governed, evidence of remediation — either formal authorisation obtained or tool decommissioned.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Also under this heading: the AI-Generated Code Review Log. Every instance of AI-generated or AI-remediated code going to production must have a record of the security testing conducted and the human sign-off obtained. The updated SDLC Policy, Board-approved, provides the framework. The log provides the evidence of compliance.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Pulling It Together: What the Inspection File Looks Like</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>An IFSCA inspection examining compliance with this circular will essentially be looking for a connected chain of evidence — not a pile of individual documents, but a coherent narrative that runs from Board-level governance through to operational execution.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The chain looks like this: the Board knew about the risk (CSRA presentation and minutes), the Board approved the response framework (revised policies and minutes of approval), management implemented the controls (SBOM, patch log, MFA register, API inventory, vendor questionnaires, AI tool register), the controls were tested (tabletop reports, drill records), and incidents were responded to as prescribed (incident response records with timestamps).</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>If any link in this chain is missing or undated, the inspection finding will reflect it. If the CSRA was updated but never taken to the Board, that's a governance gap. If the policies were revised but the Board approval isn't minuted, the revision carries less weight. If the patch log shows deployment timelines that don't match the policy SLA, that's an operational gap. If vendor questionnaires were issued but responses were never received or followed up, that's a third-party risk gap.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The documentation needs to tell a consistent story. Build it that way — not as a retrospective exercise before an inspection, but as the natural output of running the compliance programme properly.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:gallery {\"linkTo\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-gallery has-nested-images columns-default is-cropped\"><!-- wp:image {\"id\":32103,\"sizeSlug\":\"large\",\"linkDestination\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image size-large\"><img src=\"https://csatwork.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/ChatGPT-Image-Jun-5-2026-at-10_36_34-PM-1024x576.png\" alt=\"\" class=\"wp-image-32103\"/></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image --></figure>\n<!-- /wp:gallery -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">A Realistic Timeline</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Week one: Initiate CSRA update, schedule Board meeting agenda item, conduct internal AI tool survey, identify critical vendors. These are governance and coordination actions that don't require technical implementation.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Weeks two and three: Issue vendor AI risk questionnaires, begin contract review for critical vendors, circulate draft revised policies for internal review, confirm SBOM status with IT head, revise patch management SOP.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Thirty days: Board meeting to present updated CSRA and approve revised policies — Cyber Security Policy, Patch Management Policy, TPRM Policy, Incident Response Policy, SDLC Policy, AI Tools Usage Policy. All approvals minuted.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Thirty to sixty days: Technical controls implementation — MFA gap remediation, API inventory completion, SOC detection rule updates, DLP configurations, AI tool formal authorisations. All documented as implementation progresses.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Sixty days: Tabletop exercise on AI-attack scenario. Report produced and acted upon.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Ongoing: Patch log maintenance, vendor tracker updates, periodic CSRA review cycle, annual policy review cycle — all on documented schedules.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">One Final Thought</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The circular uses \"shall\" for hard obligations and \"encouraged\" for softer expectations. In IFSCA's regulatory practice, \"encouraged\" calibrated against your entity's size and risk profile is the operative standard — if you don't implement something marked \"encouraged,\" you should have a documented, proportionality-based reason why not, and that reasoning should sit in your CSRA.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Effective immediately means effective immediately. The compliance standard exists from June 4, 2026, regardless of where your implementation currently stands. What matters is that you can show genuine, good-faith progress — documented, sequenced, and Board-owned.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The entities that handle IFSCA inspections well are not the ones with the thickest files. They're the ones where the files tell a coherent, honest story of an organisation that understood the obligation, took it to the right level of governance, implemented it seriously, and documented it as they went.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Full circular here for reference:&nbsp;<a href=\"https://ifsca.gov.in/CommonDirect/GetFileView?id=91427247c5628a865846d173bc9cc2f5&amp;fileName=Advisory_on_Heightened_Cyber_Security_Risks_arising_from_Frontier_Artificial_Intelligence_Models_20260604_0359.pdf\">IFSCA-CSD/MSC/3/2026-DCS dated June 4, 2026</a></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>This guidance note is prepared for compliance, legal, and technology professionals at IFSCA-regulated entities in GIFT City. It is a practical reading companion to the circular and does not constitute legal advice. Implementation should be calibrated to your entity's specific size, nature, scale, and risk profile.</em></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->",

          "title": "The Four Fund Vehicles in GIFT IFSC, Compared: Venture Capital, Restricted, Retail &amp; Special Situation Funds",
          "link": "https://csatwork.in/gift-ifsc-fund-vehicles-vcs-restricted-retail-ssf-comparison/",
          "pubDate": "Wed, 10 Jun 2026 05:45:42 +0000",
          "dc:creator": "prashantmishra1986",
          "guid": {
            "#text": "https://csatwork.in/?p=32107",
            "@attributes": {
              "isPermaLink": "false"
