          "description": null,
          "content:encoded": "<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">A practitioner's guide to choosing the right scheme under the IFSCA (Fund Management) Regulations, 2025 — as amended up to 30 January 2026.</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Every fund manager who looks seriously at GIFT City eventually hits the same fork in the road. The IFSCA (Fund Management) Regulations, 2025 don't give you \"an AIF licence.\" They give you a&nbsp;<strong>Fund Management Entity (FME)</strong>registration — and then ask you to pick the&nbsp;<em>scheme</em>&nbsp;you actually want to run. Get that choice wrong and you've over-capitalised your FME, locked yourself into the wrong investor profile, or filed under a route that adds weeks to your launch.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>There are four scheme vehicles under Chapter III: the&nbsp;<strong>Venture Capital Scheme (VCS)</strong>&nbsp;(Reg. 18–29), the&nbsp;<strong>Restricted Scheme (Non-Retail)</strong>&nbsp;(Reg. 30–41), the&nbsp;<strong>Retail Scheme</strong>&nbsp;(Reg. 42–52), and the&nbsp;<strong>Special Situation Fund (SSF)</strong>&nbsp;(Reg. 53–60). They look similar on a slide. They are not similar in practice — they differ on investor caps, minimum cheques, structure, leverage, NAV cadence, and the FME registration tier you need before you can launch one.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is the comparison every GP asks for in the first meeting. Here it is, end to end.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Quick answer: which GIFT IFSC fund vehicle fits which manager?</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Venture Capital Scheme (VCS)</strong> — a lean, closed-end vehicle for early-stage / startup investing, up to 50 investors, that the lightest FME tier (Authorised FME, USD 75,000 net worth) can run. Best for first-time and boutique GPs.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Restricted Scheme (Non-Retail)</strong> — the workhorse private-placement vehicle. Up to 1,000 investors, open- <em>or</em>closed-ended, and the only route that maps to <strong>all three AIF categories</strong> (I, II and III), so it houses everything from PE and credit to long-short and derivative strategies.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Retail Scheme</strong> — the mutual-fund-style vehicle for the public. Daily NAV, strict diversification limits, an offer-document filing route, and the heaviest FME tier (Registered FME (Retail), USD 1,000,000 net worth).</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Special Situation Fund (SSF)</strong> — a specialised, closed-end credit vehicle that invests <em>only</em> in stressed assets and can act as a resolution applicant under the IBC. It's GIFT City's answer to SEBI's onshore SSF.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>If you remember one thing:&nbsp;<strong>the scheme you want determines the FME tier you must register as — not the other way round</strong>&nbsp;(the three tiers are set out in Reg. 3(4)). Plan it backwards from the scheme.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">The comparison table GPs actually want</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:table -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-table\"><table class=\"has-fixed-layout\"><thead><tr><th>Feature</th><th>Venture Capital Scheme (VCS)</th><th>Restricted Scheme (Non-Retail)</th><th>Retail Scheme</th><th>Special Situation Fund (SSF)</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><strong>Governing provisions</strong></td><td>Ch. III, Part A (Reg. 18–29)</td><td>Ch. III, Part B (Reg. 30–41)</td><td>Ch. III, Part C (Reg. 42–52)</td><td>Ch. III, Part D (Reg. 53–60)</td></tr><tr><td><strong>AIF category mapping</strong></td><td>Category I AIF / Venture Capital Fund (Reg. 18)</td><td>Category I / II / III AIF (Reg. 30(1))</td><td>Mutual-fund-style (not an AIF category)</td><td>Category I AIF; sub-category of restricted schemes (Reg. 60(2))</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Minimum FME tier</strong></td><td>Authorised FME (Reg. 3(4)(a))</td><td>Registered FME (Non-Retail) (Reg. 3(4)(b))</td><td>Registered FME (Retail) (Reg. 3(4)(c))</td><td>Registered FME (Non-Retail)</td></tr><tr><td><strong>FME net worth</strong>(Second Schedule)</td><td>USD 75,000</td><td>USD 500,000</td><td>USD 1,000,000</td><td>USD 500,000</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Offering route</strong></td><td>Private placement memorandum (Reg. 19)</td><td>Private placement memorandum (Reg. 31)</td><td>Public offer document (Reg. 43)</td><td>Private placement memorandum (Reg. 55)</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Filing process</strong></td><td>Green channel (Reg. 19(2))</td><td>Green channel (Reg. 31(2))</td><td>Draft filed ≥ 21 working days pre-launch; comments + fiduciary approval (Reg. 43)</td><td>Green channel (Reg. 55(2))</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Investor cap</strong></td><td>Max&nbsp;<strong>50</strong>&nbsp;(Reg. 20(1))</td><td>Max&nbsp;<strong>1,000</strong>&nbsp;(Reg. 32(1))</td><td>Min&nbsp;<strong>20</strong>; no single &gt; 25% (Reg. 44)</td><td>As specified by IFSCA (Reg. 58(2))</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Minimum investment</strong></td><td>USD 250,000 / USD 60,000 staff (Reg. 20(2))</td><td>USD 150,000 / USD 40,000 staff (Reg. 32(2))</td><td>None generally; USD 10,000 for close-end &gt; 15% unlisted (Reg. 47(2))</td><td>As specified by IFSCA</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Structure</strong></td><td>Close-ended&nbsp;<strong>only</strong>(Reg. 21(1))</td><td>Open-&nbsp;<strong>or</strong>&nbsp;close-ended (Reg. 33(1))</td><td>Open- or close-ended (Reg. 45(1))</td><td>Close-ended&nbsp;<strong>only</strong>&nbsp;(Reg. 56(1))</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Minimum tenure</strong></td><td>3 years (Reg. 21(2))</td><td>1 year, close-ended (Reg. 33(2))</td><td>3 years, close-ended (Reg. 45(2))</td><td>3 years (Reg. 56(2))</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Permitted legal forms</strong></td><td>Company / LLP / Trust (Reg. 21(5))</td><td>Company / LLP / Trust (Reg. 33(5))</td><td><strong>Company or Trust — no LLP</strong>(Reg. 45(4))</td><td>Company / LLP / Trust (Reg. 56(3))</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Corpus</strong></td><td>Min USD 3M;&nbsp;<strong>max USD 200M</strong>(Reg. 23(1))</td><td>Min USD 3M; open-end may start at USD 1M (Reg. 35(2))</td><td>Min USD 3M (Reg. 47(6))</td><td>As specified by IFSCA (Reg. 58(1))</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Investment universe</strong></td><td>≥ 80% in investees ≤ 10 yrs old (Reg. 23(3))</td><td>Broad; derivatives allowed; 20% physical assets close-end (Reg. 34)</td><td>Diversified, hard caps; derivatives for hedging only (Reg. 46–47)</td><td><strong>Only</strong>&nbsp;special-situation assets (Reg. 57)</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Borrowing / leverage</strong></td><td>Permitted, on disclosure (Reg. 25)</td><td>Permitted, on disclosure (Reg. 37)</td><td>Only temp liquidity ≤ 20% AUM, ≤ 6 months (Reg. 49)</td><td>Only day-to-day operations (Reg. 59)</td></tr><tr><td><strong>NAV frequency</strong></td><td>Annual (Reg. 27)</td><td>Monthly (open) / half-yearly (close) (Reg. 39)</td><td><strong>Daily (open) / weekly (close)</strong>(Reg. 51)</td><td>Half-yearly, per restricted norms (Reg. 60(1))</td></tr><tr><td><strong>FME \"skin in the game\"</strong></td><td>2.5% / USD 750k, cap 10% (Reg. 28)</td><td>Close 2.5% / USD 750k; Open 5% / USD 1.5M (Reg. 40)</td><td>1% of AUM or USD 200k,&nbsp;<strong>whichever lower</strong>&nbsp;(Reg. 52)</td><td>Per close-end restricted norms (Reg. 60(1))</td></tr></tbody></table></figure>\n<!-- /wp:table -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>(All figures are from the IFSCA (Fund Management) Regulations, 2025, as amended to 30 January 2026. Items \"as specified by the Authority\" are deliberately left to circulars — see the SSF section.)</em></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">1. Venture Capital Scheme (VCS) — the boutique GP's entry point</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The VCS is the only scheme an&nbsp;<strong>Authorised FME</strong>&nbsp;— the lightest, USD 75,000 net-worth tier (Reg. 3(4)(a) read with the Second Schedule) — can launch. That single fact is why it exists. IFSCA wanted a low-barrier on-ramp for first-time and emerging managers running genuine early-stage strategies, without forcing them into the heavier Non-Retail tier.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>What you're getting is a deliberately tight box:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Closed-ended only</strong> (Reg. 21(1)), minimum three-year tenure, extendable by two years with a two-thirds-by-value investor vote (Reg. 21(3)), and beyond that only with willing investors plus an exit for dissenters (Reg. 21(4)).</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Maximum 50 investors</strong> (Reg. 20(1)), each writing at least <strong>USD 250,000</strong> (USD 60,000 for the FME's own people; accredited investors exempt) (Reg. 20(2)).</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>A <strong>corpus band of USD 3M to USD 200M</strong> (Reg. 23(1)) — note the <em>ceiling</em>. The VCS is the only one of the four with a hard maximum. Cross USD 200M and you've outgrown the vehicle.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>An <strong>80% deployment rule</strong> (Reg. 23(3)): at least 80% of corpus must go into investee companies incorporated within the last ten years. This is what makes it a <em>venture</em> scheme and not a generic PE fund.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>It files as a&nbsp;<strong>Category I AIF (\"venture capital fund\")</strong>&nbsp;under Reg. 18, and the Explanation there carries that status through for Income-tax Act, FEMA and other statutory purposes — the take-on-record communication is expressly to be construed as the Certificate of Registration for income-tax purposes (Reg. 19(2), Explanation).</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Practitioner note — the January 2026 amendment.</strong>&nbsp;The placement-memorandum validity rule in Reg. 19(3) was substituted with effect from 30 January 2026. Previously a VCS got a&nbsp;<em>one-time</em>&nbsp;six-month extension at 50% of the fresh-filing fee if it missed first close. Now you can take&nbsp;<strong>rolling six-month extensions</strong>&nbsp;— 25% of the fee for the first, 50% for each subsequent one — as long as you apply while the memorandum is still valid. For a manager genuinely close to first close in a slow market, that's real breathing room. Build the extension fee into your launch budget rather than treating it as a failure cost.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>When the VCS is the wrong choice:</strong>&nbsp;the moment you want more than 50 LPs, cheques below USD 150,000, or an open-ended structure, you've outgrown it — and the regulation itself points you to the Restricted Scheme (Explanation to Reg. 20).</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">2. Restricted Scheme (Non-Retail) — the workhorse of GIFT City</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>If GIFT City has a \"default\" private fund vehicle, this is it. The Restricted Scheme is the most flexible of the four, and the only one that maps to&nbsp;<strong>all three AIF categories</strong>&nbsp;under Reg. 30(1):</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Category I</strong> (Reg. 30(1)(a)) — start-ups, SMEs, social/impact, infrastructure, ESG, and — notably — venture capital funds run <em>without</em> the Part A VCS constraints (Explanation II to Reg. 30(1)(a)).</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Category III</strong> (Reg. 30(1)(b)) — complex or leveraged trading strategies, including listed and unlisted derivatives. This is the home of long-short, multi-strategy and hedge-fund-style mandates.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Category II</strong> (Reg. 30(1)(c)) — the residual bucket: everything that isn't I or III. Most PE, private credit and real-asset funds land here.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>That category flexibility is the whole point. A single FME tier —&nbsp;<strong>Registered FME (Non-Retail)</strong>, USD 500,000 net worth (Reg. 3(4)(b)) — can run PE, credit and hedge strategies side by side, each as a separate restricted scheme.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Key parameters:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Up to 1,000 investors</strong> (Reg. 32(1)), minimum cheque <strong>USD 150,000</strong> (USD 40,000 for FME staff; accredited investors exempt) (Reg. 32(2)).</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Open- or close-ended</strong> (Reg. 33(1)). Categories I and II must be close-ended; only Category III can be open-ended (Reg. 30(2)). A close-ended restricted scheme needs only a <strong>one-year minimum tenure</strong> (Reg. 33(2)) — the shortest of any close-ended vehicle here.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Corpus minimum USD 3M</strong>, but an open-ended scheme may <em>commence investing</em> on raising USD 1M, provided it reaches USD 3M within twelve months (Reg. 35(2)).</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Leverage is permitted</strong> on disclosure and a two-thirds deviation vote (Reg. 37) — which, with Category III, is what makes GIFT City viable for leveraged and derivative strategies the VCS and Retail routes cannot carry.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>A close-ended restricted scheme may also park <strong>up to 20% of corpus in physical assets</strong> — real estate, bullion, art (Reg. 34(3)) — a flexibility unique to this vehicle.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Practitioner note.</strong>&nbsp;Watch the FME commitment in Reg. 40. For a close-ended scheme it tracks the VCS at 2.5% / USD 750k. But for an&nbsp;<strong>open-ended</strong>&nbsp;scheme it&nbsp;<strong>doubles to 5% (or USD 1.5M)</strong>&nbsp;(Reg. 40(b)). Managers who reflexively pick open-ended for \"liquidity optics\" underestimate this — the sponsor commitment on a USD 30M open-ended scheme is USD 1.5M of the manager's own money, maintained proportionally on an ongoing basis. Unless your LPs genuinely need open-ended liquidity, close-ended is materially cheaper for the GP.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Also note the extension mechanism for restricted schemes (Reg. 31(3)) was&nbsp;<strong>not</strong>&nbsp;changed in the January 2026 amendment — it remains the older&nbsp;<em>one-time</em>&nbsp;six-month extension at 50% fee. Only the VCS (Reg. 19(3)) and the open-ended-restricted corpus rule (Reg. 35(2)) got the new rolling-extension treatment. Don't assume parity.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">3. Retail Scheme — the public-facing, mutual-fund-style vehicle</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The Retail Scheme is a different animal entirely, and most private-fund GPs will never run one. It pools money from the&nbsp;<em>public</em>&nbsp;(Reg. 42) — and the regulations treat it with the seriousness that implies.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The differences start at registration. Only a&nbsp;<strong>Registered FME (Retail)</strong>&nbsp;— the top tier at&nbsp;<strong>USD 1,000,000 net worth</strong>&nbsp;(Reg. 3(4)(c)) — can launch one, and it needs&nbsp;<strong>prior approval of the Authority</strong>&nbsp;specifically to run retail schemes (Reg. 17(4)). The compliance officer for retail schemes must also be kept separate from the one handling non-retail business (Reg. 109/Ch. on obligations).</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The launch route is fundamentally different too. There's&nbsp;<strong>no green channel.</strong>&nbsp;You file a&nbsp;<em>draft offer document</em>&nbsp;at least&nbsp;<strong>21 working days before launch</strong>&nbsp;(Reg. 43(1)), incorporate IFSCA's comments&nbsp;<em>before</em>&nbsp;going live (Reg. 43(3)), and obtain fiduciary approval (Reg. 43(5)). Compare that to the green-channel vehicles, where a scheme opens for subscription the moment it's taken on record. Build the extra runway into a retail timeline.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The investor and portfolio rules reflect a retail-protection logic absent from the private vehicles:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Minimum 20 investors; no single investor above 25%</strong> (Reg. 44) — the opposite of the VCS's concentrated 50-LP book.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Diversification caps with teeth</strong> (Reg. 47): max 10% in a single company, 15% with fiduciary approval (Reg. 47(3)); 25% in a single sector, 50% for financial services (Reg. 47(4)); 25% in an associate (Reg. 47(5)).</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Unlisted limits:</strong> 15% for open-ended (Reg. 47(1)); up to 50% for close-ended, with a USD 10,000 minimum cheque once it crosses 15% unlisted (Reg. 47(2)).</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Derivatives for hedging only</strong> (Reg. 46(1)(g)) — no speculative or leveraged positions.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Borrowing only for temporary liquidity</strong> to meet redemptions, capped at 20% of AUM and six months (Reg. 49).</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Daily NAV</strong> (open) or weekly (close) (Reg. 51) — the most demanding operational cadence of the four, and a real fund-administration cost.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>One structural quirk: a Retail Scheme can only be a&nbsp;<strong>Company or a Trust — not an LLP</strong>&nbsp;(Reg. 45(4)). The three private vehicles all allow LLPs. If your structuring rests on an LLP, the retail route is closed to you.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Two upsides distinguish the Retail tier. First, the FME commitment is the lightest of all —&nbsp;<strong>1% of AUM or USD 200,000, whichever is lower</strong>&nbsp;(Reg. 52(1)) — because retail capital funds the scheme. Second, this is the only tier that can launch&nbsp;<strong>ETFs</strong>&nbsp;and act as investment manager for&nbsp;<strong>public offers of REITs and InvITs</strong>&nbsp;(Reg. 3(4)(c)(ii)). If your ambition is a listed, retail-distributed product set, you have to climb to this tier.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">4. Special Situation Fund (SSF) — GIFT City's stressed-asset vehicle</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The SSF is the newest and most specialised of the four, best understood as GIFT City's mirror of SEBI's onshore Special Situation Fund. It exists for one purpose: investing in&nbsp;<strong>stressed and distressed assets</strong>&nbsp;(Reg. 53, defined at Reg. 54).</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The defined \"special situation assets\" (Reg. 54(1)) are narrow and specific:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Stressed loans</strong> acquired under Clause 58 of the RBI (Transfer of Loan Exposures) Directions, 2021, or under a resolution plan approved under the <strong>Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016</strong> (Reg. 54(1)(a)).</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Security receipts</strong> issued by an RBI-registered Asset Reconstruction Company (Reg. 54(1)(b)).</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Securities of investee companies</strong> that are themselves stressed — under CIRP, with loans available for transfer, with ARC-issued security receipts against them, or in 90-day-plus payment default with a credit rating downgraded to \"D\" (Reg. 54(1)(c)).</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Crucially, an SSF&nbsp;<strong>may itself act as a resolution applicant under the IBC</strong>&nbsp;(Reg. 54(2)). That makes it a genuine acquisition vehicle for distressed Indian assets sourced through an onshore-IFSC platform — a structuring proposition that didn't cleanly exist before.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The mechanics are deliberately conservative:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Closed-ended only</strong>, minimum three-year tenure (Reg. 56).</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Invests <em>only</em> in special-situation assets</strong> (Reg. 57) — no general portfolio.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Effectively no leverage:</strong> borrowing only to meet day-to-day operational requirements (Reg. 59) — the tightest borrowing rule of all four vehicles.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Here's the part practitioners must internalise:&nbsp;<strong>the SSF is legally a sub-category of the restricted scheme</strong>&nbsp;(Reg. 60(2)). Its disclosure, valuation, NAV and FME-contribution norms are simply the&nbsp;<em>close-ended restricted scheme</em>&nbsp;norms borrowed wholesale (Reg. 60(1)). And its&nbsp;<strong>corpus, eligible investors and additional investment conditions are not hard-coded</strong>— they are \"as specified by the Authority\" (Reg. 58). So before you model an SSF, pull the latest IFSCA circular for the live numbers; the base regulation deliberately leaves them open. Treat the regulation as the frame and the circulars as the fill.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>You launch an SSF through a&nbsp;<strong>Registered FME (Non-Retail)</strong>&nbsp;— the same USD 500,000 tier as the restricted scheme.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">How to choose: a decision framework for GPs</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Don't start from \"which AIF category am I?\" Start from three questions in this order.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Question 1 — Who are my investors?</strong>&nbsp;Public / retail money forces you up to the Retail tier and the offer-document route (Reg. 43). Private, accredited or large-ticket investors keep you in the green-channel private vehicles. This single answer eliminates one of the four immediately.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Question 2 — What's my strategy and instrument set?</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Stressed and distressed assets → <strong>SSF</strong> (Reg. 57), full stop.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Genuine early-stage / venture, ≤ 50 LPs, lightest FME → <strong>VCS</strong> (Reg. 23(3)).</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Anything leveraged, derivative-heavy, open-ended, or broader than venture (PE, credit, multi-strategy, real assets) → <strong>Restricted Scheme</strong> (Reg. 30).</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Question 3 — What FME net worth and timeline can I fund?</strong>&nbsp;The vehicle dictates the tier, and the tier dictates the capital you lock up (Second Schedule): USD 75,000 (VCS) → USD 500,000 (Restricted / SSF) → USD 1,000,000 (Retail). The retail route also adds weeks for offer-document review. If your strategy could sit in two vehicles, the cheaper tier and the green channel usually win.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>A common structuring trap:</strong>&nbsp;managers default to \"open-ended for flexibility.\" Remember open-ended doubles your sponsor commitment under a restricted scheme (5% vs 2.5%, Reg. 40) and is unavailable for VCS and SSF entirely. Liquidity is rarely free.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Frequently asked questions</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Which GIFT IFSC fund vehicle has the lowest minimum investment?</strong>&nbsp;The Retail Scheme — it has no general minimum because it pools public money; a USD 10,000 floor applies only to close-ended schemes investing more than 15% in unlisted securities (Reg. 47(2)). Among the private vehicles, the Restricted Scheme is lowest at USD 150,000 (Reg. 32(2)), versus USD 250,000 for the VCS (Reg. 20(2)).</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What is the difference between a Venture Capital Scheme and a Restricted Scheme in GIFT City?</strong>&nbsp;A VCS is capped at 50 investors (Reg. 20(1)), closed-ended only (Reg. 21(1)), must deploy 80% into companies under ten years old (Reg. 23(3)), has a USD 200M corpus ceiling (Reg. 23(1)), and runs on the lightest FME tier. A Restricted Scheme allows up to 1,000 investors (Reg. 32(1)), can be open- or close-ended (Reg. 33(1)), has no corpus ceiling, maps to all three AIF categories including leveraged Category III (Reg. 30(1)), but requires the USD 500,000 Registered FME (Non-Retail) tier.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Can a Special Situation Fund in GIFT IFSC use leverage?</strong>&nbsp;No. An SSF may borrow only to meet day-to-day operational requirements (Reg. 59) — it cannot use leverage as a strategy. This is the strictest borrowing rule of the four.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Which fund vehicle can a first-time fund manager launch in GIFT City?</strong>&nbsp;The Venture Capital Scheme, through the Authorised FME registration (Reg. 3(4)(a)), which requires only USD 75,000 of net worth (Second Schedule) — the lowest barrier to entry of any scheme.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Is a Special Situation Fund a separate vehicle or a type of Restricted Scheme?</strong>&nbsp;Legally it is a sub-category of the restricted scheme (Reg. 60(2)). It borrows the close-ended restricted scheme's disclosure, valuation, NAV and sponsor-commitment norms (Reg. 60(1)), but its investment universe (Reg. 57), corpus and eligible investors (Reg. 58) are defined separately — several set by IFSCA circular rather than in the regulation.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Do GIFT IFSC fund schemes have to be set up as a trust?</strong>&nbsp;No. The VCS, Restricted Scheme and SSF can each be a Company, LLP or Trust (Reg. 21(5), 33(5), 56(3)). Only the Retail Scheme is restricted to a Company or a Trust — it cannot be an LLP (Reg. 45(4)).</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>What changed for fund schemes in the January 2026 amendment?</strong>&nbsp;The most significant change was the placement-memorandum extension regime for the VCS (Reg. 19(3)) and the open-ended restricted-scheme corpus rule (Reg. 35(2)). Managers who miss first close can now take rolling six-month extensions (25% of the fresh-filing fee for the first, 50% thereafter) instead of a single one-time extension — provided they apply while the memorandum is still valid.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">The bottom line</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The four vehicles aren't four flavours of the same product — they're four different regulatory bargains. The VCS (Reg. 18–29) trades flexibility for a low barrier to entry. The Restricted Scheme (Reg. 30–41) trades a heavier FME tier for genuine breadth. The Retail Scheme (Reg. 42–52) trades operational intensity and capital for access to public money and listed products. The SSF (Reg. 53–60) trades a narrow mandate for a purpose-built stressed-asset and IBC-resolution platform.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The managers who get GIFT City right reverse-engineer the decision: define the investor and the strategy first, let that fix the scheme, and let the scheme fix the FME tier and the launch timeline. Everything downstream — net worth, sponsor commitment, NAV cadence, leverage headroom — follows from that one upfront choice.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>This article reflects the IFSCA (Fund Management) Regulations, 2025 as amended to 30 January 2026. Several SSF parameters and certain thresholds are set by IFSCA circulars and should be verified against the latest issuance. It is not legal or tax advice.</em></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">About the Author</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Prashant Kumar</strong>&nbsp;is a Company Secretary, Published Author, and seasoned professional in corporate and financial services regulation. He currently serves as Company Secretary and Compliance Officer at&nbsp;<strong>Global Horizons Capital Advisors (IFSC) Private Limited</strong>, an IFSCA-licensed Investment Banker based in GIFT City, giving him direct, on-ground exposure to capital market transactions and regulatory structuring within the IFSC ecosystem.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>He brings hands-on experience across&nbsp;<strong>GIFT IFSC fund structuring — including FME registration across the Authorised, Non-Retail and Retail tiers and scheme setup under the AIF framework</strong>&nbsp;(Venture Capital, Restricted, Retail and Special Situation Funds) — alongside IPOs, direct listings, exchange listings, corporate governance, and end-to-end regulatory compliance for financial services entities operating in the IFSC and the wider Indian regulatory environment.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>His current role at an IFSCA-licensed entity in GIFT City gives him working familiarity with the practical decisions GPs and platforms actually face:&nbsp;<strong>selecting the right scheme vehicle, sizing FME net worth and sponsor commitment, navigating the green-channel versus offer-document filing routes, and aligning fund structure with investor profile, strategy and launch timelines</strong>&nbsp;under the IFSCA (Fund Management) Regulations, 2025 and their evolving amendments.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For professional discussions on&nbsp;<strong>GIFT IFSC fund setup and           "title": "A GIFT City Licence, a Nameplate, and a Cancellation: What the IFSCA Order Against LMB Insurance Brokers Teaches Every IFSC Entity",
          "link": "https://csatwork.in/ifsca-cancels-lmb-insurance-brokers-ifsc-licence-gift-city-lessons/",
          "pubDate": "Fri, 12 Jun 2026 09:35:05 +0000",
          "dc:creator": "prashantmishra1986",
          "guid": {
            "#text": "https://csatwork.in/?p=32110",

          "description": null,
          "content:encoded": "<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\"><strong>A composite insurance broker held a valid IFSC registration running till 2027. It never placed a single policy, quietly vacated its GIFT City office, and went silent on the regulator. In June 2026, IFSCA cancelled its licence. Here is exactly what went wrong — and how any IFSC entity can avoid the same fate.</strong></h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">The short version</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>On 2 June 2026, the Quasi-Judicial Authority for Enforcement at the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) cancelled the Certificate of Registration (CoR) of&nbsp;<strong>LMB Insurance Brokers Private Limited</strong>, an IFSC Insurance Intermediary Office (IIIO) operating in branch form out of GIFT City.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The headline charges were narrow: failure to commence business within the time allowed under Regulation 12(4) of the IFSCA (Insurance Intermediary) Regulations, 2021, and failure to pay the prescribed recurring fee. But the order is far more instructive than its charges suggest. It is one of IFSCA's clearest signals yet that it is actively policing the&nbsp;<strong>dormant-registration problem</strong>&nbsp;— entities that secure a GIFT City licence, build a nameplate, and then never do the regulated activity.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For anyone setting up or running an IFSC unit, this order is a compliance checklist written in hindsight.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">The background</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>LMB was a composite insurance broker already registered with IRDAI. IFSCA granted it an IIIO CoR on 31 January 2024, initially co-terminus with its IRDAI registration and later renewed to run from 18 February 2024 to 17 February 2027 — a comfortable three-year runway.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The CoR came with three things every IFSC entity receives and too few read carefully: the governing framework (IFSCA Act, 2019; Insurance Act, 1938; the Insurance Intermediary Regulations, 2021), a set of conditions, and a covering letter spelling out two obligations in plain language —&nbsp;<strong>commence business within the Regulation 12(4) timeline, and pay the applicable fee under the Fee Circular dated 17 May 2023.</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>LMB opened an office, appointed a branch head, and reported the appointment to the Office of the Development Commissioner. Then the trouble started — not because anything dramatic happened, but because nothing did.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">What actually went wrong</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">1. It missed the 180-day commencement clock — and never used the safety valve</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Regulation 12(4) requires an IIIO to&nbsp;<strong>commence business within 180 days</strong>&nbsp;of the grant of registration. Crucially, it also contains a proviso: an entity that cannot meet the deadline may apply to the Chairperson for an extension,&nbsp;<strong>at least 30 days in advance.</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>LMB never placed a single piece of broking business. More importantly, it&nbsp;<strong>never filed the extension application.</strong>&nbsp;That one omission is what converted a forgivable commercial reality — it simply could not find business — into a hard regulatory default. The safety valve existed. It was never pulled.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">2. It got \"commencement of business\" wrong</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>LMB's central defence was that opening an office and appointing a branch head&nbsp;<em>amounted to</em>&nbsp;commencement of business. IFSCA rejected this cleanly and the reasoning is worth committing to memory:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:quote -->\n<blockquote class=\"wp-block-quote\"><!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Opening an office is a&nbsp;<em>condition precedent to registration</em>. It therefore cannot also be the commencement of business.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph --></blockquote>\n<!-- /wp:quote -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Commencement, the Authority held, means taking action in furtherance of the activity for which the registration was granted — for a composite insurance broker, that means&nbsp;<strong>actually placing broking business.</strong>&nbsp;Setup is not commencement. This is the definitional clarity the whole IFSC ecosystem should note.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">3. It contradicted itself on the record</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>In its submissions, LMB claimed both that it had&nbsp;<strong>commenced business on 5 February 2024</strong>&nbsp;and that it&nbsp;<strong>could not do any business until its registration was renewed on 5 April 2024.</strong>&nbsp;The order flags this contradiction directly.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>In a quasi-judicial proceeding, an internal contradiction is often more damaging than the underlying lapse, because it undermines the credibility of every other submission.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">4. It went silent, then went stealth</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>IFSCA wrote to LMB in February, March and September 2024 seeking confirmation of the commencement date and supporting documents. Responses were absent or evasive. The \"repeated non-responsive behaviour\" became an aggravating factor in its own right.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Worse, LMB&nbsp;<strong>vacated its GIFT City premises by mid-2024 without informing IFSCA</strong>&nbsp;— even though the Letter of Approval from the Development Commissioner and the IFSC registration itself were predicated on those premises. When IFSCA officers physically visited the registered address in October 2025, they found&nbsp;<strong>a different entity conducting business there.</strong>&nbsp;It is hard to imagine worse optics for an intermediary.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">5. It picked a constitutional fight — and then surrendered it</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>LMB mounted an elaborate legal challenge to IFSCA's power to levy a recurring fee, invoking Entry 96 of List I of the Seventh Schedule, the scope of Sections 12 and 13 of the IFSCA Act, and the argument that the underlying insurance statutes do not empower a recurring levy.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Then, at the pre-hearing stage, it&nbsp;<strong>unconditionally withdrew the entire contention</strong>&nbsp;and offered to pay. That sequence is a tactical blunder: it burns goodwill and signals a defence that has run out of road. The lesson is simple — either hold a legal position with conviction or pay the fee, but do not do both.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">6. The exit gambit did not pause enforcement</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>By April 2026, LMB was negotiating a 100% sale of shares and tried to use the pending change-of-control to keep its registration alive pending IRDAI and IFSCA approvals. IFSCA separated the commercial transaction from the enforcement question and cancelled the CoR regardless.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Two myths this order quietly demolishes</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Myth 1: \"No business means no recurring fee.\"</strong>&nbsp;False. Clause 6(iii)(a) of the Fee Circular ties recurring-fee liability to the&nbsp;<strong>date of communication of the grant of registration</strong>, not to revenue. A dormant IFSC entity still owes the fee.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Myth 2: \"Cancellation is a clean exit.\"</strong>&nbsp;False. The order is explicit: even after the CoR is cancelled, the entity&nbsp;<strong>remains liable</strong>&nbsp;for outstanding dues, interest, and anything done or omitted as an intermediary. Walking away does not extinguish the liability.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">How LMB should have handled it</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The uncomfortable truth is that LMB's&nbsp;<em>commercial</em>&nbsp;failure was survivable. Plenty of new units struggle to originate business in the first year. What was not survivable was the&nbsp;<em>communication</em>&nbsp;failure. A cleaner path was available at every step:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list {\"ordered\":true} -->\n<ol class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>File the Regulation 12(4) extension application</strong> the moment it became clear that 180 days would not be enough — well before the deadline, as the proviso requires.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Respond to every IFSCA communication promptly and consistently.</strong> A short, honest status update (\"no business procured yet, here is our pipeline and timeline\") would have been worth more than silence.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Intimate IFSCA before vacating the premises</strong> — or, better, voluntarily surrender the registration if the business was no longer viable, rather than letting it drift into default.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Pay the recurring fee on time</strong>, and if there was a genuine dispute, raise it through the proper channel rather than mounting and then abandoning a constitutional challenge.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Plan the exit proactively.</strong> If the strategy was always to sell and exit, initiate voluntary surrender or change-of-control early — not as a reactive bargaining chip once enforcement was already underway.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">The IFSC compliance playbook: how to avoid this entirely</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For any entity holding or seeking an IFSC registration, the order distils into a practical operating discipline:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Treat the CoR conditions and covering letter as a live compliance checklist</strong> with calendared deadlines — not a one-time formality filed away after registration.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Build a regulatory calendar</strong> covering the 180-day commencement deadline, the recurring fee (due within 30 days of the financial year-end for years after commencement), and renewal timelines.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Designate a responsive compliance owner</strong> — a Principal Officer who actually answers regulator emails within a defined turnaround. Non-responsiveness is read as non-compliance.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Maintain a commencement-evidence file</strong> — documented client engagement, mandates, and actual transactions that prove the licensed activity is being carried on.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Intimate proactively</strong> on any material change: premises, key personnel, control, or business status. The regulator rewards transparency and punishes stealth.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Do not sit dormant.</strong> If the model is not working, surrender the licence cleanly rather than let it lapse into default.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Engage IFSCA early and cooperatively.</strong> Cooperation offered late, on issues that are already incurable, will not save the registration.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">The bottom line</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>LMB did not lose its licence because it failed to find business. It lost its licence because it stayed silent, vacated its office in the dark, treated its filing obligations as optional, and arrived at cooperation only after the damage was structural and irreversible.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The clearest takeaway for the IFSC ecosystem: in a young, ambitious jurisdiction like GIFT City, the regulator is watching for substance, not nameplates. A registration is a continuing obligation, not a trophy. Honour the conditions, communicate relentlessly, and exit cleanly if you must — because in regulatory matters, the cover-up of inactivity is always costlier than the inactivity itself.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>This article is a general analysis of a publicly issued regulatory order and does not constitute legal or compliance advice. Entities should seek specific counsel on their own facts.</em></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->",

          "title": "IFSCA vs Abans Financial Services: How I Would Have Defended This ₹8 Lakh Order",
          "link": "https://csatwork.in/ifsca-abans-financial-services-defence-strategy/",
          "pubDate": "Wed, 17 Jun 2026 11:30:36 +0000",

          "content:encoded": "<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">In June 2026, IFSCA imposed a penalty of ₹8,00,000 on Abans Financial Services Limited (IFSC Branch), upholding four separate allegations ranging from a fourteen-month Compliance Officer vacancy to delayed investor disclosures and inaccurate regulatory reporting. The order is now public, and most commentary on it has stopped at the obvious takeaway: here is what went wrong, do not repeat it.</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This article goes further. Working from the Show Cause Notice and the specific facts it raised, here is exactly how I would have approached the defence of this matter — allegation by allegation, from the day the notice landed through the personal hearing and the submissions on penalty. The aim is not to argue that Abans should have escaped liability it genuinely had. It is to show where a sharper, more evidence-led defence could have closed the gaps the entity's own submissions left open, protected the individuals named in the proceeding, and given the adjudicating authority a stronger basis to moderate the eventual penalty.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">The Background, Briefly</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Abans Alternative Fund Managers LLP was granted its Fund Management Entity licence in August 2022. In July 2024, following an internal restructuring within the group, the licence was transferred to Abans Financial Services Limited, with no change in ultimate control. IFSCA conducted an on-site inspection in September 2024, shared its findings in April 2025, and issued a Show Cause Notice in January 2026 covering four allegations. A personal hearing took place in March 2026, and the order followed in June 2026.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The four allegations were: a delay in appointing a Compliance Officer, a shortfall in the sponsor's contribution to the scheme, inadequate internal procedures and controls, failure to disclose portfolio information and annual accounts to investors on time, and inaccurate information in periodic regulatory reports. I will take each in turn.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Allegation One: The Compliance Officer Vacancy</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The facts here are not particularly flattering. The original Compliance Officer resigned, and for fourteen months no replacement was appointed. In the interim, the Principal Officer was given additional charge of the role, despite the regulation requiring a separate Key Managerial Person for that function. Candidate CVs were shared with IFSCA during this period, but none met the eligibility criteria, and the vacancy persisted.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>If I were running this defence, I would not lead with the argument that the delay was unintentional. Intent is the wrong frame entirely — a fourteen-month vacancy is a problem regardless of why it happened, and arguing intent invites the regulator to focus on motive rather than on what was actually done about the gap. I would instead want, on file before the reply was even drafted, a complete record of every candidate considered, the date each was shared with IFSCA, and any response received.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>What I would want most, though, is something that does not appear to exist in this matter: a written record of the entity proactively asking IFSCA for clarification on borderline candidates, rather than submitting names and waiting passively for rejection. If candidates kept falling short of the eligibility bar, the stronger move at the time would have been a direct query — here is a candidate's profile, here is where they may not meet the stated criteria, can you confirm whether this would be acceptable. That kind of correspondence converts a pattern of failed submissions into a documented, good-faith effort to get the appointment right under genuinely difficult market conditions. Without it, the entity is left arguing good faith in the abstract, which is a weaker position than demonstrating it through a paper trail.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>On the question of the Principal Officer holding additional charge, I would also want this decision documented, in writing, as a deliberate board-level or senior management decision taken as an interim stopgap — not something that happened by default. If that record does not exist from the time the decision was made, it needs to be created immediately for any ongoing situation, because reconstructing it later, after a notice has already been issued, carries far less weight.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Allegation Two: The Sponsor Contribution Shortfall</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This allegation involves a genuinely strong underlying argument that, in my view, was not pushed hard enough. The scheme received authorisation in January 2022, before the Fund Management Regulations, 2022 came into force in May 2022. Those regulations later introduced a waiver mechanism allowing the sponsor's contribution requirement to be waived if investors holding two-thirds of the scheme's value consented. But investors in this scheme had already been onboarded before the regulation existed, meaning that consent could not realistically have been built into the original onboarding documents.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>That much is a fair and sympathetic point about a regulation changing mid-stream. The problem is what happened next: the fund began investing in July 2022, and investor consent was only obtained in October 2022. That three-month gap, where investment activity proceeded without either the sponsor's contribution or investor consent in place, was left without a specific explanation in the submissions made.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>If I were handling this allegation, I would treat that gap as the single most important thing to address directly, not as a detail to be glossed over within the broader regulatory-transition argument. I would want a clear, specific explanation of why the fund could not have waited those three months — what the commercial cost of delay would have been, whether there were contractual deadlines or market conditions that made an immediate start commercially necessary, and why proceeding before consent was a reasonable judgment call given that the regulatory framework itself was still settling. Leaving that gap unaddressed, as appears to have happened, allows the regulator to conclude on its own that the entity should simply have waited — and that is exactly the conclusion drawn in this matter.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Allegation Three: Inadequate Internal Procedures and Controls</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Here, the entity's submissions leaned heavily on a legal argument: that the allegation rested on mere inference and surmise, supported by a citation to a Supreme Court decision on the standard required to establish a contravention. That is a real legal principle, but it was the wrong primary defence for this particular allegation, because the underlying ask from IFSCA was specific and factual — provide a detailed note on your internal procedures and controls — and that note was never furnished.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>If I were defending this allegation, I would treat the absence of that document as the central problem to solve, not a technicality to argue around. Whatever legal principles apply to evidentiary standards, they do not substitute for producing the actual document the regulator asked for. By the time of the hearing, the entity did point to a valuation policy and a gift-and-entertainment policy adopted in September 2025, but this was raised only in passing, through an annexure, with no real detail on what the policies actually covered or how they were being implemented.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>My approach would have been to treat the adoption of those policies, from the moment they existed, as something to document fully and proactively — the policy text itself, the date and authority of internal approval, and a specific note mapping each policy clause to the actual regulatory requirement it was meant to satisfy. If the regulation requires controls that protect investor interests and manage risk, the submission needs to say plainly which part of which policy does that. A passing reference in an annexure, introduced eleven months after adoption and discussed only briefly at the hearing, was never going to carry the weight this allegation needed.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Allegation Four: Investor Disclosure Delays</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This is, in my view, the allegation where the entity's defence was weakest, and where a different approach was most needed. Quarterly portfolio statements for seven consecutive quarters, covering June 2022 through December 2023, were not sent to investors on time — they were all sent together, in one batch, in April 2024. The annual report for FY 2023-24 reached investors three months late and reached IFSCA nine months late.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The submission made was that this delay was technical, venial, and procedural in nature, and did not affect the core activity of managing investor funds. I think this framing was always going to struggle, because the facts simply do not support it. A single missed quarter might reasonably be called technical. Seven consecutive missed quarters, corrected only when the regulator's inspection forced the issue, is a pattern, not a slip — and IFSCA was right to treat it that way.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>If I were running this defence, I would not have tried to characterise seven quarters of silence as a technical lapse. I would have conceded the lapse plainly and put the entire weight of the submission into two things: a clear, factual explanation of the operational cause behind the delay — whatever it genuinely was, whether a staffing gap, a systems issue, or something else specific to this entity's early-stage operations — and a detailed account of the process now in place to prevent recurrence, including a named owner for each periodic filing and a clear internal deadline with an escalation step if that deadline is at risk. Owning the lapse honestly, paired with a credible and specific fix, would have done more for this allegation than insisting on a characterisation the facts could not support.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Allegation on Reporting: Table 3.3</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>A related point, raised in the proceedings, concerned a specific field in the quarterly reporting template — Table 3.3, covering investment in debt securities on a look-through basis — which was left blank. The entity's explanation was that this was an inadvertent omission by an official, caused by a mistaken understanding, and that the relevant portfolio information had already been disclosed elsewhere in the report.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This defence had a structural problem that should have been caught before it was made: the same field was left blank in every quarterly report the entity ever filed, not just once. An explanation of a one-time mistaken understanding cannot survive that fact, because it implies a single momentary lapse, not a consistent gap across every filing.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Before offering any explanation on this point, I would have reviewed the entity's own filing history first. Having done so, the honest and more defensible position would have been to acknowledge that the requirement for this specific field was consistently misunderstood, explain clearly what that misunderstanding was, confirm the date the correct understanding was applied, and describe the steps taken to ensure the gap does not recur going forward. That is a more credible account than one the entity's own records contradict.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">The Personal Hearing</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The hearing was attended by the Principal Officer, the Vice President, and two representatives from external counsel — a reasonable composition. But composition is not the same as strategy. What matters most at a hearing like this is what gets placed on record about individual conduct, separate from the entity's failures, because the regulatory framework allows for penalties on individual officers in default, separately from the entity itself.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The clearest example in this matter is the Principal Officer being given additional charge as Compliance Officer. I would have wanted that decision documented, well before the hearing, as a considered organisational decision made under genuine resourcing constraints — not something left to be explained orally for the first time in the hearing room. The same applies to the broader remediation steps mentioned at the hearing: rather than a general reference to policies having been adopted, I would have wanted a specific roadmap on record, naming who owns each corrective step, when it was implemented, and how it continues to be monitored.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Submissions on Penalty</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The entity's submissions on quantum relied on a list of eight precedents from the Securities Appellate Tribunal and SEBI adjudicating officers, all supporting the general principle that technical or venial breaches should not attract maximum penalties. IFSCA's response to this was direct: the observations in those cases turned on their own specific facts, and could not be automatically applied to this matter.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This outcome was, in my view, foreseeable, because citing a long list of precedents for a shared general principle, without tying each one to the specific allegation it is meant to mitigate, makes it easy for any adjudicating authority to acknowledge the principle while still imposing close to the full penalty. A stronger approach would have built a separate, specific submission for each of the four allegations — addressing, for each one, whether there was any disproportionate gain to the entity, whether investors suffered quantifiable financial loss as distinct from inconvenience, whether the conduct was isolated or repeated, and the specific corrective step taken for that particular allegation. Tied to precedent in that structured way, the citations would have supported an actual proposed figure for each allegation, rather than floating as general arguments disconnected from this case's specific facts.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">The Decision on Appeal</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The order leaves Abans with the option to appeal to the Securities Appellate Tribunal under Section 15T of the SEBI Act. Whether that option should be exercised deserves a genuine, unemotional assessment rather than an automatic decision in either direction.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Against the appeal: ₹8 lakh is not a large sum relative to the cost, time, and visibility of a contested SAT proceeding, and Abans Financial Services is still relatively early in its operating history under its current corporate form. A public, contested appeal over a comparatively modest penalty could do more damage to its relationship with IFSCA than the penalty itself, particularly if the entity intends to seek further authorisations or launch additional schemes in GIFT City.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>In favour of a narrow appeal: the order's treatment of the independent valuer requirement, where IFSCA gave the entity the benefit of the doubt because the wording of the relevant regulation genuinely changed from \"may\" to \"shall\" between the 2022 and 2025 versions, suggests that arguments rooted in precise textual changes between regulatory regimes do carry real weight with this authority. If there is a similarly strong, narrow point of law buried elsewhere in the order, it would be worth pursuing specifically and on its own terms — not as a challenge to the entire order, but as a targeted point where the regulations-in-transition argument has genuine legal substance.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>On balance, my recommendation in a matter like this would usually be to pay the penalty within the prescribed window and direct the entity's energy toward the compliance directions issued alongside it, because that is where the regulator's attention will be focused at the next inspection. An appeal would only be worth pursuing if a specific point, on closer review, genuinely stands on its own legal merits independent of the other three allegations.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Conclusion</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Across all four allegations in this matter, the same pattern repeats. Where the entity's submissions offered specific, document-backed detail — as with the textual change in the valuer requirement — the regulator engaged with the argument and, in that instance, gave partial benefit of the doubt. Where the submissions relied on general characterisation — calling something technical, venial, or inadvertent without the evidence to support it — the argument did not hold, because the underlying facts, once examined closely, told a different story.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>That is the central lesson this matter offers, not as a general principle for any FME facing any notice, but as a specific observation about how this particular file was run. A stronger defence would have closed the gaps in the sponsor contribution timeline, replaced the legal argument on internal controls with the actual document requested, abandoned the technical-and-venial framing on disclosure delays in favour of an honest account paired with a credible fix, and built the penalty submission around the specific facts of each allegation rather than a general list of precedents. None of this would have changed the underlying facts. It would, however, have given the adjudicating authority considerably more to work with in moderating both the finding and the eventual penalty.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>About Me</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Prashant Kumar</strong> is a Company Secretary, Published Author, and seasoned professional in corporate and financial services regulation. He currently serves as Company Secretary and Compliance Officer at <strong>Global Horizons Capital Advisors (IFSC) Private Limited</strong>, an IFSCA-licensed Investment Banker based in GIFT City, giving him direct, on-ground exposure to capital market transactions and regulatory structuring within the IFSC ecosystem.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>He brings hands-on experience across&nbsp;<strong>GIFT IFSC fund structuring — including FME registration across the Authorised, Non-Retail and Retail tiers and scheme setup under the AIF IFSCA-licensed entity in GIFT City gives him working familiarity with the practical decisions GPs and platforms actually face:&nbsp;<strong>selecting the right scheme vehicle, sizing FME net worth and           "title": "IFSCA Managing General Agents (MGA) Regulations, 2026: India's New Delegated Underwriting Framework at GIFT City — Explained",
          "link": "https://csatwork.in/ifsca-managing-general-agents-mga-regulations-2026-gift-city/",
          "pubDate": "Sat, 20 Jun 2026 08:07:48 +0000",
          "dc:creator": "prashantmishra1986",
          "guid": {
            "#text": "https://csatwork.in/?p=32120",
            "@attributes": {
              "isPermaLink": "false"
