          "content:encoded": "<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>By Rachna Kumar</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>A product team usually asks this question at the worst possible moment—after the technology is locked, the launch date is announced, and commercial conversations have begun.&nbsp;<em>Is an FTO search actually mandatory, or is it just a “best practice” lawyers keep recommending?</em>&nbsp;The uncomfortable truth is that while no statute in India, the United States, or Europe explicitly mandates an FTO search, the legal systems in all three jurisdictions make it dangerously expensive to skip one once commercial risk becomes foreseeable. At that point, an FTO is no longer a checkbox exercise; it becomes a core part of launch risk management.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">What does “legally mandatory” really mean for an FTO search?</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>In patent law, “mandatory” rarely appears as a statutory command. Instead, the obligation arises indirectly through strict liability for infringement. If a product falls within the scope of a granted patent, liability follows regardless of intent, knowledge, or good faith. Courts, regulators, investors, and acquirers therefore assess whether a company behaved reasonably before launch. When a business knowingly enters a patent-dense space without assessing third-party rights, that omission itself becomes evidence of recklessness. This is where an FTO search crosses the line from optional to unavoidable.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Many businesses still misunderstand what a Freedom to Operate assessment actually covers. An FTO search is not about whether your idea is new or patentable; it is about whether your product can be made, used, or sold without infringing existing patents in a specific jurisdiction. We have explained this distinction in detail in <strong><a href=\"https://csatwork.in/freedom-to-operate-fto-search-product-launch-india/\">What Is a Freedom to Operate (FTO) Search and Why Every Product Launch in 2026 Needs One?</a></strong>, particularly in the context of Indian startups scaling into global markets.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">When is an FTO search effectively mandatory before product launch?</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>An FTO search becomes legally unavoidable when a product is commercially launched in a market where relevant patents exist and infringement risk is reasonably foreseeable. Although not mandated by statute in India, the US, or the EU, failure to conduct an FTO can lead to injunctions, enhanced damages, import bans, and serious investor or acquirer red flags.</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">India: when courts and commercial reality force the issue</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Under the Indian Patents Act, patent infringement is a strict liability offence. Whether the infringer intended to copy or even knew about the patent is irrelevant. Indian courts, particularly in pharmaceuticals, medical devices, electronics, and telecom, have shown increasing willingness to grant interim injunctions that halt sales at an early stage of litigation. From a practical standpoint, an FTO search becomes unavoidable in India once a product moves from internal development to commercial launch, especially where multinational competitors hold active Indian patents or where regulatory approvals are being pursued. In such cases, launching without any freedom-to-operate assessment exposes the business to immediate injunction risk and weakens its defensive position before the court.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">United States: enhanced damages turn FTO into a shield</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The United States takes the same strict liability approach to infringement, but the real danger lies in enhanced damages for wilful infringement. Courts examine whether the accused infringer took reasonable steps to assess patent risk before launch. When a company is operating in a known patent-crowded field and makes no effort to investigate existing rights, plaintiffs routinely argue reckless disregard. In US-facing products, an FTO search is therefore not just about avoiding infringement; it is about demonstrating good-faith conduct. For companies planning imports, US sales, fundraising, or acquisition exits, skipping an FTO removes one of the strongest legal shields available during litigation.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">European Union: injunction risk makes FTO unavoidable</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>In Europe, particularly in jurisdictions such as Germany, patent enforcement is fast and injunction-friendly. A single national patent or European patent can shut down an entire product line with little warning. The emergence of the Unified Patent Court has further increased enforcement leverage for patentees. For businesses selling across multiple EU countries or operating in sectors like medtech, industrial equipment, automotive, or telecom, an FTO search becomes unavoidable before launch. Even where damages may be manageable, the threat of a market-wide injunction forces companies to treat FTO as a launch prerequisite rather than a legal luxury.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Why filing your own patent does not replace an FTO search</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>One of the most persistent misconceptions is that filing a patent application automatically provides freedom to operate. It does not. A patent only grants the right to exclude others from using your invention; it does not grant permission to use earlier or broader patented technologies. Courts regularly restrain patentees who infringe third-party rights. This is why patentability searches and FTO searches serve fundamentally different legal purposes and must never be conflated during product strategy planning.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>A common and costly mistake is assuming that filing a patent application automatically provides freedom to operate. It does not. Patentability searches and FTO searches answer entirely different legal questions. A patentability search asks whether <em>you</em> can obtain patent rights, while an FTO search asks whether <em>you might infringe someone else’s granted rights</em>. We break this down with practical examples in <strong><a href=\"https://csatwork.in/fto-vs-patentability-search/\">FTO vs Patentability Search: What’s the Difference and When Do You Need Each?</a></strong>—a distinction that courts, investors, and acquirers take very seriously.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:image {\"id\":31842,\"sizeSlug\":\"large\",\"linkDestination\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image size-large\"><img src=\"https://csatwork.in/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/fto-search-patent-risk-quote-product-launch-1024x576.png\" alt=\"Quote on why an FTO search matters before product launch and patent infringement risk\" class=\"wp-image-31842\" /></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Regulatory approvals do not eliminate patent risk</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Another common assumption is that regulatory clearance implies patent safety. In reality, regulators assess safety, efficacy, and compliance—not patent infringement. In pharmaceuticals and medical devices, infringement suits frequently follow regulatory approval within weeks. Courts have consistently rejected the argument that regulatory permission offers immunity from patent enforcement. For regulated products, the absence of an FTO can be particularly damaging because competitors are closely monitoring market entry.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">The investor and acquisition lens</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Even where litigation risk appears remote, the absence of an FTO analysis often surfaces during investor or M&amp;A due diligence. Sophisticated investors view FTO as a risk-allocation tool. When no FTO exists, transactions are delayed, valuations are discounted, or indemnity escrows are imposed. At that stage, conducting an FTO becomes a defensive exercise rather than a strategic one, often under time pressure and scrutiny.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Practical guidance from real launch scenarios</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>In practice, the question is rarely whether an FTO is legally mandatory in theory. The real question is whether a business can credibly justify launching without one. Once revenue, competitors, exports, or institutional capital are involved, that justification becomes extremely difficult. A jurisdiction-specific, product-aligned FTO search almost always costs less than a single injunction hearing and provides clarity that directly informs design-around, licensing, or market-entry decisions.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The law does not compel good behaviour through explicit commands. It does so through consequences. An FTO search sits squarely in that space—technically optional, practically decisive. Businesses that understand this early do not merely avoid disputes; they build products that can survive scale, scrutiny, and serious capital.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Once a business recognises that an FTO search is unavoidable, the next question is how deep the analysis needs to go. In practice, this depends on the product architecture, jurisdictions of launch, and the enforcement behaviour of competitors. A well-structured FTO typically involves claim-level analysis, jurisdiction filtering, and risk categorisation—rather than a raw patent dump. For readers looking to understand this process in detail, we have outlined a jurisdiction-specific framework in <strong><a href=\"https://csatwork.in/how-to-conduct-fto-analysis/\">How to Conduct a Freedom to Operate Analysis: A Step-by-Step Guide (India, US, EU)</a></strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\" />\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>About the Author</strong><br>Rachna Kumar is a registered Patent Attorney with deep expertise in patent drafting, prosecution, and innovation strategy across India, the United States, and key global markets. She advises technology-driven businesses, startups, and R&amp;D teams on protecting high-value inventions through strong patents, clarity in prior art positioning, and commercially aligned filing strategies. Her work spans electronics, software, AI, biotechnology, and emerging technologies, with a focus on building patent portfolios that support scale, investment, and long-term competitive advantage.<br>Rachna frequently works with founders and in-house teams to navigate the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT), national phase entry, office actions, and infringement risk assessments, ensuring clients make informed decisions across the innovation lifecycle.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->",

While no patent law explicitly requires it, businesses launching in India, the US, or Europe often face injunctions, damages, and investor scrutiny when infringement risk is foreseeable.           "title": "What Happens If You Skip an FTO Search? Real IP Risk Scenarios for Businesses",
          "link": "https://csatwork.in/skip-fto-search-ip-risk-scenarios/",
          "pubDate": "Thu, 25 Dec 2025 05:53:08 +0000",
          "dc:creator": "rachnakumar",
          "guid": {
            "#text": "https://csatwork.in/?p=31845",
            "@attributes": {
              "isPermaLink": "false"
            }
          },
          "description": null,
          "content:encoded": "<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>(Injunctions, customs seizures, investor red flags)</em></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>By Rachna Kumar</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Most businesses that skip a Freedom to Operate (FTO) search do not do so out of negligence. They do it out of optimism. The product works, the market is ready, and timelines feel unforgiving. Legal risk, by contrast, feels abstract—until it isn’t. In real-world practice, the consequences of skipping an FTO search rarely arrive as polite legal notices. They arrive as injunctions that halt sales overnight, customs authorities blocking shipments, or investors quietly walking away during diligence. This article looks at what&nbsp;<em>actually</em>&nbsp;happens when businesses launch without understanding third-party patent rights, and why the damage is often commercial long before it becomes legal.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">What really happens if you skip an FTO search before launch?</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Skipping an FTO search exposes businesses to immediate injunctions, blocked imports, seizure of goods, enhanced damages, and serious investor or acquirer concerns. Because patent infringement is strict liability, companies can be stopped from selling even without intent or knowledge, making the absence of an FTO a material commercial and legal risk.</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Injunctions: the fastest way a product launch can collapse</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>In patent litigation, injunctions are the most disruptive remedy. Courts are not required to wait for a full trial before restraining sales. If a patent holder demonstrates a prima facie case and potential irreparable harm, products can be pulled from the market within weeks—or even days. This is particularly common in pharmaceuticals, medical devices, electronics, and industrial products where the technology space is dense and enforcement is aggressive.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Businesses often underestimate how quickly this happens. Marketing spend, distributor commitments, and customer contracts offer no protection once an injunction is granted. In India and Europe especially, courts have shown little sympathy for defendants who launched without assessing known patent landscapes. The absence of an FTO search weakens credibility at the very first hearing, when interim relief is decided.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>These consequences are not theoretical. In fact, across India, the United States, and Europe, courts and commercial stakeholders increasingly treat the absence of a Freedom to Operate assessment as a failure of basic risk management. This is why, in many real-world launch scenarios, an FTO search becomes unavoidable even though no statute explicitly mandates it. We have examined this legal threshold in detail in <strong><a href=\"https://csatwork.in/fto-search-legally-mandatory-before-product-launch/\">When Is an FTO Search Legally Mandatory Before Product Launch? (India, US, EU)</a></strong>, particularly from the perspective of injunction risk, enhanced damages, and investor expectations.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Customs seizures and import blocks: the silent killer of export models</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For companies relying on exports, skipping an FTO search creates a risk that does not even begin in court. Many jurisdictions allow patent holders to record their rights with customs authorities. Once recorded, shipments suspected of infringing can be detained, inspected, and blocked at the border.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This scenario is devastating because it often unfolds without warning. Goods are manufactured, shipped, and then frozen at ports or airports. Storage costs escalate, customer delivery timelines collapse, and distributors lose confidence. In the US and EU, customs-level enforcement has become a preferred strategy for patentees precisely because it disrupts supply chains without the delays of full litigation. An FTO search would have flagged these risks at the design or market-entry stage—when alternatives were still viable.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:image {\"id\":31847} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image\"><img src=\"https://csatwork.in/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/skip-fto-search-patent-risk-quote.png\" alt=\"Quote explaining patent risk when businesses skip a freedom to operate search\" class=\"wp-image-31847\" /><figcaption class=\"wp-element-caption\">A reminder that patent infringement risk often surfaces only after products gain commercial traction.</figcaption></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Damages and wilful infringement: when cost multiplies</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Patent infringement does not require intent, but the absence of reasonable precautions can significantly worsen financial exposure. In the United States, courts can award enhanced damages where infringement is found to be wilful. Plaintiffs routinely argue that launching without an FTO search in a known patent-crowded field amounts to reckless disregard.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Even where enhanced damages are not awarded, litigation costs themselves can dwarf the cost of preventive analysis. Discovery, expert testimony, and claim construction battles drain management time and capital. At that point, the question is no longer whether the product infringes, but whether the business can afford to keep defending it.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Investor and acquirer red flags: the quiet consequences</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Not all damage is public. In many cases, the most serious consequence of skipping an FTO search emerges during fundraising or acquisition discussions. Sophisticated investors and acquirers routinely examine freedom-to-operate risk as part of legal diligence. When no FTO analysis exists, concerns arise immediately: undisclosed liabilities, uncertain market access, and future injunction exposure.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The result is rarely a dramatic rejection. More often, it appears as valuation haircuts, expanded indemnities, escrow requirements, or prolonged diligence cycles. In competitive deals, this alone can push a company out of contention. An FTO search, even if it identifies manageable risks, demonstrates maturity and foresight. Its absence signals the opposite.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">“We have our own patent” is not a defence</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>A particularly costly misconception is that owning or filing a patent shields a business from infringement claims. It does not. A patent grants the right to exclude others, not the right to operate freely. Courts across jurisdictions have repeatedly restrained patentees whose products infringe earlier or broader third-party claims.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This confusion is why it is critical to distinguish between&nbsp;<strong>patentability searches</strong>&nbsp;and&nbsp;<strong>freedom-to-operate analysis</strong>. Patentability assesses whether your invention is new. FTO assesses whether your product infringes someone else’s granted rights. Treating one as a substitute for the other is one of the most common—and expensive—errors businesses make.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Regulatory approval does not neutralise patent risk</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Another assumption that often collapses under pressure is that regulatory clearance somehow implies patent safety. Regulators examine safety, efficacy, and compliance. They do not adjudicate patent rights. In regulated industries, infringement actions frequently follow approvals because market entry is now commercially meaningful. Courts have consistently rejected the argument that regulatory permission offers immunity from patent enforcement.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Why FTO problems surface too late</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The irony of most FTO-related disputes is timing. By the time infringement risk becomes visible, design decisions are locked, supply chains are active, and commercial commitments are in place. At that stage, even a clear infringement finding leaves limited options: expensive licensing, rushed design-arounds, or market withdrawal. An FTO search conducted earlier would have shifted these decisions upstream, where they were cheaper and strategically manageable.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>As discussed in <strong><a href=\"https://csatwork.in/freedom-to-operate-fto-search-product-launch-india/\" data-type=\"link\" data-id=\"https://csatwork.in/freedom-to-operate-fto-search-product-launch-india/\">What Is a Freedom to Operate (FTO) Search and Why Every Product Launch in 2026 Needs One?</a></strong>, the true value of FTO lies in <em>when</em> it is done, not merely <em>whether</em> it is done. The same logic underpins the distinction explained in <strong><a href=\"https://csatwork.in/fto-vs-patentability-search/\" data-type=\"link\" data-id=\"https://csatwork.in/fto-vs-patentability-search/\">FTO vs Patentability Search: What’s the Difference and When Do You Need Each?</a></strong>, a distinction that courts and investors increasingly expect businesses to understand.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">From risk to process: what businesses should do instead</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Once a company recognises these risks, the conversation naturally shifts from consequences to execution. An effective FTO is not a bulk patent list or a superficial clearance note. It is a structured, claim-level analysis focused on specific product features, jurisdictions of launch, and enforcement behaviour of competitors. This is why we have outlined a practical, jurisdiction-specific methodology in <strong><a href=\"https://csatwork.in/how-to-conduct-fto-analysis/\" data-type=\"link\" data-id=\"https://csatwork.in/how-to-conduct-fto-analysis/\">How to Conduct a Freedom to Operate Analysis: A Step-by-Step Guide (India, US, EU)</a></strong>, which many teams use as a reference point before market entry.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">The commercial reality</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Skipping an FTO search does not make patent risk disappear. It merely defers it—often to the worst possible moment. Injunctions, customs blocks, investor concerns, and litigation costs are not theoretical outcomes; they are routine consequences seen across industries and jurisdictions.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The law rarely penalises optimism. It penalises unexamined risk. Businesses that treat freedom to operate as a strategic input, rather than a legal afterthought, do not just avoid disputes. They build products that can withstand scale, scrutiny, and serious capital.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\" />\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">FAQs – What Happens If You Skip an FTO Search?</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\"><strong>1. Can a business really be stopped from selling if it skips an FTO search?</strong></h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Yes. Courts can grant interim injunctions that immediately restrain the sale, manufacture, or import of a product if patent infringement is shown at a prima facie level. Because infringement is strict liability, a business can be stopped even if it acted in good faith or was unaware of the patent. Skipping an FTO weakens credibility at the injunction stage.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\" />\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\"><strong>2. Does skipping an FTO search increase the risk of customs seizures or import bans?</strong></h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Absolutely. In the US and EU, patent owners can record their rights with customs authorities. If an exported product is suspected of infringing a recorded patent, shipments may be detained or blocked at ports. This often happens without prior notice and can severely disrupt supply chains, customer commitments, and distributor relationships.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\" />\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\"><strong>3. Can investors or acquirers really walk away because there is no FTO search?</strong></h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Yes. Sophisticated investors and acquirers treat freedom-to-operate risk as a material diligence issue. The absence of an FTO raises concerns about hidden liabilities, injunction exposure, and uncertain market access. This commonly results in valuation haircuts, indemnity demands, escrow requirements, or deal delays—even if no litigation has yet occurred.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\" />\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\"><strong>4. Does owning or filing a patent protect a company if it skipped an FTO search?</strong></h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>No. Owning or filing a patent does not provide freedom to operate. A patent grants the right to exclude others, not the right to use earlier or broader patented technologies. Courts routinely restrain patentees whose products infringe third-party patents. This is why patentability searches and FTO searches serve fundamentally different legal purposes.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\" />\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\"><strong>5. Is skipping an FTO search ever acceptable for early-stage or startup businesses?</strong></h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Only at very early prototype or internal testing stages. Once a product is commercially launched, exported, licensed, or presented to institutional investors, skipping an FTO becomes a serious legal and commercial risk. At that stage, the cost of an FTO is typically negligible compared to the cost of injunctions, litigation, or failed funding rounds.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>About the Author</strong><br>Rachna Kumar is a registered Patent Attorney with deep expertise in patent drafting, prosecution, and innovation strategy across India, the United States, and key global markets. She is part of the&nbsp;<strong>Patent Division at Eclectic Legal</strong>, where she advises technology-driven businesses, startups, and R&amp;D teams on protecting high-value inventions through strong patents, clarity in prior art positioning, and commercially aligned filing strategies.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Her work spans electronics, software, AI, biotechnology, and emerging technologies, with a focus on building patent portfolios that support scale, investment, and long-term competitive advantage. Rachna regularly works with founders and in-house teams to navigate the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT), national phase entry, office actions, and infringement risk assessments, ensuring informed decisions across the innovation lifecycle.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For discussions on patent strategy, freedom to operate, or global filing approaches, <strong>Eclectic Legal can be reached at <a>apsingh@eclecticlegal.com</a></strong>.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->",

          "content:encoded": "<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Art has always been a reflection of society, a medium through which emotions, ideas, and values are communicated. In modern culture, art’s impact is subtle yet profound, influencing thoughts, behaviors, and social trends in ways that are often overlooked. Its quiet power lies not in loud statements or grand spectacles but in the way it shapes perception, inspires reflection, and connects communities across diverse backgrounds.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">1. Art as a Mirror of Society</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Art serves as a mirror, reflecting societal values, struggles, and achievements. Contemporary artists often tackle issues such as identity, inequality, and environmental concerns, encouraging viewers to engage critically.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Ways art mirrors society:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Visual storytelling through paintings, murals, and installations.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Photography capturing moments that define cultural and social movements.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Digital and multimedia art that addresses current global topics.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>By reflecting society, art fosters awareness and conversation, making it a subtle but influential force.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">2. Emotional Impact and Personal Reflection</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>One of art’s most significant contributions is its ability to evoke emotion. Art invites personal interpretation, creating intimate experiences that resonate with viewers on an individual level.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>How art affects emotions:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Colors and textures evoke specific moods or memories.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Abstract forms stimulate imagination and curiosity.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Narrative-driven works encourage empathy and introspection.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Through these emotional connections, art quietly shapes how we understand ourselves and others.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">3. Art in Public Spaces</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Modern culture increasingly integrates art into public environments, making it accessible to everyone. Public art enriches communities by creating shared experiences and cultural touchpoints.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Examples of public art’s influence:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Street murals that beautify neighborhoods and communicate social messages.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Sculptures and installations in parks, plazas, and city streets.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Interactive art experiences that engage audiences in participation.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Public art encourages interaction, dialogue, and community pride, demonstrating art’s power beyond galleries.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">4. Art and Technology</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Technology has expanded art’s reach and influence, allowing it to permeate everyday life in unprecedented ways.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Technological impacts on art:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Digital platforms allow artists to share work globally.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Virtual and augmented reality create immersive artistic experiences.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Social media fosters direct engagement between artists and audiences.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Online marketplaces enable access to art for new collectors and enthusiasts.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>By blending creativity with technology, art quietly shapes modern culture and broadens its accessibility.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">5. Art as a Tool for Education</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Art plays a critical role in education, fostering creativity, critical thinking, and empathy. Exposure to art at an early age develops cognitive and emotional intelligence, shaping how individuals interact with the world.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Educational benefits of art:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Enhances visual literacy and observation skills.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Encourages problem-solving through creative expression.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Builds emotional awareness and communication abilities.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Provides historical and cultural context through artistic interpretation.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Art in education ensures that future generations understand its subtle yet transformative power.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">6. Art and Personal Spaces</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Art’s quiet power is also visible in homes, workplaces, and personal spaces. Thoughtfully placed art can inspire, calm, and energize daily life.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Ways to use art in personal spaces:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Choose pieces that reflect personality and values.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Rotate artworks periodically for fresh perspectives.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Use art to define the mood or style of a room.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Combine visual and tactile elements to create sensory experiences.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Incorporating art into everyday life reinforces its influence beyond formal exhibitions.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">7. The Social and Cultural Dialogue</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Art encourages dialogue across cultures, generations, and perspectives. Its subtle influence lies in the conversations it sparks and the shared understanding it fosters.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>How art promotes dialogue:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Exhibitions and galleries as spaces for discussion and exchange.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Collaborative projects that bring together artists and communities.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Digital platforms that allow commentary, critique, and engagement.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Through dialogue, art nurtures empathy, connection, and cultural awareness in modern society.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->",

          "content:encoded": "<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>A contemporary artist’s studio is more than a workspace; it’s a sanctuary where imagination comes alive. Every object, tool, and corner reflects the artist’s creative journey. From the light streaming through windows to the scattered brushes and unfinished pieces, the studio embodies both discipline and experimentation. A typical day in the life of a contemporary artist blends routine, exploration, and reflection.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Morning Routine: Preparing for Creation</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The day often begins early, taking advantage of natural light that highlights textures, colors, and details. Morning routines help the artist focus and set a productive tone.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Common morning habits include:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Sketching:</strong> Quick, informal sketches to warm up the hand and mind.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Journaling:</strong> Recording ideas, inspiration, or reflections from previous work.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Material experimentation:</strong> Testing new colors, textures, or mediums.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Studio setup:</strong> Organizing brushes, paints, and tools for smooth workflow.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>These practices help center the mind, preparing the artist to engage fully with the creative process.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Immersion in Work: The Flow State</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Once the studio is ready, the artist dives into their main project. This phase often brings a state of <strong>flow</strong>, where time passes unnoticed, and every action is guided by intuition.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>During this stage, artists focus on:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Experimenting with techniques, colors, and textures.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Layering materials to achieve unique effects.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Embracing mistakes as part of the creative journey.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Moving seamlessly between painting, sculpting, and digital work.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The environment supports this flow through flexible workstations, proper lighting, and inspiring surroundings.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Midday Breaks: Refreshing Creativity</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Even immersed artists need to pause. Breaks prevent fatigue and allow ideas to incubate subconsciously.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Break activities often include:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Eating a light meal while reviewing sketches or notes.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Taking short walks to gain perspective and observe surroundings.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Performing simple studio tasks like cleaning tools or organizing materials.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>These pauses often spark new insights or lead to creative breakthroughs.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Afternoon Focus: Refinement and Documentation</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Afternoons are dedicated to refining work and documenting progress.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Key afternoon activities:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Adding details and adjusting composition for visual harmony.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Photographing pieces for portfolios, galleries, or social media.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Preparing works for exhibitions or client presentation.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Artists balance creation with documentation, connecting the studio experience to a wider audience.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Evening Reflection: Assessing the Day</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Evening is reserved for reflection, planning, and relaxation.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Typical practices include:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Reviewing sketches, notes, and works-in-progress.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Planning future projects or experiments.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Engaging in peer feedback or collaborative critique.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Relaxing through music, reading, or quiet observation.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>This phase reinforces learning, growth, and creative clarity.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Tools and Environment</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>A contemporary artist’s tools and surroundings are crucial for productivity and inspiration.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Common elements include:</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Brushes, paints, canvases, clay, and sculpting tools.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Digital tablets, computers, and design software.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Mood boards, found objects, and inspirational reference materials.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Studio lighting, furniture placement, and ambient sounds that enhance focus.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The studio is both functional and inspirational, reflecting the artist’s identity and style.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Key Takeaways</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:list {\"ordered\":true} -->\n<ol class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Creativity thrives with structure: A morning routine and organized studio support focused work.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Flow is essential: Deep immersion enables experimentation and innovation.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Pauses are productive: Breaks allow ideas to incubate and prevent burnout.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Reflection sustains growth: Reviewing and planning informs future creativity.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Environment matters: Lighting, layout, and materials shape inspiration.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>\n<!--           "title": "When the Fund Manager Is the Fraud Victim — And Still the Noticee: Lessons from IFSCA's Interim Order in the We Founder Circle Matter",
          "link": "https://csatwork.in/ifsca-we-founder-circle-fme-cyber-fraud-order/",
          "pubDate": "Wed, 15 Jul 2026 15:28:41 +0000",
          "dc:creator": "prashantmishra1986",
          "guid": {
            "#text": "https://csatwork.in/?p=32250",
            "@attributes": {
              "isPermaLink": "false"
            }
          },
          "description": null,
          "content:encoded": "<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>On 13 July 2026, IFSCA's Quasi-Judicial Authority for Enforcement (QJAE) passed an ex-parte ad-interim order against We Founder Circle Angel Accelerator LLP (IFSC Branch), a registered FME managing a CAT I Angel Scheme at GIFT IFSC.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Here's what makes this order worth every fund manager's attention:&nbsp;<strong>the FME was itself the victim of a cyber fraud.</strong>&nbsp;No allegation of misappropriation. No suggestion of diversion by insiders. And yet, the regulator directed it to deposit USD 100,000 in an earmarked account and barred it from launching any new scheme.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>That is the headline lesson — and it deserves unpacking.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">What Happened</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>In April 2026, the FME pooled USD 100,000 (approx. ₹94 lakh) from 17 investors for a proposed SAFE investment in a US startup, BentoLabs AI, Inc. On 30 April 2026, the amount was remitted through banking channels.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>It was then discovered that fraudsters had infiltrated the email communication chain between transaction participants using impersonation email IDs, and circulated manipulated bank account details. The funds landed in an unintended beneficiary account with Bank of America — held in the name of an entity conveniently styled \"Sherrygold LLC DBA BentoLabs AI Inc.\"</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>A classic Business Email Compromise (BEC). The FME's own systems, per its submission, were not compromised.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>To its credit, the FME moved quickly on paper:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Notified remitting and intermediary banks and initiated SWIFT recall (4 May 2026)</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Filed an IC3 complaint in the US, an FTC fraud report (shared with the FBI), and a cybercrime complaint in India (4–5 May 2026)</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Self-reported the incident to IFSCA on 9 May 2026</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Where It Went Wrong with the Regulator</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The order's factual narrative is a case study in how&nbsp;<em>not</em>&nbsp;to manage post-incident regulatory engagement:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>May–June 2026:</strong>&nbsp;IFSCA sought facts, held in-person meetings with the Principal Officer and Financial Controller, and received investor complaints — including a collective complaint on 16 June 2026.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>10 June 2026:</strong>&nbsp;IFSCA asked for a resolution plan with timelines within one week.&nbsp;<strong>No response was furnished.</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>17 June 2026:</strong>&nbsp;The Principal Officer was summoned. IFSCA directed a concrete plan —&nbsp;<em>either allot units or refund the investors</em>&nbsp;— by end of that week. The FME asked for 15 days.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>30 June – 10 July 2026:</strong>&nbsp;The FME sought \"one to two months,\" then time till 8 July, then reported that detailed discussions had been completed with only&nbsp;<strong>4 of 17 investors</strong>, and asked investors themselves for another 2–3 months.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>More than two months after the incident: no units allotted, no refunds made, no definitive plan. That timeline — not the fraud itself — is what triggered the interim order.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">The Legal Hook: Regulation 118 and the Code of Conduct</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>QJAE anchored its prima facie findings in&nbsp;<strong>Regulation 118 of the IFSCA (Fund Management) Regulations, 2025</strong>&nbsp;read with Part A of the Third Schedule — the Code of Conduct. The specific clauses invoked are telling:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Clause (b):</strong> The FME is responsible for acts of commission <em>or omission</em> by its employees and service providers</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Clause (c):</strong> No contract or termination absolves the FME, its partners or officers of liability to the scheme or investors</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Clause (h):</strong> Investors must receive adequate, accurate and timely information about the scheme's affairs</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Clause (k):</strong> High standards of integrity and fairness in all dealings</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Clause (l):</strong> High standards of service, due diligence, proper care and independent professional judgment</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The finding is blunt: pooled investor money was required to be invested in BentoLabs AI per the term sheet; it went to a third-party account instead; and despite two months of \"recovery efforts,\" investors had neither units nor refunds. Prima facie, that is a failure of due diligence and of fiduciary obligations —&nbsp;<strong>irrespective of who perpetrated the fraud</strong>.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">The Directions</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Exercising powers under Sections 12, 13(1) and 13(4) of the IFSCA Act, 2019 read with Sections 11(1), 11(4) and 11B(1) of the SEBI Act, 1992 (delegated to QJAE under Section 23), the order directs:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:list {\"ordered\":true} -->\n<ol class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Deposit USD 100,000</strong> in the FME's GIFT-IFSC bank account within 60 days, separately earmarked, not to be withdrawn without prior IFSCA permission</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>The IFSC Banking Unit</strong> must ensure no withdrawal without proof of IFSCA approval</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Freeze on new schemes</strong> in GIFT-IFSC until the deposit is made</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The FME has 21 days to file objections and seek a personal hearing.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Seven Learnings for FMEs at GIFT IFSC</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>1. Victimhood is not a defence to fiduciary failure.</strong>&nbsp;The Code of Conduct doesn't ask whether you intended the loss. It asks whether you exercised due diligence and protected investor money. A BEC that succeeds because bank account details were accepted over email is, in the regulator's eyes, a controls failure — yours.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>2. Payment verification controls are now a regulatory expectation, not best practice.</strong>&nbsp;Every FME making cross-border remittances should mandate out-of-band verification (callback to a pre-verified number) for beneficiary account details, prohibit acceptance of banking changes via email alone, and document the verification trail. This single SOP would have prevented this entire matter.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>3. Self-reporting buys goodwill, not immunity.</strong>&nbsp;The FME did the right thing by intimating IFSCA within days. But self-reporting is the&nbsp;<em>start</em>&nbsp;of regulatory engagement, not its conclusion. What the regulator measures thereafter is remediation velocity.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>4. Missed regulatory deadlines are accelerants.</strong>&nbsp;Read the order's Section B carefully: the inflection point was the FME's failure to respond to the 10 June email within the stipulated week. From there, every extension request compounded the impression of drift. When a regulator gives you a one-week deadline, silence is the most expensive response available.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>5. \"Issue units or refund\" is the binary the regulator works with.</strong>&nbsp;Cross-border recovery complexity, SWIFT recalls, FBI coordination — none of it suspends the investor's entitlement. If money is stuck, the FME (or its sponsors) may effectively have to make investors whole from its own resources. The deposit direction operationalises exactly that.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>6. QJAE's interim toolkit is fully operational.</strong>&nbsp;This order confirms the enforcement architecture: SEBI Act Section 11/11B powers, exercised through Section 13 of the IFSCA Act, delegated to QJAE. Ex-parte interim directions — deposit, earmarking, business restrictions — can arrive&nbsp;<em>pending investigation</em>, on prima facie findings alone. The bar is investor protection, not proof of culpability.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>7. Investor communication is a compliance obligation, not a courtesy.</strong>&nbsp;Detailed discussions with 4 of 17 investors, two months in, was cited in the order. Clause (h) of the Code of Conduct converts poor investor communication into a standalone violation. A structured, documented, all-investor communication cadence within days of an incident is now the defensible standard.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">The Bigger Picture</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>GIFT IFSC's fund management ecosystem is scaling fast, and angel schemes — with their small teams, cross-border deal flow and email-driven closings — are structurally exposed to BEC risk. This order tells every FME that cyber fraud sitting&nbsp;<em>outside</em>&nbsp;your infrastructure still lands&nbsp;<em>inside</em>&nbsp;your liability.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The practical mandate is clear: build payment verification SOPs, wire them into your operations manual, test them, and — if an incident occurs — treat regulatory timelines as sacrosanct and investor restitution as the first workstream, not the last.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Because in the regulator's framework, there is no such thing as an FME that is merely a victim. There is only an FME that either protected investor money — or didn't.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:separator -->\n<hr class=\"wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity\"/>\n<!-- /wp:separator -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><em>The order (IFSCA-AIF/98/2026) is an ex-parte ad-interim order based on prima facie findings; the Noticee has 21 days to respond and the investigation remains open.</em></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->",
          "excerpt:encoded": "IFSCA’s ex-parte ad-interim order against We Founder Circle Angel Accelerator LLP offers a critical compliance lesson for every FME at GIFT IFSC. Although the fund manager was itself a victim of a USD 100,000 cyber fraud, IFSCA directed it to earmark an equivalent amount and restricted new scheme launches. Here are seven key lessons on fiduciary responsibility, payment controls, investor communication and regulatory response.",

          "content:encoded": "<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Section 188 has been amended three times since 2013 — and each amendment quietly rewrote a rule most of us memorised in our student days. \"Special resolution\" became \"resolution.\" Imprisonment became a civil penalty. The voidability option moved.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Which version is sitting in your memory?</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>We've built a&nbsp;<strong>20-question knowledge test on Related Party Transactions under the Companies Act, 2013</strong>&nbsp;to help you find out — before an exam, a Board meeting, or a due-diligence call does it for you.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">Try These Before You Start</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Q1.</strong>&nbsp;A related party transaction crosses the Rule 15 threshold. The shareholders' approval required is by — ordinary resolution or special resolution?</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Q2.</strong>&nbsp;Mr. X is a director of ABC Ltd and also a director of PQR Ltd (a public company) in which he holds 1% along with his relatives. Is PQR Ltd a related party of ABC Ltd?</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Q3.</strong>&nbsp;A ₹80 lakh transaction is entered into without Audit Committee approval and isn't ratified within three months. Voidable at whose option — the Board, the shareholders, or the Audit Committee itself?</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>If you paused on any of these, the quiz will be twenty minutes well spent. (And yes — every one of them is a real question from the test, and at least one of the \"obvious\" answers is wrong.)</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">What the Quiz Covers</h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:list -->\n<ul class=\"wp-block-list\"><!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Who is a related party</strong>&nbsp;— the Section 2(76) limbs, including the private-vs-public company trap and the group entities added in 2017</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>The approval matrix</strong>&nbsp;— Audit Committee (Sec 177), Board resolution at a meeting (Sec 188), and shareholders' ordinary resolution above thresholds</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>The arm's-length exemption</strong>&nbsp;— what it switches off, and the four things it doesn't</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>Voidability, ratification and penalties</strong>&nbsp;— the three-month clock, the 2017 and 2020 amendments, and penalty vs punishment</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li><strong>The paper trail</strong>&nbsp;— Section 184 disclosures and the Section 189 register (MBP-4)</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading -->\n<h2 class=\"wp-block-heading\">How It Get one wrong and the scheme is defective from launch.\",\"cards\":[{\"tag\":\"CORPUS\",\"title\":\"Twenty crore a scheme\",\"law\":\"Each scheme of the Alternative Investment Fund shall have corpus of at least twenty crore rupees; each scheme of a social impact fund shall have a corpus of at least five crore rupees.\",\"means\":\"The floor attaches to each SCHEME, not to the fund as a whole. Provided further that this clause shall not apply to an accredited investor.\",\"means\":\"One crore is the general floor; twenty-five lakh for insiders; and the floor does not apply at all to an accredited investor.\",\"watch\":\"The accredited-investor carve-out disapplies the clause entirely — it is not a reduced figure.\",\"link\":\"Accreditation recurs across the regime.\"},{\"tag\":\"INVESTORS\",\"title\":\"One thousand per scheme\",\"law\":\"No scheme of the Alternative Investment Fund shall have more than one thousand investors.\",\"means\":\"A per-scheme ceiling, counted scheme by scheme.\",\"watch\":\"Where the AIF is formed as a company, the Companies Act, 2013 applies in addition.\",\"link\":\"Contrast with the angel fund concentration rule.\"},{\"tag\":\"FORM\",\"title\":\"Units in dematerialised form\",\"law\":\"The Alternative Investment Fund shall issue units in dematerialised form subject to the conditions specified by the Board from time to time.\",\"means\":\"Physical unit certificates are no longer the default position.\",\"watch\":\"Inserted by amendment — a point where older material is out of date.\",\"link\":\"See the amendment tracker.\"}],\"summary\":\"Four gates per scheme: corpus twenty crore (five crore for a social impact fund); minimum investment one crore, twenty-five lakh for employees and directors, and disapplied entirely for an accredited investor; not more than one thousand investors; and units issued in dematerialised form.\",\"tip\":\"Check the four gates scheme by scheme, not fund by fund. Regulation changes are cited to the amendment regulations; GARUDA and Inoperative Fund are cited to the Master Circular.\",\"tip\":\"Keep a living amendment register with three columns — the change, its effective date, and whether it is regulation or circular.
